Dorfromantik is a peaceful, tile-based strategy and puzzle game developed by Toukana Interactive. It offers a relaxing gameplay experience where you place hexagonal tiles to build idyllic landscapes—fields, forests, rivers, villages, and more—while trying to complete quests and achieve high scores.

Pros:

Calming, meditative gameplay with no time pressure.

Beautiful, minimalist art style and soothing music.

Simple mechanics that still allow for strategic depth.

Great for short or long play sessions.

Cons:

Dorfromantik is like Carcassonne in a simpler and more casual form, with the satisfying logic of Sudoku where every tile placement feels like solving a puzzle.

[b]What makes it great:[/b]
✔ [b]Relaxing vibe[/b] with no timers and no pressure. You can play at your own pace and simply enjoy the process.
✔ [b]Endless creativity[/b] as every map turns into a living landscape filled with forests, rivers, villages and railways.
✔ [b]Accessible but deep[/b] because it is easy to pick up yet rewarding when you chase high scores or unlock new tiles.
✔ [b]Visually rewarding[/b] since watching your small village grow into a sprawling diorama feels genuinely satisfying.
✔ [b]Perfect in short bursts[/b] but also dangerously easy to lose hours while building your world.

[b]Verdict:[/b]
Dorfromantik is not about winning but about creating. Every placement feels meaningful, every map tells its own little story and the result is a meditative puzzle that keeps pulling you back.

This game has become one of my favorite games to sit down and be challenged as well as being able to have a relaxing game at the same time. Another easy to learn game that really provides a challenge without overtaxing your brain.

   The premise is to match 6 sided pieces of varying make ups, including: water, railroad, forest, houses, grass and field, as you are giving one piece at a time to match onto the playing field. You can rotate pieces to fit them together with an already placed piece. You do have a limited amount of pieces to start a regular game but you can add back to your total by completing quests. Trying to get a high score is the goal in a classic game. 

   As you play a game another goal is to build out to a piece that is away from the main starting area, doing score gets you score and special pieces to unlock. The game has seven modes to keep you occupied with a change of pace. A tutorial is first, then classic,  creative, quick, hard, monthly and custom. The tiles can be customized to certain looks with the use of biomes, which you unlock as you play. You can choose what biomes you want to appear in a game. 

  This game is really a no rush game, you can take your time as much as you like to find the best location to place pieces. You really have to way the pros and cons of piece placing as getting perfect placements can get you big scores but you have to continuously complete goals/quests done to keep getting more tiles. 

   A great addition to the game is the awesome music, you kind of lose yourself in it as you play. Very original, and enough tracks to not get bored of any of them. I now have to talk about the art style, it's AWESOME! It fits this game perfectly and is conducive relaxation. I just love the little animations that begin with some of the tiles when you place them.

    This game is highly recommended if you love strategy/puzzle games that let you work your brain while also relax. You will be spending many hours blissfully gaming with Dorfromantik.

Dorfromantik. On the surface a simple, tile based puzzle game. But hidden behind it's cute, cardboardy art style is a menacing demon of complexity. If you enjoy puzzles, this game will tickle your brain in the best and worst ways. With an extensive selection of randomized tiles, you will soon find yourself entrenched in creating tiny villages, giant forests, winding rivers and interconnected systems of railroads. The amount of discoverable "secret" tiles that you can unlock through in-game quests are astounding, and make for an incredibly compelling experience. If you enjoy brain teasers I would throughly recommend picking this up.

[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is a wonderful city builder game that aims to provide the most calming and relaxing experience possible by keeping the gameplay minimalistic yet extremely addictive. Since [i]ISLANDERS[/i] was released in April 2019, several other games using more or less the same mechanics appeared on Steam, but none of them managed to capture its inner brilliance. After having experienced [i]Dorfromantik[/i] fully, I strongly feel that it has the potential to be a worthy competitor, if not even better than [i]ISLANDERS[/i] in some ways.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2435045617
The core ideas of the two games are the same: you begin with an empty environment that contains an already set default tile, then you build up your landscape by placing down title by tile, expanding in all directions and gaining points by arranging them in an optimal way. While [i]ISLANDERS[/i] offers a choice between two packs of buildings belonging to the same type as long as you don’t have enough tiles, in [i]Dorfromantik[/i] you are by default given a stack of random tiles, with only the topmost one always being usable. The gameplay is thus simplified a lot, and the decision making shifts towards determining what the optimal spot for placing this tile is, based on the existing configuration.

The tiles are randomly generated mixes of five different elements (houses, fields, trees, water, railroad), featured in various shapes and amounts, but most of the times it's a combination of 2-3 different elements, with the water and railroad bits being more difficult to handle than the rest. Some of these tiles give you a quest when they're placed on the map, requiring you to connect a certain amount of tiles to them.

The core gameplay basically consists in [i]domino[/i]-ing these in such a way that they form separate areas, in preparation for upcoming quests which are essential for game progress. Completing quests is what gives you survivability (they add new tiles to the stack) and increase the score, together with placing tiles in optimal spots for bonus points. Just like in [i]ISLANDERS[/i], you might want to group related tiles together even outside quests, building up those points in preparation for the moment when you receive a quest tile that you can place down nearby for instant or almost-instant completion. However, one crucial difference between these two games is that the placement of building in [i]ISLANDERS[/i] is done based on the radius of the master building, while in [i]Dorfromantik[/i] the tiles can be chained together over any range, as long as the elements keep the connection among two adjacent tiles. In [i]ISLANDERS[/i], gathering points is done through pixel-perfect placement and cramming together the maximum amount of buildings of the same type, both horizontally and vertically, while in [i]Dorfromantik[/i] the hexagonal grid expands only in 2D, allowing only a strict placement but the points can be collected from any amount of linked tiles.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2435045591
There are two types of quests: those that require you to have a minimum amount of elements in the connected tiles, and those that ask for an “exact” number. While the ones from the first category are pretty easy to complete initially, those that appear mid-game towards the end game have considerably increased requirements. For example, the first quests are connecting 10-30 trees - easily doable with only a couple of tiles, while later this value scales towards several hundreds, requiring you to already have connected several tiles with the same elements. The quests that require you to have an exact number of elements linked are substantially more difficult because you will need to wait for the right tile to drop. That’s where you truly become a slave of the RNG, praying that you get a tile containing not 5 houses, but 2 only - because that’s what you need in order to complete the quest (and connecting a 5-houses tile would ruin it). For some of these quests, there's an optional requirement to close the opened edges, which further complicates things due to the fact that you’ll need to preplan the positioning so that you can easily close these off for extra tiles. 

Completing quests will not only award you points, but also add new random tiles in your stack - and without tiles you can’t progress further. Therefore, finishing as many quests as possible should be your main priority, in order to generate the maximum amount of tiles in the stack. In practice though, because the RNG is what controls your gameplay (more or less), you’ll end up having several quests that can’t be completed and in the end you’ll just run out of tiles, while waiting for those fitting ones. Unlike in [i]ISLANDERS[/i], where you need to reach a certain score in order to progress to the next island, here you can start as many game sessions as you like, with the score having an influence only on the additional challenges that you get in one gaming session. There are always 3 random challenges attributed (like building a water chain that is 50 tiles long or reaching 5000 points) which are made available in a progressive manner (as soon as you complete one, you unlock the next tier of the same challenge). Additionally, special tiles exist on the map - if you expand enough to reach them and complete their quests you will receive a random reskin for an existing tile.

In my opinion, one thing that is missing from the game is the ability to undo your moves, even for a limited amount of times. It happened more often than not that I misplaced a tile, thus breaking my existing configurations, and there was no way out from that. Several other people requested this functionality but the developers agreed to take this into consideration only in a later update. Also nice-to-have would be the ability to postpone some tiles for later use, thus saving some of these randomly generated tiles for quests with exact requirements, instead of wasting them on the current configurations. However, the devs are inclined to keep the gameplay unchanged, in order to not overcomplicate it with such features.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2435045637
The game can be played with the mouse only or with a combination of mouse and keyboard that you use to rotate the tiles and the camera. The quest requirements are visible
 on the map above the quest tiles and are instantly updated when you hover a potential placement spot with the currently active tile. This way you can easily see if you can get progress towards a quest by placing it on that spot, plus, all the tiles connected to the current one are highlighted. The opened edges are also highlighted on hovering the quest tile. The game makes it as easy and comfortable to you as possible and gives you all the information you need, leaving you only with the decision of where to place the tile.

In terms of achievements, prepare to spend at least 40-50 hours in it, if not even much more. The achievements are awarded for completing the challenges which grow exponentially in difficulty as you progress through the game, plus several challenges (reaching highscores for example) will have to be completed multiple times. 

[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is a game worth playing and playing again. It never gets old, there's always a new goal to pursue and with each new gameplay there's a soft nudge towards bettering your strategies, while still keeping everything casual and chill. It's a game in which you can lose yourself for 20 minutes or for hours, in short bursts or in lengthy sessions, and you can play it as casually or as hardcore as you choose. Also, a Creative mode is in the works - I for one am excited to see how that will play.

Yes, Countryside Romance is addictive, so I decided to try the game after I obtained it. My initial plan was to do one or two games then play a strategy game which had a new DLC. Then 3 days and 48 hours later I realized I totally ignored all other aspects of my life.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Dorfromantik is a simple but genial puzzle game. You start the game with 40 tiles and you need to place them on the board/map. Each tile has 6 edges and random objects placed on all of the edges. These could be: grassland, water, railroad, forest, house(s), some agricultural object (wheat probably). You can’t choose what tile you get, you will get them randomly and you need to build up an as big as possible countryside idyllic world using those tiles.

How to do that?

Eventually you would run out of tiles so you need to finish quests, like create a connected system of 50 houses, 10 railroads, etc. These quests show up on tiles you could place, but it keeps increasing and its required number is in relation with the size of your current biggest, expandable area. So when you have 50 connected houses and you could still expand that, then you will get quests which ask for 60-75+ houses, when you have 200 it will ask 220-250+. The additional amount is asked keeps increasing as you progress in the game. 
Don’t be afraid, if you closed your forest with 1500+ trees and now your biggest expandable forest has only 200 trees, then you won’t get a tile with 1700+ trees quest requirements, it will be again only 250-400+.

The reward for solving quests is 5 new tiles and when you place tiles perfectly (all 6 edges bordering the same type) you will get an additional tile too.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Loving it! Well worth the cheap asking price. Don’t hesitate if you like puzzles or relaxing games, just click the buy button. 97% of the players could be wrong, but I don’t!:-D

This game has become my 'second job'. It takes a while to get your head around all the possibilities but once you do. Even at 158 hours in I just learned/realized something that allowed me to get my new high score – 17770. Now I’m looking forward to playing again with my newfound knowledge.

The game is a mix of so many others, The obvious settlers of Catan, memory (where do I need that tile with one house next to one forest?), matching (I got a perfect perfect tonight! That’s 7 perfects at once). So much planning and very high stakes; one wrong click could ruin your entire game (I understand the debate but an undo button would really change the game).

I’m a lifelong player of video games (I refuse to call myself a ‘gamer’). This game has brought together so many things I love and have missed in video games. From a simple idea, with simple rules comes a game with such depth and complexity; its replay value is astronomical (see 158 hours in 19 days).

It is a steal for the price, get it, play it, enjoy it and play again.

This is a relaxing casual game with just enough challenge to keep it interesting. If you've had a hard day and just want to play something to relax and zone out, this is a good candidate. The artstyle is fantastic. The way some of the tiles will slightly change to match the neighboring tiles is neat. The little animations made me smile when I saw them for the first time. Relaxing? Yes, but also... strangely stressful. Under this whole aesthetic of idyllic central European countryside there's a surprisingly deep game of matching tile edges, managing groups, closing off regions, fulfilling quests. You can, of course, ignore all of that and play creative mode exclusively, but I'd feel like this would be a waste of game.

There are two reasons to pay attention to these systems. One - score. That one might not seem that important, but it's fun to try to beat your own high score! Besides, it often leads to achievements, which in turn unlock new tiles and biomes. And two - it replenishes your tile pool. See, your pile of tiles is always limited - and once you run out, it's [strike]game over[/strike] session complete. So if you want to keep expanding your little world, you have to keep paying attention to these things.

The mixture of those systems and the incredibly chill aesthetic - both in terms of look and the soundscape - create a very unique and potent brew that just washes your worries away. And I think this is the main reason why the game is so beloved by many.

For example: this one time, I had a mental breakdown so severe, my entire concept of reality collapsed and even thoughts of suicide didn't bring any solace. I got out of it with the help of therapy, philosophy and some research, but what kept the mortifying existential dread at bay was this game. The chill feeling was strong enough to make me forget I spent too long gazing into the abyss, and undoubtedly made my recovery quicker.

With all that said, I wish the game had more object types on the tiles. There are only 3 common ones (there's more, but they're much less common): houses, trees, and fields. I get it, that's rural Europe for you, but we also have mountains! Meadows! Swamps! Admittedly, the devs are from Berlin (I think), and the state of Brandenburg is almost completely flat - so maybe that's what they were going for.

I wasn't sure if I'd like Dorfromantik, but it entered my life when I needed it, and returned some kind of peace to my soul. I won't claim it would do the same to you, but I'd say it's nice to place a few tiles every now and then.

reviews.developer_response:
Thank you for the detailed information! We take your feedback very seriously and will act accordingly. To give a little context, we are a 4-person indie team and always try to address all issues to the best of our ability, including privacy related topics. We've already taken legal advice on this to be compliant with the GDPR, as well as technical support from the Backtrace team to be able to implement it properly. Backtrace is a crash report tool that helps us find issues and bugs in the game and fix them as soon as possible.
We have no interest in collecting user-related data to identify individual players at all, which is why, to the best of our knowledge, we have already independently filtered out user-specific data from the data to be transmitted. Our sole interest in using Backtrace is to improve Dorfromantik (for which it is very crucial, for example, whether 100 reported error messages come from a single game session or from 100 different game sessions).
However, in order to be able to investigate the matter thoroughly again, whether data is still being transmitted by Backtrace by mistake, we have decided to deactivate the tool completely and thus remove any data transmission from the game for the next patch until we have solved the problem and found an appropriate solution.

If you would like to send us more information, please do not hesitate to do so via the official contact email. Thank you very much!
- Sandro

reviews.review:
Dorfromantik is the ultimate procrastination tool masquerading as a game. 
It's a digital version of adult coloring books, a puzzle on steroids, a black hole of tile-matching goodness that sucks you in and never lets you go.
A virtual puzzle but instead of just fitting them together, you get the satisfaction of creating a unique new world.
It's like meditation but with less incense and more pixels.
If you're looking for a stress-reliever, a  zone out or just something to kill time, give Dorfromantik a try. 
The only downside is that you might find yourself neglecting your responsibilities to play this game.
Just don't blame me when you realize you've spent the entire day trying to get perfect tiles instead of doing work.

I did not find this game relaxing.

It bills itself as a relaxing puzzle game in the style of Carcassonne - take the next tile, place it where it fits best, and continue until the end of the game. It's the "until the end of the game" part where the relaxation turns into stress.

Each game you're provided a limited number of tiles. When you run out of tiles to place the game ends. To increase the number of tiles in your stack you're given "quests" to complete. These quests fall into two categories: "get N or more tiles of this type in a group" or "get exactly N tiles of this type in a group". A river with exactly 5 tiles, a city with 10 or more houses, a forest with 30 or more trees, etc. These quests grow in magnitude as the game progresses (River with 20 tiles! City with 100 houses! Forest with 400 trees!)

Instead of trying to place tiles to where they best 'fit', matching their features with the terrain, you're forced to cultivate large groups of like features to appease the quest system. You can't have a handful of small towns, you have to have a massive metropolis (that 300+ house goal isn't going to complete itself!). You can't have a countryside with sporadic forests, you have to have a dense wilderness. You can't have several small farms, you have to make an industrial-scale agricultural zone.

This is made worse by the "exact number" quests. You'll simultaneously be dealt a quest for a 200+ group of houses at the same time as a group of 12 (no more, no less) houses. You need to place the tiles close enough to eventually satisfy the former goal while not yet connecting them lest you sabotage the latter. Here's hoping the tiles are contiguous and of the right type: not too large so as to go over the exact number needed, yet not too small so as to "cap" the group and prevent it from expanding further. 

The result is a micromanaging nightmare, trying to place your tiles in the exact ways needed to satisfy the quest system while at the mercy of the random tile generator. There is no time to relax, you have to worry exactly how best to place the next random tile so as to put a stopper in the ever-dwindling count of tiles left to place. All you can do is hope that the next tile has exactly two houses so you can complete that 12 house group quest and get 10 more tiles to complete the 200+ grain quest in order to get 10 more tiles to complete the 400+ forest quest which will give you 10 more tiles to complete the 30+ river quest which will get you 10 tiles to

Everything in the game from the art style to the music is designed to be relaxing. Everything except the game itself.

I refunded my purchase.

Simple concept, high replayability. 8/10.

One point off for the horrible code optimisation. This game should run on a potato, as the suggested specs say. Yet, towards mid game (7-8k+ points) it begins to slow down on my laptop. Such a game should run smoothly even for occasional players gaming on a refurbished 10-years old family laptop with integrated graphics.

There is a lot to like about this game, but the randomness of it is crippling. You can play for an hour, and then a run of bad tiles will bring all your hard work to a premature end - and there's literally nothing you can do about it. You can't swap tiles, sell tiles, recycle tiles, trades tiles, or merges tiles - if the randomness decides your time is up then your time is up.

Buy it now.

I mean, sure, technically it's "Early Access."

And technically it's "missing features."

Only technically.

What's already here is infinitely, and immaculately playable. It's simple. It's clean. It's both casual and engrossing. You can play it for 15 minutes or 15 hours. Just click a tile, and then the next, and then the next... and suddenly you have a sprawling landscape that can never be the same as another.

It's remarkably simple, yet relaxing, creative and replayable.

This is a real winner here, especially for the low price.

It ain't even done, yet.

I bought this game because I wanted to be able to play a chill game either to relax or to play it along with a stream/movie/yt video on my other monitor. (This works perfectly btw)

Little did I know that I would descend into madness. 

PART 1: Ignorance is Bliss
I didn't know how the point system works so I just kept building cute little maps and I was pretty proud of myself for increasing my points after every run. I was happy as long as the world made me want to quit real life and instead get on the cute little train on tracks that looked like a 5-year-old designed it. But I wanted to get even more points and so instead of going for aesthetics I was paying more attention to maximise points. 

PART 2: Perfect Tiles = Dopamine
One thing led to another and I ended up watching a 40 minute YouTube video talking about the point system, some general tips and the overall thought process when putting tiles together. Basically, you have to try and match each side of the hexagon tile with an adjacent tile, for example house borders house. If you are able to match all sides perfectly you add more tiles (and points) to your stack. The 'goal' is to not run out of hexagons. Another way to accomplish that is to fulfil quests that will pop up randomly. Tasks involve connecting one type of tile (e.g. tree, field, house..) to reach either a specific number or plus. 

This awakened something in me that has been absent for most of my life; ambition. I started to get the hang of it and my maps were getting bigger and I finally reached over 10k points. I considered that an achievement; my friend called it an addiction. Apples and Oranges. Every time I completed a matching set of tiles and the "perfect" animation popped up with the cute sound feedback, I got a small dopamine dosis that kept me going. Coffee? No. Chocolate? No. Perfect tiles? Oh yeah, that's the shit!

Conclusion:
What started off as a game to past some time quickly turned into a personal challenge. Don't get me wrong though, I can still relax while also trying to be more efficient about it. Sometimes I do get a little grumpy when there is a tile that fucks you over and doesn't fit ANYWHERE :) But, on the other hand, you feel the opposite when you finally see a tile you were waiting for the past hour. 
There is also a creative mode for all the people who don't want to deal with points and quests and prefer to build aesthetically pleasing maps. 

10/10  I dream about putting tiles together. No, I don't need help.

Dorf Romantik is a tile placement puzzle game where the player will create a rural landscape.

The player is given a supply of hex shaped tiles featuring houses, trees, rivers, lakes, wheat fields and train tracks, and you’ll decide where to place them, ideally matching together tiles of the same type. Some rare tiles have tiny trains, boats, or animals, which will move around the map when placed.

In the classic game mode you have a limited number of tiles, but can earn more by completing quests which ask you to connect a number of the same tiles together, or by making perfect placements where all edges match. Your objective is to earn the highest score possible before you run out of tiles. 

Each run should take around 1-2 hours, but unfortunately the simple gameplay mechanics felt a bit repetitive after only a few runs. I also don’t like that the tile generation is completely randomised. I always seem to end up with some blank voids in my map that I can’t fill in because I just never get a tile that fits properly.

There’s also a creative game mode where you have unlimited tiles to expand endlessly without worrying about quests and high scores, although you’re still limited by the random generator and you can’t earn achievements.

Despite my criticisms, I think its fair to say this is a good game that just doesn’t suit my own personal preferences.

This game will intrigue the following kinds of players:
- If you are looking for something relaxing to fill some free time
- Puzzle elements
- People who like to create something pretty and who likes to share it with others.

This game will bore players who are looking for an action, fast paced shooter, survival, material gathering experience.  THIS IS NOT IT!

PROS:
- No time constraints:  You can walk away in the middle of the game, do something else and come back and continue where you stopped.
- Save game:  You can save to continue another day.
- Objectives:  You are given objectives to complete so that you receive more tiles.  This is relaxing and will not tire you out.
- Free build mode:  No constraints here.  You have unlimited tiles to create something amazing.

CONS:
- Many tiles can still be added to build on this game's diversity.  Things like bridges that will connect villages over a water barrier, Tunnels to connect railways under a forest barrier etc.
- No undo button:  If you place the tile wrong, you are stuck with it.
- No tile placement score indicator:  You can not see how much score a tile placement will give you until you score is adjusted.

I played this game when it was a free demo, i kept playing when it was an Early Access title who felt like a full fledged game and i will continue to play it for a long long time.

Why? Because it's a beautiful passion project made by some game dev students who keeps bringing you back.
Those guys were very clear from the start about the direction of the game and it shows. Up to this day i would be fine with the normal mode alone and i would still recommend this game but they didn't stopped there. They added so much more. Biomes, challenges, modes... but i digress. Here's why the core gameplay deserves your time. 

At the start you will get immersed in a relaxing little microcosm of your own making. Little villages, forests and other tiles will be your brush strokes in order to realise your idyllic landscape. You will make tens of beautiful pictures and then you will slowly begin to realise what's hiding beneath. The hidden mechanics who will skyrocket your highscore, will broaden your vision and let you finally realise that this game, apart from being a relaxing pretty picture simulator, is actually a quite deep puzzle game.
And that's when the real fun begins.

So, relax, put some music and enjoy a game who deserves all the love that can get, all with a more than fair price.

[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is a relaxing strategy game where you place tiles to grow beautiful and ever-expanding landscapes with plenty of replayability. 

[h3]Gameplay & Features[/h3]

[i]Dorfromantik[/i] (translated as the German word meaning “village romanticization”)is a game that is highly relaxing, challenging, and fun where you place tiles to create ever-growing landscapes filled with villages, trains, boats, waterways, wheat fields and lush forests. You start off with a stack of procedurally generated tiles and place them down on available slots, rotating them for the best fit. In the process you create forests, villages, and bodies of water. Get bonuses as you continue to grow each landscape. Special tiles will appear that give you quests and as you complete them you will unlock new tiles with new quests. 

This game is truly relaxing with no time pressure or building constraints to worry about. The only real concern is your point score, if you aim to beat the challenges in the campaign mode. 

Different game modes are available in this game. Classic mode is your standard game experience, Quick mode (tasks you with 75 tiles while scoring the highest possible score), Hard mode is like Classic but harder with more complex tiles and Monthly mode that offers challenges with different custom rules and a fixed biome every month where you compete with others against an online leaderboard. Custom mode lets you design your own game and rules and share them with others. 

Some of the challegnes are very difficult. I am over 36 hours in and still have not achieved them all. 

[h3]The Visuals & Audio[/h3]

The art style of [i]Dorfromantik[/i] is charming, hand drawn and idyllic. When all the tiles come together they form works of art in and of themselves. You can even select which biome you wish to play in (changing the season and color of the map). Biomes that you can choose from are Standard, Fjord, Enchanted, Sakura, Lavender, Blossom and Midwinter. 

The music is relaxing. I can not review the soundtrack DLC available as I have not purchased them. But it is a game that you can play and listen to your own music while you play. In-game audio is not necessary to play the game. 

[h3]Overall Experience[/h3]

I love this game, it is one I keep coming back to when I need to relax. There are so many game modes with different biomes you can play depending on what you're in the mood for that session. I highly recommend this game for something to pop into when you need to de-stress. For the amount of replayability this game offers, the price is great even at full price. The challenges range from easy to very hard but depending on what mode you chose it is up to you if you even want to do challenges. A game I highly recommend for everyone who enjoys puzzles and beautiful scenery. 🌄

🌾 Dorfromantik is a relaxing city-builder/strategy game in which you build a city, hex tile by hex tile. I am not usually good at these kinds of games, so I was initially somewhat on the fence about buying it, but I am so glad that I did! Let me tell you what I love about this charming game: 🌾

🎮 Dorfromantik's Gameplay:

Dorfromantik's gameplay is chill, relaxed, and easy to learn. I love that you don't have to be good at the game to enjoy it and that it has a gentle learning curve; much more merciful than some strategy and puzzle games I have played in the past.

I am still learning strategies to make bigger cities than my attempts before, but I never feel frustrated at the end of a run; it's very comfy, and it's very satisfying to reach different goals. ^^


🎨Dorfromantik's Artstyle:

The game's visuals are charming and colorful, with different varieties in different biomes. I enjoy the pleasant, simple, yet detailed style! I love the different architectural styles of the buildings in each biome, as well. ^^


🎶 Dorfromantik's Soundtrack:

Dorfromantik's soundtrack is as comfy as the game itself; I found myself humming and singing along to its chill, relaxing melodies. I thoroughly enjoyed it, and I could see myself listening to it even casually while doing other tasks!


Overall:

Dorfromantik is, at its core, a very relaxing game. To me, it meets a perfect balance between challenging you to try to get a higher score, and simply being enjoyable to play casually on its own; no matter how long or short your run may be.

To conclude, I must say that I love Dorfromantik! It is a beautiful game, and I find it very therapeutic. The gameplay is fun, the biomes are beautiful, the music is enjoyable, and I love everything about it. I am so glad that I decided to try this game despite my hit-or-miss experiences with some other similar types of games. ^^

8/10! Very, very good game! I would highly recommend it if you like chill and relaxing games, or more casual city-builder sims. ^^

I always say that the biggest sign of the enjoyment of the game is how eagerly I come back to play it. I tried again, this time playing for relax instead of high scores. Still, I lost interest, because I found that other games provide also this kind of fix better for me.

Still, regardless of how simplistic Dorfromantik might look (and it is), it packs a surprising amount of strategic depth, which I have to praise. I think the combination of simplistic, fast, yet clever and also visually pleasing gameplay might explain overwhelmingly positive reaction of players. I am OK with it, this combination just did not work for me at this time. In my case, the simplicity was a double-edged sword, because there was just not enough content to justify spending hours on simply besting the scores.

Dorfromantik offers several compelling reasons to give it a try. It runs very smoothly on Steam Deck OLED. You can limit the Refresh Rate to 60Hz/60FPS to safe some battery. 
The game is designed to be soothing and calming, featuring a puzzle-like gameplay where you lay down hexagonal tiles to create beautiful landscapes.
With its voxel-based graphics, Dorfromantik provides a visually pleasing experience that stands out for its simplicity and detail. Each tile placement contributes to a picturesque, ever-evolving world.
While the rules are simple, creating the most efficient or aesthetically perfect layouts can be indeed challenging. 
While you can play in a free-building mode, the games Classic mode - which I play mostly - includes tasks and scoring systems. You can aim to beat your high scores or complete specific objectives.
There's a significant amount of creativity involved. You decide how your villages, forests, rivers, and railway networks will look. But of course there’s a twist - the tiles you receive are completely random. So you’ll never have the full control of how your landscapes evolve over time. 
Although primarily a single-player game, Dorfromantik allows you to share your creations online. You can see how others have built their landscapes, providing inspiration and/or new ideas.
The best part is, that there's no rush to complete levels or beat timers. Play the game in your own speed without having any pressure. The game ends, when you run out of tiles.  
If you're looking for a game that combines strategy with relaxation, offers a creative outlet and doesn't demand a huge time investment, Dorfromantik might just be what you're looking for.

[u] Little Summary [/u]
In Dorfromantik, you place down hexagonal tiles and get points based on how well neighboring tiles fit one another. Tiles want to neighbor around other tiles that share similar features such as trees, waterways, or towns. Certain tiles can feature quests which revolve around getting 'X' amount of features in an area of tiles. For instance, quests may ask for a forest containing 100+ trees or a town with a specific number of buildings.

[u] My Thoughts [/u]
First off, Dorfromantik got me hooked with its easygoing gameplay along with fantastic graphics and music. The game basically boils down to just moving the camera, rotating tiles, and placing tiles where I think they'll fit best. Yet with such simple controls, I could craft beautiful landscapes whilst completing quests, going for achievements, and looking to beat my high score.

All in all, I recommend that you too try out Dorfromantik so that you can craft worlds out of your own deck of tiles.

Alright, fellow gamers, let’s talk about Dorfromantik. Developed by Toukana Interactive, this chill puzzle-strategy hybrid is available on PC and basically designed for those evenings when all you want to do is vibe. It’s like Carcassonne had a baby with Bob Ross, and then that baby went to therapy and decided to just relax for the rest of its life.

[h2]Gameplay Vibes[/h2]
This game is all about placing hexagonal tiles to build a gorgeous, sprawling landscape. Think forests, rivers, villages, and fields—each tile placement earns points if the edges match. It’s deceptively simple at first, but when you’re gunning for a high score, the pressure ramps up. One bad tile? Game over for your dreams of hexagonal perfection.

You can play this casually while sipping tea or hardcore strategize like you’re prepping for a chess championship. Either way, it’s addictive. People are out here playing 800+ hours and still learning new tricks—what kind of sorcery is that?

[h2]Graphics and Style[/h2]
Visually, Dorfromantik is pure serotonin. The soft, pastel art style feels like a warm blanket, and the way tiles subtly adapt to neighboring pieces? Chef’s kiss. It’s simple, clean, and designed to be soothing, not overwhelming.

There are no explosions, no neon chaos—just peaceful fields, happy little trees, and the occasional “Oh no, I messed up that train track!” moment.

[h2]Music and Sound[/h2]
The soundtrack? Absolute zen. It’s like the game whispers, “Relax, friend. Just place the tile and breathe.” The music is perfect for zoning out or unwinding after a stressful day. But, fair warning, if you’re chasing a high score, those peaceful tunes won’t stop you from cursing at a mismatched border piece.

[h2]Replayability and Multiplayer[/h2]
This isn’t a multiplayer game, but honestly, it doesn’t need to be. The replayability comes from mastering the art of tile placement and beating your own scores. That said, some players wish for more tile variety or expansions, and I’m here for it. Hexagons may be the bestagons, but a little spice never hurt anyone.

[h2]What Works, What Doesn’t[/h2]

[h2]What Works:[/h2]

Relaxing vibes mixed with just the right amount of challenge.
Gorgeous visuals and a calming soundtrack.
Endless replay value for puzzle and strategy fans.

[h2]What Doesn’t:[/h2]

If you’re expecting a city-builder or combat, this ain’t it.
Perfectionists beware: one wrong tile can ruin your day.

[h2]Who Should Play This?[/h2]
If you’re into puzzles, strategy, or games that make you feel like you’re meditating while gaming, this is your jam. It’s also perfect for winding down after a long day. However, if you’re all about fast-paced action or need a multiplayer component, you might want to pass.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
Dorfromantik is the gaming equivalent of a cozy night in with a cup of tea and a sleeping cat on your lap. It’s simple, relaxing, and oh-so-addictive. Just be prepared to look up at the clock and wonder how it’s suddenly 5 AM.

[hr][/hr]
Dorfromantk's basic premise is extremely simple: You're given a stack of hexagonal tiles which you'll have to place next to each other in order to gain points. Each tile contains various biomes like forests, villages or fields, each of which takes up one or more of the tile's edges and can be rotated before placement. Ideally, tiles should be arranged in such a way that the biomes of neighbouring edges match, which results in bonus points. Once enough points are collected, you're rewarded with new tiles, challenging you to keep going for as long as possible before running out.

While this sounds rather simple at first, especially given the complete lack of a time limit, things quickly become difficult with more biomes and special landscape features, mainly rivers and railroad tracks, which can to any other biomes. To make things more interesting, you're also given quests as you progress, tasking you with creating enclosed landscape types of certain sizes in order to earn additional points. As each game progresses, required point amounts increase drastically, meaning you'll have to stay on your toes to keep up.

Through these simple rules, Dorfromantik creates a genuinely mesmerizing gameplay loop, which can trap you for hours on end as you chase the next tile refill to keep your run going just a little longer. Getting perfect placements and finishing quests provides a genuine rush, especially once you're in the late game, when every boost in points matters. As the game progresses, this also creates some really scenic landscapes, with only railways and some rivers tending to end up rather ugly.

To add replayability, Dorfromantik provides you with a bunch of challenges to complete, many tracking your actions over the course of various games, such as perfectly placing a certain number of tiles or passing a set number of points for placing a single tile. Each of these comes in multiple stages, acting as neat milestones as you get better and better. Soe of them also require you to change up your tactics, with the most notable one challenging you to not rotate tiles at all.

Through all of this the game manages to keep its simple premise fresh for quite a while. When trying to play perfectly, Dorfromantik can feel quite challenging, as you have to hunt for ideal tile locations and have to plan ahead, yet doesn't feel very mentally draining, striking a rather perfect balance that's plain fun. For even more variation, you can also participate in monthly challenges, which put some twists on the basic gameplay and feature leaderboards for a bit of competition.

As for visuals, the game looks great, using simple graphics to create a cozy, lively world, underlined by some light, if not exceptional background music. Interactions also feel very nice, with good sound design making every action feel impactful and a very intuitive control scheme.

Summary: 10/10

Dorfromantik sets out to be a tile puzzle game. To do this it doesn't copy successful games like Carcassone or other tile placing games and instead creates its own. You have quests which range from minimum size, maximum size on first deployment, fully enclosed or exact match. All of these come for nearly all types of terrain (grassland excluded). If this was the only way to earn new cards in the standard mode, I wouldn't praise the game. By just doing blind quest runs on high efficiency, a player can easily do the 30k goal. The game truly shines in its placement bonus. For perfect tiles which have no error on an edge, the player gets another tile to place. Doing this can ensure reaching above 30k without much effort. This is where the "puzzle" aspect comes in. 

At some stage it is clear what tiles are more common by pure statistic and why "dirty" tiles (many terrain types) are best left on some lone side of your set. Preparing perfect slots for your plans is much easier if more chaotic and reasonale tiles are chose. Less uniform triple sides and more "one-slot grassland". Keeping your enclosures to 1-2 terrain types is as much part of the puzzle logistic as it is gambling on one of the complex tiles fitting the one accidental 3 terrain one you let slip in to finish a quest.

Again, if this was all this game offered you'd perhaps consider it an 8 or a 9. It delivers but is it truly the puzzle game for you? Worry not, this game has monthly challenge with highscores, alternative ruleset modes and a sandbox mode where you can simply build the little map of your dreams with romantic villages in an early industrial landscape.

If one was petty, the lack of a "road" tile to connect the towns would be a deduction of 0,5 points as would be the lack of mountains or hills for more personality of the landscape. Since this game is a beautiful complete package, this shall not be done. Although a DLC to add mountains and or roads would have been appreciated.

If you like puzzling and would like to test some hexagonal puzzles, Dorfromantik is a game for you. Yet, even if you are not the sandbox mode may strike the fancy of the artist in yourself; build a beautiful map of your own.

Suggested Improvements to the Devs:
- Add a level mode with different puzzle scenarios. You can easily create biomes that differ per each 10 levels or something like that to change the visuals/music to keep things exciting.

- The knock-off game I play on my phone, has a tile that when connected to adjacent tile types, it fills a meter. Once filled, it gives additional tiles, which incentivizes the player to not lock off that tile type. Obviously, I'm not suggesting to copy them, and it is similar to the quests in the game, but it acts more like a continuous quest and a challenge to not block off that tile type. [h1]Experienced on the Meta Quest 3[/h1]

You can view my 3D in VR gameplay here (SBS 3D): https://youtu.be/r2A6vqXIACY

Yes, you can play Dorfromantik in 3D in VR using the Geo 11 3D driver (search for it, it's free). You just need an app like Bigscreen or Virtual Destkop to view the 3D content in VR. It's like playing a game in a 3D movie theater.

Visuals look great, except for the lighting issue with the water tiles. It's not that big of an issue, but it otherwise looks really good, especially on close-up view. You will need to use a gamepad because the mouse cursor does not render by default as well. 

This experience in 3D in VR proves that this game would be perfect with VR support. Mixed Reality with the tiles would be heaven sent. I hope the developer sees my video and decides that VR support is needed. It is the best way to play this game as the 3D visuals really pop in this game up-close.

If you’re looking for a simple game that takes minimal effort to play, yet fully engages you, then Dorfromantik is a fine choice. I purchased this game at the start of a much needed break. At that point, my mind was too foggy to do almost anything else, so I stuck to playing this game before bedtime. Put on some mildly stimulating sounds in the background, and you’ve got an excellent activity to help you recover from severe fatigue.

The gameplay is extremely simple, yet there’s just enough mechanics to keep you making meaningful choices at every turn. If you want a high score, it’s essential that you balance quest progression and perfect fits. Whilst getting perfect fits is very satisfying, especially when it’s multiple instances at once, you’ll hamstring your play-through by aiming for perfection. It is, indeed, common to make concessions, which isn’t particularly satisfying, but doing so does not lead to ugly seams in your features. Creating a pretty world is, of course, half the fun. In this regard, I think the game does a good job early on, though the larger the map grows, the noisier everything becomes. You don’t get many tiles that comprise of just one feature, so woods, fields and villages tend to look stringy instead of blobby, which I’m not a fan of. Rail- and waterways should be placed with care, because their ends don’t accept anything but more rails and water respectively. This means that time and time again, I end up building nonsensical, webby rail and river networks because it’s safe and effective to do so, though it never looks good. Why do some quests require you to close rivers anyway? Where’s the water going and coming from? In terms of progression, there’s various one-tile features to unlock, as well as different biomes which change how parts of the map look. I like having focal points in my world, but the fact that special features are just one tile makes them pretty insignificant on a larger map. Furthermore, you don’t get that many unique ones, because you mostly unlock skins for existing ones instead, which I struggle to differentiate in many cases. Lastly, growing your map ever more provides a good challenge, but when you’re doing especially well, it can take over 10 hours to run out of tiles, which is way too long for a game you might only play every now and again. The pace gets progressively worse as well, because instead of completing quests at a steady rate, you’ll be working on several similarly large ones simultaneously, which can take a very long time to finish.

Dorfromantik costs quite a lot for what you get, but if you’re in need of something to occupy your mind while everything else is too much effort, this game should give you sufficient value in return. See if you can spot the pumpkin with the c: face.

Dorfromantik is a relaxing tile placement game. You start with a stack of hex tiles you place one at a time, some of them give you little quests that when completed give you more tiles and you get points for matching the edges of the tiles.

My problem with this game is motivation. I have never been one to chase High Scores, and that is all there is to do in this game. There isn't much to unlock, no threshold where things change, no levels, no victory condition... and this is the important part, if you try to play by the rules of the game the map you end up making is kind of fugly. Don't get me wrong, there are quaint little villages and forests and wheat fields, but they are not connected in any sort of cohesive way. Rivers that dead end, railroads with a million intersections going nowhere, and lots of holes with no tiles. You can build a beautiful landscape but then you have to actively ignore points. And that, to me anyway, is bad design. 

I hate comparing games, but I do think this game is very similar to the minimalist city builder Islanders. In Islanders you place buildings in a very similar fashion, trying to maximize points with adjacency, but the map ends up looking better if you ask me. Islanders is also played in rounds. Once you get enough points you start over at the next island, and honestly, dorf could really benefit from that. Create multiple smaller maps instead of a big chaotic one.

I am clearly in the minority here, lots of people seem to enjoy the maps they create in drofromantik, but I never found them satisfying so could not get much enjoyment out of the game.

Brilliant art design, great sound and music. Fun concept, but ultimately, it has far less depth than it feels like it should. This is not a "city builder", as the stylistic elements of the terrain are just arbitrary representations of numerical values on edges of a hex tile. You could replace all of the graphics with just a top-down view of hex pieces with a number (1, 2, 3 etc) on each edge and the game would remain totally unchanged.

What really makes me unable to recommend this one though is the execution of the water and train lines. The game has a frustratingly low skill ceiling, and a large part is the punishing nature of the RNG around the water and train track tiles. It is very difficult to do much strategic management of either water or train tracks because their appearance is infrequent and random, and when they do appear, they give often hefty demands on multiple directions at once. The problem is that both of these tile types are parasitic with the game's core strategic concept of building outwards in a methodical balanced fashion. Sure you can argue that balancing this tension is the challenge of the game, and you would be right, but you have so little agency with the water and train tracks that there is no real balancing that can be done and therefore not much depth to the game.

I'm a huge fan of board games, tile laying games and more specifically - Carcassonne. One thing I've always disliked though, is the competitive nature of the game. My pleasure of Carcassonne comes from laying down the collection of tiles, creating an aesthetically and beautiful landscape.

Another game I love is Triple Town (similar to 2048) a simple puzzle game which I can happily knock out regularly on my phone. Building up that simple village and being constrained within the land grid makes it a challenging but relaxing game too.

Dorfromantik combines both the beauty of tile laying while implementing the challenging puzzle mechanism of Triple Town. Being constrained to laying a set number of tiles you're continuously challenged to preserve your remaining playtime, there is no time limit, the limit is the amount of tiles left in your portfolio. Sure you can ignore the basic rules and build something nice and idyllic however you will eventually run out of tiles and end game.

The goal of play here is to always plan ahead, can you maintain the challenge of placing the perfect tile formations before your tiles run out? The true beauty of this game is creating something that's equally challenging as the best puzzle games out there, while also creating a calm and reflective atmosphere with the ever growing biomes, animal showcases and music.

Dorfromantik is a chill puzzle-game. The main mechanic is to place hexagonal tiles to the ever-increasing landscape you have built. Once you are out of tiles, the game starts again from zero. You get more tiles during the game by achieving certain goals which are randomly generated. For example, you need to create a forest containing a certain number of trees or a river of certain length. The graphics are very nice and give the game a cozy vibe.

Even though the game is relaxing, it can be very challenging to achieve all goals and achievements and get new highscores (It took me roughly 100 hrs to get all achievements, with some idle time in between). Very neat little game, also a great fit if you like to watch videos on a second screen while playing :)

In Dorfromantik, you will build a beautiful landscape with several different tiles that must be connected to other tiles with similar geographic features. Dorfromantik can be played where you must get as many points as possible to keep playing or else you will lose the game. This is done with the connection of tile features to tile features to form large masses of the same feature for bonus points. On the other hand, it can be played in sandbox mode where you build whatever you want with no losing conditions. Either way, Dorfromantik serves to be an incredibly relaxing game that you can play in whatever situation you find yourself in, alone in your room, or during times of boredom to quickly pass the time.

Dorfromantik is one of those games which really pushes at the limitations of a yes/no reviewing system. It's a satisfying puzzler with a strong, distinct art style, but it hasn't made a lasting impact on me, and I wouldn't feel strongly about playing it ahead of other good puzzle games.

It is superb for that purpose. Even on a larger map, the natural districting that the scoring system encourages leads to being able to have a strong intuition as to where to place the next tile at a glance.

However, nothing about it makes me want to play it where there aren't similar restrictions on my ability to freely use my time. This isn't the case for all turn-based games or all puzzlers: one that springs to mind is a free game on the store called Handshakes, where I found the gameplay satisfying enough to want to play outside of working hours. Your mileage may vary, of course.

Quick Description:
-Dorfromantik is a really peaceful, well designed management puzzler.  This game is great.  It has a really cool visual style, has a really tranquil soundtrack, and is super easy to learn but offers some strategic decision making w/ every choice you make.  While I do think there is a good amount of depth, my favorite part of this game is how easy it is to play while doing other things.  It's a great pallet cleanser after playing a really demanding game.  Having said that, some ppl are able to string together crazy high scores that I could only dream of, so clearly this is a skill based game w/ a decent learning curve.  

Consensus:
-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  I recently compared this game to Can't Live Without Electricity, and I think there is a good amount of overlap between the two.  I do prefer CLWE, but I think this game is really fun too.  I also think this is an easier game to learn, feels less chaotic, and has such a cool visual aesthetic.  I think the price point is spot on, but is really easy to recommend if there is any form of discount available.

[h2] DORFROMANTIK – tranquility, creativity, and peaceful strategy! [/h2]
[h3] Personal experience: [/h3]
I’ve spent nearly 10 hours in Dorfromantik, and I can confidently say it’s a perfect choice for those who want to unwind and enjoy a calm, thoughtful experience. There’s no pressure here—just you, nature, and the satisfying task of building a beautiful, ever-growing world.

The game feels like a digital version of a quiet countryside evening. The visuals, music, and gameplay work together to create a truly relaxing atmosphere. Even after many hours, the game continues to surprise with its cozy charm and simple depth.
[h3] Pros and cons: [/h3]
[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Visual style: Soft, pastel colors and clean design make for a peaceful and visually pleasing experience.
[*] Gameplay: Easy to pick up, but creating the perfect landscape tile by tile is deeply satisfying.
[*] Atmosphere: Calming music and slow pace help clear your mind and relax.
[*] Replayability: Each new run feels like building your own little world from scratch.
[/list]
[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Repetitiveness: The gameplay can become a bit repetitive after long sessions.
[*] Lack of challenge: Players looking for fast-paced or competitive mechanics may find it too laid-back.
[*] Lack of clear end goals: Some might miss having a strong objective or final reward.
[/list]
[h3] Result: [/h3]
Dorfromantik is a wonderful game for players who value peaceful, creative gameplay and want a break from intensity. Whether you’re listening to music or just want to wind down, it’s a lovely and rewarding way to spend your time.
[b] My rating: 10/10 [/b]
[i] I recommend it to anyone looking for a peaceful, feel-good experience with a cozy vibe and no pressure. [/i]

Dorfromantik is intended to be a cozy puzzling experience where you place down pieces so that the corners are of the same type, eg. houses on houses, trees on trees, etc. and you are given missions to complete that want a minimum number of tile types, a specific number of tile types, and for you to "close" a patch of tiles. Doing these actions gives you more tiles and if you run out then it's game over.

On a casual level, this game is great. I love seeing the world come slowly to life, along with the brain teasing conundrums you run into when you get low on tiles. There's also a creative mode so you can just build whatever you want. However, I personally think high level Dorfromantik is fundamentally flawed in a way that could only be fixed from redesigning the whole game from the ground up. You see, completing quests is not the only way for you to get tiles. If you create a "perfect" tile (aka all 6 of its sides are matching), you get an extra tile. This might not sound like much, but then you realize that in later parts of the game this means you get 1 tile for placing a tile plus the rewards from missions means you can effectively go infinite (and people have). The problem is that perfect tiles are so important that they make missions pretty much worthless- it is actively better to squander a mission and never close patches of tiles in favor of making more perfects. This also means that the pace of the game slows down exponentially as your board gets bigger, as you find yourself scanning for tens of minutes for just the right place to use your tile.

This wouldn't be a problem for most players since it's a "casual" game, but then paradoxically the game wants you to reach ridiculous scores to complete its meta-progression quests, which means inevitably you will stumble upon this truth if you want to get better. Some people may enjoy this style of gameplay, but I find that it clashes with the atmosphere of the game and building a little land of your own, as you're no longer thinking about how your tiles look placed down and more at the cold hard numbers.

All that being said, I'm sure for a lot of people this scratches that OCD itch, and more power to them. It's not like I'm immune to it either, I just would have liked it if the game incentivized you better when you become really skilled. I may not enjoy it much anymore, but I'm still giving it a positive review because I definitely got my money's worth of entertainment out of it before I began to have issues.

I think I'm at a point where I can give this a fair review now.

So what is it? It's probably best described as a tile-laying board game but specifically designed to be played digitally, and solo. You get a stack of hexagonal tiles and place them on a board, trying to connect fields/woods/plains/villages/rivers/railroads. The placement rules are relaxed except for rivers and railroads, which HAVE to connect. However, if you want a higher score, you're going to want to place tiles that connect correctly on most or all sides. There are also dynamic quests attached  to some tiles (e.g. connect a woods area with X amount of trees) that reward you with more tiles if completed.

The game is excellent, but it certainly won't be for everyone. If you're playing for a high score, a single match could easily take you 1-2 hours or beyond. And it's only really excellent when you're tackling it that way. Its good casual fun otherwise, but you would probably get bored after the first handful of games if you don't enjoy the challenge.

The good thing is, you can go at your own pace, the music is zen and its a nice relaxing but thoughtful session. If you like solo board games, or have the patience for jigsaws, or love a bit of sudoku for some brain exersize, the chances are you will really appreciate this game.

I like Dorfromantik for the most part. It's really meditative when you get in the flow, and the music is calming.

For some reason I thought there would be levels, but it's just one main level where you try to beat your high score (plus a creative mode, too, which is nice).

There will be quests and requirements that get you thinking about tile placement and how to achieve better scores. You'll get better as you practice.

In the menu you will also see challenges you can work towards as you play the game. You can get new tiles/skins by completing them. They are linked in with the Steam achievements. There are base challenges such as "place 250 tiles in total" and "gain a highscore of 10,000". But the other challenges you need to unlock.

This is where I feel a bit iffy. To unlock a new challenge, a pre-placed tile will appear on the board, slightly further out. You then have to build up to that point to "uncover" that tile. It will have its own quest which you must fulfil to add the challenge to your menu.

These extra challenges will be things like "score two perfect placements at once" or "build a forest with at least 250 trees". In my opinion, these should already be unlocked from the get-go. It feels weird to have to obtain the challenge card first - especially if you've already done some of these requirements! I don't know, I just like getting achievements without stipulations...

That aside, it's a good puzzle game. It's pretty to look at and my favourite part is the different biome tiles which give you different colours across the board.

I'll keep playing for sure. I recommend this game on sale.

This fun and addictive game is about placing landscape tiles. The hexagonal shapes have various possible landscapes for each side. Your task is to match them to like-sides. There are plains, housing, fields, woods, water, and train landscapes. If you can match all 6 sides on a piece, you score 60 points for a perfectly placed piece. This all makes each and every play-through different.

Complete tasks to gain more tiles, such as laying 63 trees touching each other, or 18 adjacent fields, BUT that number needs to be exact; not too many and not too few.

Sound easy? Give it a try!

The notion that this game is a "relaxing" strategy game is a downright lie.  Essentially a tile-matching game, the nature of this game is that you have a limited number of tiles to play, yet if you can make a perfect match on every edge of a tile (which usually means on other tiles that you "complete" the edges for after playing more tiles), you get another tile.  There are also "quests" to make "runs" of a certain size, but before too long, those are for things like "a river 120 tiles long" or "1,600 trees in a forest", and you get 5 tiles for completing something it takes 120 tiles to make.  So basically, anything less than constant, relentless perfection is [b]FAILURE!![/b]  

Also, the achievements that are the only progress this game has require constant perfection.  As in, one of them I was given recently was "place 250 tiles in a row that are perfect placements" (another is that you aren't allowed to rotate tiles anymore), and somewhere around 230 perfect placements in a row, I apparently either placed a tile imperfectly [i]and didn't know it[/i] because the game's interface is [i]way[/i] too subtle about a faint red line (which can be occluded by quest markers or buildings) to actually see it every single time when playing sessions for hours.

So, again, play this game for the "relaxing" time of having felt like you were getting good at this - you're over a thousand tiles into a game, the map is huge, you have a score of nearly 100k, and 80 moves in the bank, and then you just keep getting railroad pieces you just can't match, and have to expand more out to the edges, and suddenly, without you [b]ever[/b] making a bad move, you're at less than 10 moves left and you're left with the inescapable feeling you just [i]ruined[/i] a run you spent the last week on in a single day and everything you did for the past week was an utter waste.  Due to the sheer randomness, even tiles that [i]should[/i] be common, like plains with two farms on opposite ends of the tile that I set up at hour 1 of my second game was a tile that [i]didn't come until 30 hours into the game, or several thousand tiles later[/i]!!  Due to the nature of how perfect tiles work, you've sunk 6 moves in the hole if you can't fill in a perfect match to a tile you've left as a hole, and you have breathing room of maybe 120 tiles, so you can afford to be waiting on as little as 20 tiles that are a "hole" when there are tens of thousands of permutations of tiles that might appear.  Even more insidiously, however, is that every single piece along the edge (where you keep your odds of leaving matches open by having less confirmed edges) is essentially a frozen drain of a tile until every edge is completed, making an expanding map an increasing debt you inevitably drown within. 
 Every single tile you have to skip and just hope you get a matching tile for it later as you advance forward is like a bleeding wound sucking at your nerves for [i]hours[/i] as you try to hold out until the match gets dealt to you by a merciless RNG that I [i]swear[/i] is [i]explicitly[/i] designed to hold out on pieces you need.  You know, "relaxing", like inescapably being cornered and drowned by debt.

But OK, it's horribly depressing and ruins your whole day that the game you looked forwards to playing after getting home was a total disaster through the game's own fault, but you can get back on the horse after taking a bit to recover from the crushing disappointment of your second game coming to a crashing end, right?  Well, haha, sucker, you still need to get nothing but perfect moves, and in the sixth tile of the game, you get handed a windmill with only farm edges and there hasn't been a [b]single[/b] farm edge yet.  RNG SAYS FUCK YOU, YOU LOSE!  START OVER, LOSER!  Oh, look, now you get an all-city tile before there's been any city edges to match it to!  YOU LOSE AGAIN, LOSER!  After playing my second game (for about 30 hours gametime,) it took about 15 tries to find a single game where it was even [i]possible[/i] to get established, and it quickly fell into a death spiral of no matching tiles after only another 4 hours trying to get my hopes up.  This game is just relentless kicks in the kidney by the RNG.  What [i]you[/i] can do about it doesn't matter, you just have to wait for the RNG to [i]let[/i] any strategy you might have start to matter.  Even if you have a perfect strategy based on looking up the game's probability chart to give yourself the best odds, it's still luck.  You're still watching the Sword of Damocles that is the tile counter swing down with every tile you don't get what you need, and [i]that isn't "relaxing"!![/i] 

Speaking of strategy, this game even trains you to play it wrong.  Early on in the game, plains are much more common (presumably to make it "easier"), but this just puts you into a mindset that the strategy is to leave edges that are plains open because early in the game, they're easier to match (ESPECIALLY tiles which have rails, where woods-edges are nearly non-existant), only for this to [i]very much not[/i] be the case later in the game when an invisible switch is flipped and it's time for nothing but tiles with two rail edges, two river edges, a woods edge, and a farm edge with no plains in sight.  All those edges you left hours ago with plains exposed when those were common are now massive liabilities because the game taught you on one set of rules [i]then changed the rules on you without telling![/i]  In short, the game is deliberately tricking you into failing.

Basically, there's a reason I never play games that are entirely determined by RNG.  Leaving your fate up to chance is always only going to end in bitterness and depression.

Yeah, sure, this game has a "creative mode" with no move limits or score where you can "just enjoy making the scene you want", but this game's output is to art what static from a radio on the wrong frequency is to music.  It's pure randomly-generated noise, best exemplified by the railroads, which tend to be a tangled knot of spaghetti that goes nowhere and has no trains on one giant track, but two trains on a single track that have to phase through each other to travel down the single linear path.  It's just endless blobs of the same random stuff mashed together for no reason because this game encourages playing to the mindless procedural generation method of generating content.  There is zero ability to enjoy placing random tiles down for no reason, it doesn't even qualify as a game.

Rails in particular are poison to the game, as rail tiles are [i]vastly[/i] rarer than most other tiles.  A recent event popup even has a challenge where the dev mentions that there are "no rails to ruin your maps" because in this game, rails are apparently a force of pure evil and chaos that just exist to ruin all of civilization.  When I had holes in my map that I just couldn't fill, they were almost always because I had to wait for a rail of a particular shape to fit the spaghetti mess of rail tiles I'd had excreted onto me by the game.

At its core, it is a zen/methodically paced puzzle game involves you matching similar sides/types to other pieces. The game rewards you for building maps with as many perfect matches as possible while also fulfilling challenges such as X piece wanting to be apart of a 200+ house section, or a 400+ tree forest. I personally enjoy playing the game in the evenings or quiet weekend afternoons as a way to relax while having something to do (a lot of ADHD and ASD people struggle to actually relax or meditate, and for me this is really relaxing as it gives me dopamine for achievements, doesn't leave me alone with my thoughts, and provides flow-state). The music is pretty ambient, but there is no big sound cues other than those for achievements and perfect matches, so you can put on your own music of choice and not miss anything. The achievements are pretty in-depth and skill focused, so while the skill floor to play the game is low, it has a higher skill ceiling, which I like. On that note, there are creative modes, quick modes, harder modes, as well as a monthly mode with leader-board. Technically all the modes have leader-boards, but I find the monthly to be the most enjoyable and rewarding competitively as you are limited in space vs the hard mode which is just harder challenges. TLDR if you are looking for a cozy relaxing game, and enjoy the task of matching or sorting things for fun, doing puzzles, or other sorts of spacial strategy games, I would highly recommend this game.

Dorfromantik is a delightful gem of a game that has truly captured my heart. If you're seeking a relaxing and visually stunning experience, look no further because this game is an absolute masterpiece.

First and foremost, the artwork and design in Dorfromantik are simply breathtaking. The hand-drawn landscapes are so charming and picturesque that you'll often find yourself just gazing at the scenery. The attention to detail and the vibrant, calming colors create a tranquil atmosphere that's perfect for unwinding.

The gameplay is easy to grasp, yet it offers a surprising depth of strategy. The concept of placing hexagonal tiles to build a pastoral landscape is both intuitive and creative. You'll quickly find yourself engrossed in the challenge of creating the most beautiful and harmonious world possible. The game strikes a perfect balance between being relaxing and engaging, making it suitable for both casual players and those who enjoy more in-depth, thought-provoking experiences.

The relaxing soundtrack complements the gameplay beautifully. It enhances the tranquil ambiance and is just a joy to listen to while you immerse yourself in the world of Dorfromantik. It's a game that encourages you to slow down, take your time, and appreciate the simple pleasures of life.

One of the most appealing aspects of Dorfromantik is its endless mode. There's no rush or time pressure, and you can play at your own pace, creating your dream landscape without limitations. This design choice allows for a highly personalized and meditative experience, making it the perfect game to unwind with after a long day.

Dorfromantik's replayability is impressive as well. Each new game offers a fresh opportunity to experiment with different tile placements, develop new strategies, and improve your high score. It's a game that you can return to time and time again without it ever feeling repetitive.

In a world filled with fast-paced, high-stress games, Dorfromantik is a breath of fresh air. It's a peaceful, engaging, and visually stunning experience that will soothe your soul and provide hours of enjoyment. If you're looking for a game that helps you relax and appreciate the simple beauty of creating your own idyllic world, Dorfromantik is a must-play. It's a true work of art in the gaming world, and I can't recommend it enough!

I don't usually love puzzle games, but this one is so satisfying, relaxing and fun that I have been playing it constantly. I like it so much more than I thought I would. It is inexplicably fun to create beautiful landscapes one tiny step at a time. By the end, when I look back, I feel proud and accomplished as well as extremely satisfied.

I had Dorfromantik on my Wishlist for some time, always waiting for a sale greater than 20%. The overwhelmingly positive reviews intrigued me, but I was not moved to purchase. One day a streamer on Twitch was playing it, but I didn't recognize it at first. "Wow this game looks great! This is right up my alley! What's the name?" "Dorfromantik". 

From that moment I've been hooked. I downloaded it that day, and have already sunk over 8 hours into it over the weekend. Even my partner loves it, and she never games. There is something so rewarding about placing the tiles - especially when they match up perfectly - getting points, and watching your beautiful map grow bigger and better, that hits all the right spots. Hidden behind the very simple mechanics and beautiful design is an incredible depth and loads of strategy. Sure you can have an amazing time tinkering around and creating a cute little countryside, but you can also spend minutes agonizing over each tile placement and thinking ahead to reach those high scores.

Between this depth of play, the ease to enter and exit a game, and the gorgeous graphics and sounds, you'll be hooked just like I was. Fans of the board game Carcassone will feel at home, and to a lesser extent Settlers of Catan or Ticket to Ride. Even if you don't game, and ignore the quests and points, just making a really cool map with all the beautiful and varied tiles is bound to bring enjoyment.

Dorfromantik will undoubtedly be at the top of my favourite games list for some time, which is crazy to think that I had slept on it so long. I encourage you to give it a go!
