A nice puzzle game to play every now-and then. 

The store page explains it quite well. You try to place down randomly-generated hexagonal tiles so that their borders match neighbouring tiles. For example a tile might have trees on three sides, houses on one side, and farm fields on two, and you'd want to place it so that the edges with trees are placed against the side of another placed tile that also has trees, while the side with houses is against the side of another tile with houses, etc.

Railways and rivers are a bit different as they have to be connected so that one railway track/river goes into another without ending at the edge of a tile.

You only have a limited number of tiles, but you can get more with "quests". A quest can be generated by a tile when you place it, or by special tiles that appear on the map, with the quest activating when you reach the tile. A quest is visible as a little speech bubble above a tile with a number indicating that you will be rewarded with more tiles if you connect that number of a specific feature to that tile. For example, it might say to connect 20 houses to that tile. Most tiles have multiple houses on them, so you won't need to connect 20 tiles with houses, but the connection needs to be continuous, with no other features like fields or water separating some houses from others, even on single tiles. It is the same with trees, water, etc.

You earn points every time the side of one tile is matched with a side of another with the same feature. You also earn an extra tile every time you get a perfect placement (a tile with all its sides matching the features on neighbouring tiles). Once you run out of tiles it's game over and you get your score.

There are at least a few different modes to play around with: 
- classic (normal gameplay)
- quick play (awards fewer tiles so games don't last as long)
- hard mode (tiles have more difficult/varied feature combinations)
- creative mode (unlimited tiles and can place any you want)
- custom mode (allows you to specify some parameters like how often features appear on tiles, add a time limit, etc)
- monthly challenge (everyone is provided with an identical seed and a limited area to place tiles, you can look at leaderboards to see how your results compare to others)

This game is beautiful and the gameplay gets off to a strong start. Although my first game went well (I placed 780 tiles with a score of 42k) it also revealed to me that there are some serious flaws with this game's design. In particular, I would highlight four principal design failures:

1. As the size of the map expands, it becomes increasingly difficult to remember the ever-expanding wishlist of specific tile arrangements you're waiting for. It also takes longer and longer to find the correct place to put a tile as the number of possible placements continually increases. The result of this is that the pace of the game drags and the game increasingly feels like a tedious administrative chore. This problem could be fixed by having a button you can click in order to highlight any particularly good locations for a tile (e.g. 3+ matching sides). 

2. The number of possible tile combinations is so high that the chances of getting the right tile combination become very slim, particularly once you have more than 3 sides to match. This leads to a sense of frustration which is at odds with the intended relaxing game experience. This problem could be fixed by including a new type of tile - a wildcard tile - which automatically morphs into the perfect tile once placed. This could be a special quest reward, for example, or perhaps could be awarded each time you achieve a certain number of natural perfect placements.

3. The mechanics of the river and railway tiles are fiddly and frustrating. The difficult of managing these pieces, combined with the ridiculous water station tile, means that the only viable tactic is to create an area just for them on one edge of the map. This leads to an unnatural and aesthetically displeasing map. These tiles should be removed as base tiles and instead should be overlay tiles that you place on top of existing tiles (as in Civilization V). This would not only alleviate issues 1 and 2 above, but could allow for more variety of quests (e.g. a quest to connect two closed town areas with a railway, a quest to create a railway which bridges over two different rivers or spans a large area of water, a quest to create a river which travels through three pure forest tiles, etc.).

4. The gameplay is fundamentally just not interesting enough. More thought needs to be put into how to make a game which has mechanics beyond tile rotation. This game needs things special base tiles which actually do something (as opposed to being purely cosmetic), overlay tiles that go on top of existing tiles to allow placement of rivers, railways and roads, a greater variety of quests, maybe even power-ups which could be won by closing an area (e.g. dynamite to destroy a previously placed tile, an axe to turn forest into plains, etc.), etc.

There is the foundation of a good game here, but it needs significantly more development to make it enjoyable to play.

This is a funny game. Better said, this is a game that has funny tags. If you look up above at the most relevant tags you see "City Builder", "Turn Based Strategy" and "Puzzle". Of those three I'd say only puzzle is 100% relevant. Especially in terms of what you'd really expect from these tags traditionally. When you think "City Builder" you normally think of games like Tropico, Cities: Skylines or Simcity. Yes, you can build a very large town by connecting lots of house tiles that could constitute a city, but it's not what you think it is. Same goes for Turn-Based Strategy yeah, you lay down one tile at a time. So one could call that a turn. But it's not like Civilisation or Total War where there are clearly defined turns as such.

That being said, was this a delightful discovery? Absolutely! It's addictive, soothing and simply fun. This game is to me, a classic example of "don't judge a book by it's cover" and "you should really give a wide net of games a go!". While I do enjoy board games and this game very much feels like one, it certainly was not what I was expecting. And it turned out to be an incredibly pleasant surprise!

The graphics and feel of the game are all very lovely. My only criticism is the music. I think it's ok, but honestly, I think they could have been a bit more adventurous with it and gone with something a bit more melodic rather than something that feels like it would play in the background at a spa. Like I get what they were going for, they wanted something calming and inoffensive to try to appeal to as many people as possible, but I don't generally agree with this sort of thinking. Things designed by committee are rarely good. I think they should have let the composer be a bit more adventurous.

All in all. Very solid game that definitely deserves the overwhelmingly positive reviews it currently enjoys! Recommended!

A lot of the reviews for this game paint it as a chill, calm, no-stress puzzle game. And it could be played that way, if you didn't care about the score, unlocking additional challenges, or completing quests. If, however, you're the kind of person who does care about your score, unlocking additional challenges, or completing quests, it's a stress-filled RNG nightmare. You start with six quest types (or challenges) unlocked, and as you progress through the game you can reach preset tiles on the map and complete their quests to unlock a new quest type (or challenge).

For instance, you may encounter a preset tile with a bit of forest and a quest to connect 500+ trees to it, and if you succeed at the quest you can unlock one of the remaining challenges. It doesn't seem to matter what kind of quest tile you encounter when it comes to unlocking the next challenge, and no consideration of which quest tiles have been placed at map generation is made when the game rolls your starting tileset. This is where the problem comes in. You can run into a til that wants 40 or 50 more field tiles attached to it, but the rest of the game you get primarily water or forest tiles, or city tiles, or even meadows, and you can just never complete that quest. This can go on for game, after game, after game, with no end in sight.

Pure RNG like this just ruins games, and it's such an easy fix, that games like this wind up infuriating me, rather than providing enjoyment or relaxation. So if you care about the score, the leader boards, or you're a completionist, I'd advise steering clear of this one.

Casual puzzle game with hidden depths. Place tiles down on an a playing area to slowly construct a map, with periodic challenges set by the game to build chains of contiguous tile sets. The hexagonal pieces score points for corresponding with matching tiles (the egde of one tile with trees if placed adjoining another tile with trees scores points) with the objective being to construct something that is randomly generated but aesthetically pleasing. Ultimately, the game is very one dimensional -- they could have integrated systems to allow you more flexibility in tile placement while still retaining the core themes of the puzzle.  E.g. some sort of tile inventory, more flexibility on tile placement, something where the puzzle edges aren't all fixed and can be adjusted, allow you to cycle through tiles, etc.  Edit:  They could also add a system where it is easier to see when a tile placement is optimal, because if you're trying to be careful and strategically place your tiles, it's extremely tedious to find optimal placements when your board is large -- again some happy medium between doing it for you and being able to help filter information so it's not so tedious.

[h1]UPDATED REVIEW[/h1]
[h2]Dorfromantik – The Perfect Balance of Relaxation and Gentle Brain Exercise[/h2]

I’m back with an updated review because this game has continued to live rent-free in my head for years now. Dorfromantik remains, without question, one of the most genuinely relaxing games I’ve ever played on Steam—yet it somehow never slips into the “mindless clicking” category that so many cozy games fall into. It’s the rare title that can be both a warm blanket and a satisfying little puzzle at the same time.

[h3]Pure, Uncluttered Calm[/h3]
From the moment the soft piano starts and you place your first tile, the game whispers: “Slow down. Breathe. Nothing is chasing you.” The color palette is deliberately muted—soft greens, warm browns, gentle blues—no neon explosions, no flashing UI, no overwhelming particle effects. It’s visual chamomile tea. I’ve fallen asleep mid-session with the game still running (in a good way). I’ve played entire sessions while half-watching a sitcom or waiting in queue for a World of Warcraft raid. I’ve even used it as white-noise background while working because it demands so little yet gives so much gentle satisfaction.

There are now multiple modes (Creative, Classic, Hard, Custom, Monthly Challenges, and the incredible new Biomes updates), so whether you want to zen-out and build an endless perfect countryside or chase high scores like a little strategy gremlin, the game has you covered.

[h3]Surprisingly Deep Under the Simple Surface[/h3]
Don’t let the cute hex tiles fool you. When I really want to focus, I catch myself sitting forward in my chair, tongue half-out, calculating three moves ahead like it’s competitive chess. The flag system creates the most elegant “just one more tile” loop I’ve ever experienced. It’s a Pavlovian jackpot machine done right—every perfect placement gives you that delicious ding and a shower of points, and suddenly two hours are gone and you have a 15,000-point landscape you’re stupidly proud of.

[h3]It Runs on Literally Anything[/h3]
I’ve had Dorfromantik open at the same time as World of Warcraft, multiple Chrome tabs, Photoshop, and Spotify. My laptop didn’t even notice. If your computer can run Solitaire, it can run Dorfromantik in 4K at 60 fps. Ultimate “second monitor” or “laptop on the couch” game.

[h3]An Actually Educational Game That Doesn’t Feel Like Homework[/h3]
As a parent and someone who spent 11 years in PTA leadership (board member → auction chair → Ways & Means VP → President at two different schools), I cannot overstate how perfect this game is for developing young minds.

It quietly teaches:
[list]
[*]Basic counting and number sense (those flag quests are brilliant)
[*]Spatial reasoning and planning ahead
[*]Evaluating trade-offs and opportunity cost
[*]Patience and deliberation (no timer!)
[*]The joy of fixing mistakes (undo exists!)
[/list]

Kindergarteners who can count to 20 love it. Middle-schoolers get real practice in logic and resource management. My own teens still fire it up when they need something calm but engaging.

Honestly, Toukana could easily release a “Dorfromantik: School Edition” with lesson plans and class leaderboards—I would have fought tooth and nail to get it funded back in my PTA days.

[h3]Room for Growth (My Polite Wishlist)[/h3]
I love this game so much I just want a few small quality-of-life touches:
[list]
[*]Color palette options or seasonal themes (look at how URBO handles customizable colors—gorgeous and accessibility-friendly). Maybe even let us use the classic Windows/Unity color picker!
[*]An optional transparent/floating landscape view so we can admire our work from new angles with no distractions. Some bright colors can feel blinding, especially for older players or those with neurodiversity needs.
[*]Larger stack sizes or an “endless big build” mode (500–1000 tiles instead of the current limits)
[*]A more detailed scoring breakdown or in-game compendium. I’m a technical writer and I still don’t fully grasp every nuance of maximizing points—my math-minded husband got it instantly while I’m still experimenting years later. A proper “scoring academy” mode would be amazing.
[/list]

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
Dorfromantik is digital comfort food with a side of brain vitamins. It’s the game I recommend when someone says they’re stressed, when a parent wants something educational that doesn’t feel like spinach, or when a friend wants “cozy but not boring.” It’s the game I gift more than any other.

If you only buy one chill game this year, make it this one. And devs—if you ever do make that school edition, call me. My old PTA self still has connections.

Thank you, Toukana, for continuing to support and expand this little masterpiece. My landscapes (and my blood pressure) thank you.

At first glance you may mistake Dorfromantik as some sort of chill city builder, but it actually is a very not-chill rogue-like jigsaw puzzler. The twist over a normal jigsaw is that you are allowed to "misplace" the pieces, e.g. the terrain depicted on an edge of the hex piece doesn't have to match the neighboring pieces. However, only "perfect" placements (where all 6 edges have a matching neighbor) grant you an extra piece to play with, and stave off your inevitable death.  

And therein lies my central complaint of the game: Poor UI when it comes to perfect placements. As you play and build out the puzzle, the number of gaps in it will steadily increase as your surrounding terrain restricts appropriate placements. A single hex hole will only have 1 perfect matching piece after all, and there tens of thousands of terrain combinations (albeit some are more common than others). It's up to you to keep a mental list of all the combinations you need, vs what's currently in your hand. 

Fine. What's frustrating is that you'll eventually forced to place a non-perfect tile to achieve a mission or just survive for another piece placement, and these ruined tiles are nearly indistinguishable from the perfect ones. You may think you have the exact piece for a given opening, only to find out you don't get as many perfect placements as you originally thought (or any at all). In my final run I was so fed up with this trial-and-error, that I eventually just slammed down my pieces to end the game, even though I could have spent more time finding more optimal placements to continue playing and get a higher score.

If there was a clearer indicator in the UI for marking non-perfect tiles, that would greatly relieve the montony and stress of filling in the gaps, as the barrier for finding a sufficient neighboring piece is greatly reduced.

Other thoughts:
[list]
[*]Matching terrain can sometimes be difficult to tell due to irregularity in the representation (related to the problem above). But at the very least matching edges light up white when you're testing piece placement.
[*]The unlocks and general progression could be more enticing. They're all just reskins, that's it. The biomes are pretty cool as they change the palette of a region via a gradient, but the rest are features that are so small that you're not really going to notice them on a large map. And they tend to be samey anyway.
[*]A "session" or run takes quite a long time. My 18 hours recorded was only from two sessions after the tutorial. If you play cautiously and optimally you'll live longer, but also the gameplay becomes a slog as you have infinitely-increasing choices of where to place tiles.
[/list]

There was some fun to be had, but overall Dorfromantik is a stressful chore.

Nice, relaxing experience, but after a while it gets repetitive, boring and even tiny bit frustrating. So you quit faster than you would anticipate. While I've had quite a bit of fun playing the game, I couldn't stop thinking how this game could be better. I like its visual style, changing biomes, those little ships and trains cruising through the map. Dorfromantic has relaxing atmosphere and brings joy from looking at those unique lands you can build there. But also I was always a bit frustrated because I couldn't really find any special strategy that could help me survive longer in a game. At some point you just get not enough new tasks and start to slowly spend more tiles than you are awarded with. So often after each completed task you wait for new one to start and you waste tiles waiting for it to show up. So many times you have like 3 field tasks, 2 with water, and all the tiles with forrest/city/train tracks are just waste. New tiles are 100% randomized and you're never awarded with tiles that you need - which would be great idea - you can either get lucky (rarely, due to high number of possible combinations), wait for ages for 100% matching tile or simply use one that matches partially. It would be so cool to get a special tile as an award - one that can be placed in any place and will fit all surrounding tiles. Or if you could swap current tile with different one. No. Obviously carefully considering each move can prolong the game, but eventually you will run out of tiles anyway. And while this is intentioned - what I don't like is the fact that final result is mostly dependent on that random nature of the game. If you scored higher than usual - it's luck, not your newly invented strategy or smart decisions. So it quickly becomes boring, as I don't see any incentive to play again if it's just luck that can get me further than before. It's definately worth checking out, spending some time with it, but the novelty and discovery evaporate quite fast and you're left with a bit of disappointment.

In need of a really nice chill game? This game is for you.
It is not a game you would play end to end in a sitting. It is one you would play it over multiple sessions when you just want to relax. 
Gameplay
In the beginning, you start with a stack of random tiles. The idea is to match as many as you can together to expand your playing field. You will be challenged to keep the groups together to reap the rewards of more tiles for you stack to keep you playing further. The challenge then is do you close out a group, or risk it for further rewards. Also occasionally in game play, you will extend you tiles outwards and a greyed out special tile will appear approx 10 tiles from the current edge of your tiled map. If you build to these before your tile stack diminishes you will be given a new tile type.

What a fantastic game! You can pick it up just to relax and build a little Dorf (village) without worrying about perfection, or, when you're feeling analytical, strive to perfectly place every tile. There are a few different gameplay styles (encouraged by leveled achievements), and to truly master the game, you'll need to learn them all - or you'll run out of tiles and the game ends.

Perfection will result in lots of snaking connected fields, like farmlands or forests, while you hunt for the perfect tile to connect them. Placing those perfect pieces will earn additional tiles.

Caring less about perfection will have you focusing on completing quests, closing fields to get flags, and exploring to find bonus tiles. All will give you additional tiles.

Or, just play creative mode, where you have an endless supply of tiles, can skip tiles you don't like, and can generate perfect tiles to place in any spot.

Dorfromantik is barely a game... it's a console (Switch) game that should probably have been a mobile app.  It's selling point is that it's "casual" which means "incredibly shallow" in terms of gameplay.  The idea is that you create an idyllic village scene by placing various tiles around.  In an attempt to make some kind of game out of this objectiveless sandbox, there's a few limits to what you can and can't do... you can run out of tiles, and you've given what seem to be procedurally generated "quests" that just involve specific arrangements of tiles (like placing three tiles with "forest" edges together, how challenging).  You might as well play dominos with only one player, that's pretty much what we're dealing with here, only slightly more visually appealing.

From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard, there's some minor technical foibles that aren't helping.

The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the mid 2000s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.

Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies.  Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for.  These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers.  The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game.  Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone.

This looks and feels like a mobile app, but it doesn't seem to have made it to the app stores.  It's unclear why this was put on Steam/Nintendo Switch instead of the app stores it seems to have been designed for.  Maybe it was removed, maybe it was rejected by Apple and Google (they do have more rigorous quality standards than Valve does for Steam, after all).

Regardless, for all intents and purposes "Dorfromantik" might as well be a mobile app, it has the same limitations and dumbed down qualities.  It's impossible to recommend such a game to PC gamers.  We don't spend all this money building gaming rigs so we can pretend they're iPhones and play games that might as well be mobile apps.

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Another unusual point, the software contains stock/store assets and other packages, but the "developer" here hasn't credited the people who actually did the work for the software (a scarecrow asset, a number of Unity packages for UI and graphical effects and so on).  While this isn't necessarily against the license for the use of those assets, and it's not an unusual practice for this kind of code reuse, claiming the work of others as your own without crediting them (I checked the credits) is highly unethical.

All of that might be forgiven, but the pricing can't be.  Dorfromantik has the almost comically optimistic (if it wasn't so sad) price of $14 USD (plus TWO soundtrack DLC's for $6, making this games true cost a whopping $28 USD, near AAA pricing), for which you could easily get any number of recent AAA games.  The developer seems to genuinely think this is a better game and thus should cost more than the entire Mass Effect trilogy, The Witcher 3, Subnautica, Deep Rock Galactic, the list goes on.  I know, right?

You wanna talk about city building?  This costs more than Cities: Skylines!!!

This is also competing with over 9,000 free games available on Steam, many of them far better than this massively overpriced product.  Given the defects and quality issues with the software, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the questionable ethical nature of the developer and/or their associates (as outlined above), this is impossible to recommend.

Cosy yet addictive tile-based builder where the goal is simply to build a peaceful, bucolic landscape with as high a score as possible. 

You start with a fixed number of hexagonal tiles. Each tile can have some combination of grass, field, trees, houses, water or train track. You proceed to fit them together one-by-one, creating a landscape in the process. The size of your stack of tiles dictates how big a landscape you can build. Initially, not that big it would seem. However, you are given 'quests' as you proceed (build a forest with this many tress, a town with this many houses, a river this long etc), and as you complete these quests, you will gain more score and new tiles will be added to your stack allowing you to extend your landscape further. And this is really it. Once the stack is empty, it is over and you are left with a wonderful landscape and a high-score to chase. 

Simple but with just the right amount of engagement to make it fun but not so much to ever make it stressful. The art style is wonderful, the animations are relaxing, the music is chill. Runs can last from 30 mins to a couple of hours depending on well you are doing (but you can suspend at anytime and resume later). Also works wonderfully on Steamdeck. Highly recommended.

Steam told me I might like this game based on other games I've played. Steam was correct. Easy to pickup, tough to master.

Tiles have 6 sides and a handful of things that can go on a tile (as far as I can tell they're randomly generated) so it's up to you to find the best spot for whichever tile you're served until you're out. Two kinds of quests pop up as you play, either prompting you to link a certain amount of stuff together (like, link 10 trees together as an example), or having you close off what you've already made with the proper tile type. Completing quests gets you more tiles, more tiles gets you more points, and that's the loop.

My high score after 14 hours was about 14,000 - which felt like a herculean task and an impossible feat (I told my wife about it at dinner knowing she wouldn't care but I was THAT excited) - however I've seen numbers much higher and I'm actually quite low on the leader board. I don't believe there will be a day that will pass by without me playing at least one round.

TL;DR: Boring. Overpriced. Missed potential.

As I approached the end of the first level I just put tiles wherever, to finish quickly and get to the next level. [b]But there is no next level.[/b] It's the same one, over and over. There's some unlocks, but not enough to hold interest.

At this price point I expected a full game, but this feels like a basic tablet app, or the "casual mode" to a more fleshed-out game.

[h3]Potential[/h3]

Here's where this review gets long. I'm gonna talk about how much potential this game has, and share some ideas, because tbh that's what makes it so disappointing, how much more it could have been.

It could have:

- New levels with their own challenges, restrictions, reskinned tiles, and special tiles unique to that level or area. Eg, a city area with factory tiles instead of farm tiles and trams instead of trains; a beach biome with more water tiles and no farms; a fairy kingdom with oversized mushrooms and dragonfly flight routes instead of train tracks; a zoo world where you get bonus points for grouping birds/mammals/fish etc, or a theme park world where massive roller coasters replace train tracks... there's endless possibilities with this game's engine.

- More mechanics besides "put tree next to tree", eg. bonus points if you put a train station next to a village of >10 houses, or if you connect villages via railways. Atm you're incentivised to keep everything separate, [i]especially[/i] train tracks which heavily restrict their adjacent tiles.

- Having a choice between 2 tiles would be great. I actually enjoyed the game for a while when I was imagining how I would build the area, with its history and current culture -- but despite being simple, the system is too restrictive to give you any lasting sense of creative freedom. Having a choice of 2 tiles instead of 1 would give players a feeling of control and authorship, and let them steer the direction of their current world so each new one feels less repetitive, without disrupting the core score chasing mechanic too much. (Yes, there's a Creative Mode, but I need some restrictions and goals to keep me interested and motivated).

There's [i]just so much[/i] you could do with this game's concept, I could go on for ages with other ideas. I'm still gonna try another run, maybe try to unlock everything and see if my opinion changes, but as said, atm this feels like either an app store game or an early access build.

Dorfromantik is a very laid back game.  There isn't a story line or even an ultimate goal.  There are quests and points, but ultimately they don't matter.  The object of the game is to create a landscape however you want with the tiles that you're given.  Sure you can produce your own goals like try to play as long as possible by earning more tiles, or scoring the most points possible, or try to unlock all the tiles that the game has to offer, but at its core this game is a creative endeavor to do the best you can with what you have. 

I can see the appeal of the game if you want something just to pass the time with.  The game is pretty, and the music is soothing.  But ultimately, for me, the payoffs of the game just aren't enough for me to want to keep playing.  Honestly it does feel like a .99 game you might find on an app store under "relaxing sim/puzzler" but sim and puzzler is used rather loosely here.  There is no real simulation of people, no economy, no resource gathering beyond tiles.... It's a terrain generation game.  

 There are goals and quests....  Each tile is hexagonal, and each side has a "biome."  You can line up biomes together to make larger villages.  Some terrains have hard rules like railroads restrict the end of the tile to only railroads.  Some tiles come with quests where you might need to connect 100 forest together in a continuous chain/blob, others ask that you get precisely X houses no more or less.  Sometimes there is a tile in the distance that is highlighted that you're supposed to build and connect to.  You get extra points for placing a tile that perfectly matches the biome to its 6 neighbors. The tiles, as far as I can tell are randomly generated, so you have to work with what you have if you want to maximize your score.  Some events like getting a perfect match gives you more tiles, but you start off with 100 tiles.  When you run out of tiles, the game is over, and you start over, with anything you've unlocked from the previous playthroughs.  There really isn't any penalty for not matching biomes up well, nor failing to complete quest objectives.  

There are also a creative mode which lets you generate/change the tiles to whatever you want so you can paint the map to how you like, stripping all of the loose game mechanics entirely from the game.  So if it frustrates you that the game "ends" you can turn that off.  

I can see how this game can appeal to a certain kind of game player in a certain mood, but ultimately, this game is not for me.

So, I've been playing this off and on after work as a way to relax and get into something simple that helps me to relax; which, to be honest... is probably exactly what this was intended to be and I love it for that.

It's a puzzle game where you attempt to match up tiles with towns, fields, forests, rivers, and railroads in order to up your score. As you fulfill certain quests (like x amount of forest tiles strung together) you acquire more tiles. Line up a tile on all sides with the corresponding tiles? You get another tile. Eventually you WILL run out of tiles but the objective is to rack up your score while simultaneously keeping as many tiles as you can coming back to your stockpile therefore keeping you in the game longer and further increasing that overall score.

It's an easy-to-grasp (and jump into) premise but addictive and thoroughly enjoyable with endearing graphics, audio, and musical score. I highly recommend for those who like puzzle games at all and need something to relax to!

Dorfromantik is a peaceful building strategy and puzzle game where you create a beautiful and ever-growing village landscape by placing tiles. You can explore a variety of colorful biomes, discover and unlock new tiles and complete quests to fill your world with life! It's a relaxing game that allows you to immerse yourself in a quiet, peaceful world at any time and take a break from everyday life. It's perfect for those who enjoy games like Catan and other tile-based games.

In Dorfromantik, you start with a few tiles and have to build a landscape from hexagonal tiles. You can create pine forests, patchwork fields, meandering rivers, spidery train tracks, and higgledy-piggledy little red-brick towns.  You can choose from a variety of biomes and discover and unlock new tiles.  

The game has a relaxing soundtrack that helps you unwind while playing.  It's perfect for those who want to take a break from their busy lives and enjoy a peaceful game.

I liked the game initially, I really did. And I still do love the quaint visuals and how the world comes together as you build it. But soon I realised that the game didn't really have the depth to achieve any of the goals I wanted from it.

As a relaxing game it fails because your continent soon grows too big to manage effectively and then you'll find your game ending sooner than you'd like because you ran out of pieces. You have the ability to port your game over to sandbox mode, which is nice, but by default it automatically borks up the colours and alienates your world from you. And by removing all the quests and connection bonuses alongside the introduction of the tool that'll make pieces, it instantly gives you a sense of pointlessness. What I really wanted was to just have the regular game continue. Let me go into piece 'debt' and continue playing because I want to accomplish all those quests. Or just give me 10 extra pieces and a slap on the wrist and say I didn't get the gold medal. Whatever, at least I still have a reason to keep playing...

As an engaging puzzle game it also dropped off for me because I realised I was just doing a computer's job. It's not very difficult to constantly scan the exterior of your board and compare the next piece to all the available slots. I made myself a document containing data on all of the available placements on my board and what each side required. Then when I got a new piece I could just look at my spreadsheet and it'd tell me if this piece fills any of the holes I needed it to. If you could communicate the game data to an AI, it could play this game. Which means it's not really a game, nor a puzzle. It's just work.

Absolutely enchanting little puzzle that knows exactly what it wants to be and succeeds at being that with flourish and taste. It feels extremely board-gamey to me, landing in a lovely niche right between Carcasonne's tile placement mechanics and Calico's hex-based puzzle elements. Dorfromantik scratches just the right itches for me for a thinky tile game with nice aesthetics and casual vibes but deep strategy and a long - but not unlimited - lifespan per game.Progression is tied to score (as far as I can tell, having not played much and avoided spoilers for anything that might unlock down the line) and all game modes seem to be available from the outset, which means that [i]actually playing the game[/i] is the core gameplay loop rather than unlocking or achievement hunting. That, sadly, is an often overlooked element of design especially in games with roguelite progression systems, which this technically has, but Dorfromantik neatly sidesteps that by being a good, fun game first and allowing for progression as a nice cosmetic bonus for skilled play.All around excellent, and while I don't think it's probably for absolutely everybody I do think absolutely everybody should give it a try before deciding, because it's utterly wonderful.

Fantastic game for what it is: Casual, relaxing, a modicum of puzzle gameplay and the feeling of setting up an itty bitty diorama of a town.[hr][/hr]I usually put this game on when I have a migraine or need to sit through a work from home meeting that I don't have anything to contribute towards. It's absolutely perfect for that, and if it sounds enticing I highly recommend it.[hr][/hr]The gameplay consists of placing 6-sided tiles that randomly have different attributes on each side. You link up waterways, plains, houses, railways, forests, and blank areas together and get bonuses for connecting certain amounts of tiles or maximal amounts of tiles. There are certainly min-max strategies to getting high scores, but it's never interested me to take this game that seriously.[hr][/hr]The more connections you make successfully, the more tiles are added to the stack allowing you to build further. There are special tiles to unlock by hitting certain milestones or physically stretching your towns in one direction for a while, like a little scene of a deer in a clearing in a forest or a tugboat on a river.The vibes? Immaculate. Chill background music and adorable visuals give this game a really cozy charm. The game is exactly what it looks like, so you can easily tell if this game is for you or not.[hr][/hr]I love a game that has a clear vision for what it is and achieves on it. I wish more games were as well executed as this one is.

Oof. I really wanted to love this game- the art is so pretty and cute, and the tile placement thing seemed like such a neat twist on city builders, which I *love*. Before We Leave had a similar hex-based aesthetic, which I thought worked really well.

However, the game is extremely rigid, lacking even the flexibility of solitaire: you can't reshuffle your tiles or use anything other than your top tile. And you can only place tiles directly adjacent to other tiles, making it basically impossible to plan routes for things like rivers and railroads.

Overall, while I liked the aesthetic, I realized after about an hour and a half it was tedious and frustrating more than fun and relaxing.

The music fits the vibe really well and the controls are easy enough to pick up, and I'd give it a pass for how the different land types do not blend well at all, but the gameplay just isn't enjoyable.

This is a tile-placing game, not unlike Carcassonne, except that you're working with hexes rather than squares. Each quadrant of the hex can contain one of the following: meadow, forest, city, fields, water, or train track. Your goal is to place the tiles such that each biome forms continuous groups, which is both worth points and aesthetically pleasing. The tiles are weighted so that you don't usually end up with a chaotic mess on every tile; normally there'll be a "theme" to the tile - such as woodlands, which will generally have three or four of the corners filled with trees, maybe with some meadows or houses/city on the other sides. Water and train tracks are annoyances, since you can't mismatch tile borders like you can with anything else - if you want to cap off a train track, the tile you're placing must have a track ending on it; which makes it harder to complete perfect tiles around them.

You start off with 50ish tiles, and there's only two ways to earn more - completing missions, which requires you to expand one biome to either a minimum size, to an exact size, or to close out a zone so that it's fully enclosed by other biomes, each of which earns 5 tiles; or to place 'perfect' tiles - a tile that is surrounded on all sides by biomes that match that tile - which earns 1 new tile per perfect tile.

Anyway, the game is very relaxing with pleasant music and the graphics are beautiful. It's easy to pick up, but tough to reach ever higher high scores. There's a bunch of achievements, which unlock unique tiles or new map themes.

Considering this is the second copy of Dorfromantik I own, I other being on the Nintendo Switch, I do recommend it.

The game is straightforward, you place hexagonal tiles adjacent to others, build a scene and continue going until you run out of tiles to put down. They can be rotated to match sides for bonuses. Simple enough, but the hook is keeping your pile of tiles flowing.

While you can simply go for making a pretty scene, there is something satisfying about using lots of tiles to make a large diorama of your own design. Getting more tiles through completion of challenges, and perfect matches does not impede the relaxing style either.

As you play, you will unlock new tiles like a Beaver Dam, or Old Tree that can crop up in you your tiles for more variety. On top of that, you will unlock new themes like Enchanted or Fjords which you can toggle for extra appeal or flavor. They can all be on at the same time too, so you can get a whole cornucopia of variety if you so choose.

When your game ends, you can continue it in Creative Mode if you really liked how it turned out, or you can start a again. You can also save your maps that you might have taken a liking to, so even if you can't add anything else to it, you can show it off or just admire the boats, trains and nature sounds.

Overall my recommendation of Dorfromantik is Recommended.

Anyone who has played the board game Carcassonne will immediately recognize Dorfromantik as being based on the same sort of domino-like idea, but Dorfromantik is still significantly different. The main thing is that it's a solitaire game. It's also a little more elaborate and challenging due to the hexagonal tile design, and the game rules are somewhat customizable.

I'm not really a big player of these types of games and mostly got it because my niece and nephew like this sort of game (it's good for younger kids) but even I still think it's pretty good for what it is. In addition to the standard , quick, and hard modes, there is also a custom mode and a monthly challenge mode. The custom modes have a seed which ensures the same sequence of tiles for anyone who uses the seed, thus multiple people can compete to see who can get the highest score with the same tile sequence and restrictions. There's also a "creative" mode that, while I wouldn't call it a "true" creative mode, lets you just freely place tiles and delete/discard them to see what sort of map you can draw.

The UI is also simple and well designed, so any kid old enough to use a mouse will probably be able to figure it out pretty much immediately.

This game highlights the problem with Steam's yes or no system.
The game is painfully repetitive, and within two hours you've pretty much seen and done all there is to it. Yes, you might unlock a new tile that serves no purpose at some future point, or even an equally purposeless different colour scheme, but you can't work towards it because you have no idea what specific action beyond "Complete a quest" will do so.
Dorfromantic is essentially 6-sided dominoes with pictures instead of dots. It's easy enough for a 5 year old to pick up in 5 minutes, but the tactics and concentration can take MUCH longer to master.
The game's repetition is its greatest flaw, but much as I found it unimaginative to play, there's something beautiful and mesmerising about it. The gentle music and the cute little landscapes had me thinking about the game FAR more than I actually played it. They combine to create something truly blissful. That said, the concentration and tactics required to master it are not at all relaxing - in fact, it's more like a stressful exam. The game depends upon what appears to be random tiles, but that randomness can also be your downfall where, no matter how flawlessly you play, you may simply never receive the tiles you need to attain the high scores or unlock more cards or specials.
I would give this a 7 out of 10 if Steam had scores, and it's great to see Toukana continuing to enhance it. I WOULD buy this again, especially at just £7.69, but it's all about the atmosphere, not the game play.

You can connect trees and a house, but that is only when you have no other options.
Place them so ideal as possible and make the country you are creating as big as possible.
Some pieces have tasks attached, for example grow a town as big as 500 houses.
When you complete these tasks you receive extra pieces to place.
Go as far as possible until you have no more pieces to place.

This is easily one of my new favorite puzzle games. The replayability is really good and the challenge/achievement system is staggered in a way that ensures you don't get them all right away. Unlocking certain achievement paths happens in game when you reach certain preplaced tiles and finish the quests they give you. 

If you focus on unlocking all of the quest paths, you could probably unlock them all in under twenty hours. I, however, didn't know this was how you gain access to them, so I've racked up over 60 and haven't unlocked them all. I'm fine with this, but want to reassure you that, if you don't want to play this many hours before completing the game, you may not need to.

Aside from the achievements, the things I enjoy most about this game are the visuals, the turn-based play style, and the random selection of tiles ensuring replayability. Each game progresses slightly differently and you can take your time thinking about the right move before making it. As you unlock new biomes/seasons/skins in the game, the color and style gradient between the tiles gets more and more complex, leaving you with a really pleasing rainbow of a landscape. It's very nice to look at.

You ever played Carcassone, a boardgame about earning points by placing tiles? You know, you get a tile per turn, you gotta place it in ways that would help you secure more points. This is literally it but with hexagons and singleplayer, and more freeform - and because there's no other player competing for the meeple figurine placement, there's way more creativity involved to make a prettier landscape. Also, no meeple placement either.

This one can be both seriously challenging if you feel like going for high scores, and at same time super comforting, allowing you to create endearingly comforting rural landscapes with towns, railways and rivers. There's some unlocking to do trough achievements too, adding new visual bits, and those may take time but aren't that super tough to actually secure, since the game is really gripping so it's a matter of time till you unlock everything.

It looks like the Catan games; but now it is just a relaxed building mode. You have a stack of tiles. You need to connect the tiles with the same sides to score points and fulfil quests. [b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

TLDR: So peaceful, gentle, and relaxing. 

So I absolutely played Dorf Romantik incorrectly.
Now anyone who’s played a single minute of this game will be scratching their heads at that. “What? How did you manage that?!” I can hear them ask. 

Simply put: I played to win. That is not how the game is meant to be played, and DR did everything it could to show me that. Being the hard headed fool that I am, I didn’t listen until too late. 
Dorf Romantik is all about the journey. There is no winning, there is only going as far as you can, and trying to love what you’ve built along the way. 
The game has you placing tiles to design a map. Rotate them, match sides, spread out, uncover secret tiles, and complete quests to earn more tiles to place. That’s it. There is no story, there are no enemies, and there isn’t a higher purpose. It just… is. 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Peaceful in a way that most games simply aren’t. If you allow yourself to get lost in the ambiance, focus on the puzzle aspect, and just let the world go, you can be comfortable for a while. 
[*] The music, ambient noises, and artwork are lovely. They’re fitting and relaxing. 
[*] This has a one more tile, one more game, or one more hour type of addictive play.
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The tile unlock system is tied into the achievement unlock system, which is tied itself to quests given by the mystery tiles. This is VERY poorly explained in game, and the moment I realised I needed to achieve to unlock more tiles I began hammering the achievements, only to find they weren’t unlocking because I had to unlock the achievements options by completing mystery quests… this was so convoluted and unintuitive that I can only describe it as ‘frustrating’. 
[*] There is no way to turn off some of the unlocks. For example I really didn’t enjoy building in the ‘night’ zone. The grey made it hard to see, the tiles just weren’t as nice in my opinion, and I found the experience off-putting. That it keeps pushing itself into my game, forcing me to move away from promising developments or breaking my flow is not a pleasant experience. 
[*] This isn’t really a game, as I’ve come to expect. No levels or real measurable progress. While I very much love it, I can’t help but feel like it’s missing something. But that just feeds back into my opening statement, really. I’ve come with the wrong mind-set. Nothing makes this clearer than every achievement complete, and no maps saved. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] A title swapper. Allowing you to change out a rouge tile placed for necessity earlier with the perfect tile later (but not if it would undo a quest or take tiles away from you).
[*] A tile painter, allowing you to ‘paint’ a terrain type on a tile edge. 
[*] More variety. New quests (link areas, functional settlements, rotations challenge), new tiles (bridges? train stations? harbours?), but also controls to turn on and off the unlocked content that we like. 
[/list]

So, I got it because I heard good things and I like tile-laying games like Carcassonne, and it seemed like a nice tile puzzle game.

What I wasn't expecting was a deep strategy game. The core element of the game is the fact that if you get a perfect tile (6 matching sides), you get extra tiles to place. So while you're trying to complete objectives, you're also looking at perfect placements so you can keep upping your score.

Add to that the fact playing unlocks new tiles with new graphics that also affects the art style of the map, which is also lush.

So, yes, this is one of those deceptively challenging puzzle games that hits the right notes.

I'm nominating this for the Labor of Love Steam Award nomination, because you can feel that labor of love in this game.

This is my go-to game when I wanna do some chill gaming but still want something engaging and challenging. How "hard" it is really just depends on how interested you are on getting a high score, and then how motivated you are in trying to beat your high scores.  

The "deck" of tiles are finite meaning your game ends when you run out, but you gain more by completing tasks (connecting a certain number of a type of tile, such as a railroad, a river, a forest, a town, or a meadow), but your score is multiplied by how many matching sides you create EG you may be focusing on completing your 15 tile railroad but each tile also has 6 sides, and so ideally you want to complete your railroad task only/mostly by placing railroad tiles that also match as the other sides - you'll be torn between perfection and efficiency. This means you have to use some foresight when placing tiles so that you set yourself up for success and don't accidentally lock yourself into an area such that you can't complete a task IE by overlapping tasks that then require very specific tiles to complete both.  You want to diversify your placement a bit so that you have options and get the best score with each tile, but you also want to complete tasks so you can get more tiles.  It becomes incredibly satisfying when you not only keep your score climbing but you see your sprawling city stretching into different biomes, forming interesting patterns and such.

Sometimes I don't play for a couple months and might have been spending my time in more high intensity games, but there are days when I will start a Dorfromantik game and literally spend hours just on one game.

Dorfromantik is a well-designed puzzle game with unlimited replayability.

If you need something to quickly pick up and waste some time, Dorfromantik is a good choice for that. There are various modes (Classic, Quick, or Hard) that count towards achievement goals, but there are also Creative mode and Custom mode, which are just for fun.

The gameplay is rather simple at first glance but has some more depth once you try to get higher scores. The more different types of tiles there are, the more difficult the game gets, but that's not all, tiles can also have mixed types, so they become dead ends of sequentially placed types.

The nicest thing about Dorfromantik is its art style and how they dynamically change depending on the biome they are in or what other tile is next to it. Sounds are alright and the gamepad layout takes some time to get used to.

TL;DR - an incredibly relaxing game you will accidentally lose hours of your life in, but unfortunately, losing sometimes feels out of your control.

The game is structured around completing missions that are attached to hexagonal tiles you're issued, usually in the form of connecting a certain number of tiles of a given type together. When you complete a mission, you are given additional tiles, extending how long your game can run. As you get further along, the missions become harder, and so it becomes increasingly important to get perfect placements to earn more pieces instead. However, many of your runs will end waiting on the random number generator to give you the right tile to fill a space, and instead fighting to find a place for a complex railway intersection tile. Also, some details of the game that are important for having longer-running playthroughs are never told to you. For instance, you can only have so many active missions at once, and so in some cases, it's important to deliberately terminate missions that are too difficult to complete.

There are multiple game modes, including a custom game mode that lets you tailor the proportions of tile types for your playthrough to make it easier on yourself, or to create a challenge, which you can share with your friends. They also have a monthly mode, offering unique challenges to compete with others on.

Achievements are handled in a somewhat unique manner, in that you can only achieve them when they are one of your three assigned achievement missions for a playthrough, and you can't earn higher-ranked achievements at the same time as the lower-ranked ones. And don't expect to get them easily - towards the end, achievements require each to be your playthrough's central focus, and they can't be earned in the custom game mode. Each achievement you earn also unlocks a unique decorative tile that the game will sometimes issue instead of the basic version.

Dorfromantik is a decent pick-up-anytime puzzle game if you just want to chill for a moment. The concept is very straightforward: try to match the same sides as much as you can and make all the forests, fields, rivers, railroads, etc... as big/long as you can or until you reached the required number. A bit like the boardgame Carcassonne, though you are allowed to mismatch. You are limited on pieces, but you can earn more pieces by finishing goals and making multiple matches with a single piece, which could make the game go on endlessly.
The game has a lot of achievements, but you can't just go for them until you have unlocked being able to do them, which is randomly decided when connecting to a special piece. It gives the game a little bit of a challenge and a goal besides just going for the highest score.
Other than that, there's not much to do in this game besides trying to make patterns or such, so it is not for everyone and can get boring after just a few games if you want more of a challenge. Still, even at the full price, it is worth a go!

A casual, fun, "boundless" puzzle game.  

Starting from one placed tile you begin the game with a stack of 40 randomized hex tiles with each tile being a set of different environments.  By matching the edges to like sided edges you can create a grouping of that particular environment, influencing your placement score.  The game play mode offers a series of different tasks/quests to be unlocked through manipulation of the hex tiles, spinning them (or not in the case of one achievement) to get the best combinations to fulfill the objectives unlocking new tiles/achievement lines.  Through the finishing of these tasks you get additional tiles added to your queue and the game continues until you run out of tiles.

Additionally there is a free play mode where you can cycle through tiles at your leisure building your own idyllic landscape without being bound by the normal game play mechanics.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
This might be my favourite game of all 2021/2022. Never have I seen such a nice Early Access phase. Now with full release it is my favourite puzzle game to just play, relaxe and forgett about everything else.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You place hexagonal pieces on a playing field. The adjacent sides should be identical (field to field, forest to forest, etc.). New pieces are unlocked by perfect placements (all six sides placed correctly) and completion of quests (create X amount of fields, trees, etc.). The game ends when the part table is used up.

[h1]Artstyle / Music[/h1]
It looks simple, but everything fits together perfectly. On special parts, which are unlocked through quests, three-dimensional animals (deer, foxes, swans, ...) also move around.
The music is very realxing and chill.

[h1]Bugs[/h1]
It probably sounds crazy, but despite my 100+ hours in Early Access, I hardly experienced any bugs. I have never lost game saves or the like.

[h1]On a special Note[/h1]
The developers do a really awesome job supporting the game. There is a community Discord Server for general conversation, questions and also reporting bugs.

Dorfromantik is a nice casual puzzle game that is definitely worth giving a shot! The name means a romantic village/small town in German.

You basically get a new tile to place everytime and you have a fixed amount of tiles, which can be increased by completing some quests. This is the puzzle element in the game to make as big villages you can make without running out of tiles. You can actually make some really beautiful looking towns and countrysides! I really really like the art style and the multiple themes they have for every tile. One run im making a frozen winter-ish town and next game there is lush fields in pleasant spring. It's a very calming experience and something great that you want to play in between doing some other tasks or just stress relief. Whenever i play it i feel like im in some countryside just sitting on a ledge near a farm and watching the sunset, those feels.... And also it was developed by a small indie team from Berlin, so grats guys! Spiel ist sehr Gut! :)

Very relaxing, soothing game — but a real time-eater!

The game's simple enough — you get a random tile (which is any combination of grass, woods, water, train tracks, fields and houses) which you then place on the game board. How you place it matters, as it scores points (and points mean prizes in the form of extras tiles, etc), and you get the most points by joining and linking areas of the same type. You also get missions to complete (e.g. 10 linked tiles of water) that net you even more points, or even a special tile.

Easy.

Except it isn't, because the challenge is how to deal with unfavourable tile draws without the game board spiralling out of control into unchecked sprawl of useless tile placements... Thing is, drawing a card you can't use is slightly mitigated by the fact you get a slight preview of what's coming, but still, if you're trying to close out a fields mission and all you're drawing are trees, water and houses... sigh...

Strangely, this game manages to avoid being stressful, despite RNG unfairness, mostly due to the zen peacefulness of the tile placement, which at core is a soothing, repetitious act, and this is the game's real niche — it excels as a winding-down, de-stressing activity... But be careful when playing — a "quick half hour session" can easily become an hour or more, simply because you become enrapt in the tile placement, creating your beautiful landscapes...

This game is definitely worth your time (if you like this sort of thing), and as a further inducement there's a sandbox mode where you can create "perfect" worlds (you still get random tiles, but you can skip ones you don't want, and clone ones you do)

[h1]Hidden Complexity in a Simple Puzzle Game[/h1]

This seemingly simple puzzle game will surprise you with its intricate gameplay mechanics and vast array of randomized tiles. As you dive deeper into the game, you'll find yourself creating sprawling landscapes with interconnected systems of railroads, tiny villages, and giant forests. 

The "secret" tiles you unlock through in-game quests only add to the depth of the game. While the cute cardboard art style may deceive you, this game is a true menace of complexity that will keep your brain tickled for hours on end.

[b]The normal price may be a bit high, so it's worth waiting for a sale. But if you're a fan of brain teasers and enjoy a challenge, this game is definitely worth picking up.[/b]

The fastest way to explain Dorfromantik would probably be "Carcassone Solitaire" and, while reductive, it certainly gets the point across. In a slower way: Dorfromantik is a single-player tile placing game where the objective is literally score attack but, in a broader sense, is about perfect tile placement. A game of Dorfromantik, like Carcassone, ends when the number of tiles remaining is zero but. unlike Carcassone, you can replenish your tiles by completing - and I use the word rather loosely here- challenges. This tile says it wants to be connected to 37 tiles of wheat/field, so you better connect EXACTLY AND NO MORE THAN 37 tiles of wheat/field but this railroad says ay buddy how you doing can I get uh at least 50 railroad tracks and you go sure I got a the train equivalent of a Jormungandr over here lemme just slap you in there.

And that gives you 5 more tiles.

I mentioned perfect tile placement. When you surround all six sides of a tile with a perfect match, which you'll know when its perfect because that side will glow white as opposed to red, you get bonus points as well as another tile back. So, playing well enough can, theoretically, make the game never end.

If you like Carcassone, you'll like this. If you like light single player puzzle games, you'll like this.

I really HATE to give this game a Down Vote because it truly is quite a neat game.

The only reason I'm giving this a Down Vote is because of two things...

1. Four Excruciatingly painful Achievements to shoot for namely:

*Planner V
*Planner VI
*Puzzler V1
*Puzzler VII

2. RNG

These four Achievements, actually a lot of the Achievements for this game will require you to rely on a good Tile Roll because I've come really, really close to getting at least Puzzler VI with only five (tiles) remaining to complete the Achievement which is to plop down 200 consecutive tiles that do not have any incompatible edges, so that eant I've already plopped down 195 of said tiles with only thirty tiles on my stack remaining. "You still have Thirty tiles to use, so what's the problem then that's plenty enough", you might say. The problem is, this game's RNG loves to piss you off. In those thirty remaining tiles it'll most likely hand you four or less of what you actually need and the rest will be tiles that'll screw you over.

So yeah, fun and pretty chill game actually, until you try and shoot for the game's Achievements and the game's RNG decides to screw you over and be a huge pain.

I'm sure many others have said this, but it bears repeating. This game is so chill. So perfectly chill. I've only played about 10 hours, but it really feels like so much more, mainly because I play a little bit here and there and feel so relaxed after playing a round. It's a little like game therapy. Which is what the game designer's intention was, apparently. 

The graphics are clean and pretty, with an eye to detail when you zoom in, though it's not busy. There is some movement, windmills gently spinning, clouds drifting lazily, boats chugging in the water - this all adds to the peaceful ambiance. The color palette is warm and soothing.

The game play is fairly simple, reminding me of Carcassonne with some of its expansions added in. It is possible to really focus on strategy as far as where you place pieces. The level of commitment is entirely up to the player. Sometimes it's nice to place pieces just to make a cool design, but if one plays with an eye towards completing various goals that pop up with different pieces, the game begins to open up with unlockables that include new pieces and goals. Some of these goals include growing bigger forests, rivers or farmlands. There is a lot of luck involved in which pieces you'll draw from your pile next, which is sometimes frustrating if you are looking for a particular piece. For my play style, this isn't a big deal. I like completing the goals, but they are not my main focus, which is really just winding down from a hectic day.

This might not be the most played game in your library, but I guarantee it will chill you out, assuming that is what you're looking for. Of note, the developer is constantly updating the game with cool little additions. New tiles and themes have been released on a pretty steady basis. I find that whenever I fire it up, there are always new touches that surprise me and add to my enjoyment.

For me, a thumbs up is the perfect rating system. This is a 10/10 game, a 100/100, even! Shucks, I'd sell my middle child for this game. I think you'd have to be a monster to not enjoy this game on some level. Even a monster should enjoy it, methinks.

This is an amazing game. I play it for hours at a time while listening to my my favorite podcast (Small Town Murder). Even after 177 hours, I still find it as enjoyable as when I first purchased.

Pros:

Very aesthetic. Playing is a very calm experience, and it's very cool to scroll around to see the world you've built.

Completing quests is pretty rewarding, especially juggling quests that require you to "close" an area vs those that require you to connect a huge one.

Placing a tile in a "perfect" spot is very satisfying, especially if you get a chain going.

---

Cons:

The game wants you to be strategic, but seems to actively keep you from doing so. You can only see the next two tiles, AND those tiles are randomized, which means long-term strategy is heavily diminished in favor of RNG.

The core gameplay is simply taking the one tile that's available to place, spinning it around in a few spots that you need filled, then placing it somewhere random(ish) if it doesn't fit in any of those spots. Not super engaging.

The main challenge of the game is going for high scores, but a "high score run" takes at least two hours. You can save in-between runs, but I find myself always wanting to start a new run rather than continue an old one when I return to the game.

Dorfromantik is a puzzle game where you create an idyllic landscape using hex-tiles.

At the start of the game you are given a a number of tiles. The aim of the game is to match the corresponding sides of randomised tiles to score points and complete objectives. Completing these objectives awards you more tiles. For example, you may get a city tile that requires +50 houses. If you connect enough tiles and sides to have that number of houses, then you complete the 'quest'. This also applies to trees, rivers, train tracks and fields. 

My placing more and more tiles you end up creating a randomised landscape that's different each time. The game's simple graphics and gentle soundtrack, accompanied by the occasional moo from a cow or choo from a passing train, make the game a joy to watch unfurl. There is also a creative mode if you don't want to bother chasing points. I would put this game in the same category as Townscaper or Islands, it's very simple  but you can lose yourself for hours. 

A relaxing puzzle/city builder, Dorfromantik is well worth your time. Make a cup of tea and enjoy!

However, over enough time (2-3 "cities") I found myself getting bored. I suspect this is how the game it designed and it's a reasonably priced game so I am generally positive on it, but please be aware: 
1) The game never meaningfully changes. All mechanics are presented as-is early on, and the only changes I found were cosmetic (new looks for tiles). If you aren't having fun early, you won't later.
2) It can be frustrating because the tiles you get are random and sometimes really hard to place intelligently

With those being said, the game is extremely accessible, and relaxing. Some of the results can be really nice  looking and it's fun creating pretty landscapes.

Bigger isn't always better, and attempting to make every goal are two issues of mine that often led to me running out tiles early and prevented me from getting bigger scores.

I think if I had one main issue, it's that the need to connect the outlying quest tiles to unlock new goals and eventually tile types wasn't made very clear.  I kept wondering why I had clearly made a forest of 500+ trees on several occasions but didn't get the achievement until I re-read some stuff about the game.  I may have missed something somewhere in the tutorial, but it would be nice if this was made a bit more clear up front.

Tetris if it were a city builder.

Although I use the term "city builder," I feel like it needs clarification when describing this game.

The main attraction of city builders is the satisfaction one gets when creating something complex and/or beautiful. In most city builders, these creations are premeditated in that they stem from an idea of something you'd like to make. In Dorfromantik, your creations are almost entirely a byproduct of your pursuit for survival and high scores (unless you prefer Creative Mode). 

After finishing a long session in Dorfromantik, it's satisfying to look back at all you've done. Although you don't plan for the end result to look the way it does, there is a sort of natural beauty in the score/survival driven creation. There is a history to each board.

That being said, I think you'll be disappointed if you're not into high scores and your main motivation for buying this game is its city building and creation aspects. I like how the city building aspects manifest in this game, but I don't think they are all that engaging when separated from the scoring/survival aspects.

One more thing. It's easy to fall into a trance-like state while playing this game. That makes this game perfect for those moments when you want to engage your mind with little effort. If you've ever played a lot of Tetris, you know what I mean.

In short:
If you like Tetris & city builders, buy this game.
If you like Tetris & not city builders, buy this game anyway.
If you don't like Tetris, find God.

Be warned, this can be super-addictive. Getting that perfect tile to place just where I need it gives me a real dopamine rush, and it's hard to break that cycle (especially if you have ADHD) since you'll inevitably have created another several spots waiting for more perfect tiles. I've had to uninstall this game a few times so I can get things done or sleep! Lastly, if you're a completionist you'll still be challenged, as it's quite difficult to unlock new tiles. [b]Dorfromantik[/b] scratches that itch for a game I can pick up super easily to kill some time, but is still interesting enough that I can get hooked and end up playing for an hour or more.

It's a very relaxing game, and the gorgeous soundtrack is a perfect complement - I just wish it was on Spotify so I could carry on listening to it after I'm done playing :D

The core of Dorfromantik is to place a series of hexagonal tiles next to each other on a large grid. Connect the same types of tiles together for a few bonus points, place a tile that matches on all 6 sides and you'll score a 'perfect' and get a bonus tile. Sometimes you get 'quest' tiles which need to be connected to a large, connected string of a certain type of tile in order to get a big bonus pile of tiles.

This all seems simple in its premise, but once you get into it you realise there's much more strategy than first meets the eye. Firstly, you're always running out of tiles with every tile you place. If you reach 0 tiles, the game ends. You can make a profit on tiles by completing quests, but what if you get a quest that needs a large forest and you've not got any forests large enough? Or any forests with open edges to carry on adding to? Some quests also need a specific number of items - e.g. be connected to exactly 36 houses - if you only have one megacity in the middle of the map that you add all house tiles to, you'll fail that mission instantly.

Strategising and keeping your map in a certain way to prepare for as many missions as possible is the heart of the game, but it's not as tedious as it might sound. Paired with the beautiful soundtrack, calming visuals and cute atmosphere effects (birds, animals etc. roaming around on the tiles), you watch your map slowly come to life as you try to survive as long as possible without running out of tiles.

In short; Dorfromantik is a relaxing and easily-replayable 'pick up' puzzle game. It's easy to play but also easy to lose, so once you've learnt the basics you can begin strategising to get the high scores needed to unlock more and more of the overall meta quests.

Very nice and well crafted strategy game. It's extremely basic and easy to understand, but allows for depth through the multitude of choices the game gives you every single turn. Every tile is a important and impacts the future of the map you're on. The differing quest variants force you to think ahead and make often times, decisive decisions. Overall, really fun, relaxing, and simple while not sacrificing player agency or how skilled a player can get.

Honestly, I'm not sure I will play this very often, because the zen focus causes me to lose all track of time and far too much sleep. It's an experience very much like the last time I worked on a large jigsaw puzzle until I realized blearily it was 3am. My 15 hours was only 2 games, split into maybe 4 play sessions, as I can't help but search for the best place for every tile once I'm more than a hundred tiles in. If you have a hyper-focus problem like me, then consider yourself warned...

There's a fair bit of hidden depth to the gameplay beyond tile edge matching. You learn to pay attention to quests (which reward more tiles to your stack to continue playing if you, say, grow a forest enough or close off a set of fields), assess their relative attainability, and choose between incompatible options. And, after a couple of games, it's also become obvious that really getting to know the tile set's ins and outs would help - it's broad but not complete, so when you place that 3rd or 4th tile adjacent to an open hex, you might be creating a hole that is easy to fill or guaranteed to cost you points later. Some tiles with more than 2 types of terrain only have one handedness (clockwise or counter), for instance, and rivers and tracks in particular have pretty limited patterns of terrain on their other edges. Whether I actually want to spend the time to take notes (or study someone else's notes on the web) just to get better at this dangerous time suck of a game, I don't know yet :)
Finally, we can have..peace.

Dorfromantik is a great game. Very relaxing and easy to lose yourself in, it's hard to describe other than as a zen, "city builder" puzzle game. You just place randomized tiles on a board, optimizing for points if you're going for scores--or appearance if you want to lean more into the sandbox and worldbuilding aspects. As useless as "this game is like X" comparisons often are, I'd put this somewhere around Mini Metro/Motorways; but instead of a minimalist aesthetic mimicking subway lines or road maps respectively, Dorfromantik goes for a very cozy art style that's easy on the eyes and really drives home the relaxing vibe the whole game has. The ambient audio and gentle music also contribute strongly to that feeling.

Really, I've got nothing to complain about, major or minor. It's a wonderful game that's an absolute time sink--there's been sessions where a single game has gone on for well over an hour and I haven't even felt the time pass. It's definitely worth picking up if you're looking for something to relax and zone out with, and is an easy (strongly) Recommended from me.

If I had to describe it in one sentence, I’d say [i]Dorfromantik[/i] is essentially therapy bottled up and sold in a video game format. It’s fun and cozy, and I’d recommend it to anyone who’s a fan of city builders. Heck, I’d recommend it to Joe Blow down the street.

This is a low-stress game that I find myself thinking about even during periods when I’m not actively playing it (a testament to how unforgettable it is, which I wasn’t expecting), and a game I often itch to return to when I’m stressed out. If you’re looking for something pleasantly simple to escape to after a long day (or a long life), then this is the perfect candidate.

My only qualm is that it does get rather repetitive and somewhat boring after a few hours. The good thing is that it’s really easy to pick the game back up, even if you haven’t touched it in a few months.

All in all, I’d say it’s absolutely worth buying — the concept is great, and the quality is exceptional.

In the end, it becomes simply more frustrating than relaxing, and I wouldn't say that resulting landscapes look that good. Waters and forests are nice, railroads and cities are OK, but those yellow/purple fields are unbelievably ugly.
