I have played this game for 91 hours as of this review, and personally I have enjoyed it a lot. The game rewards patient and thinking, instead of spamming tiles. There is diversity in the two different categories of tiles, being water/train and house/tree/farm. The water train station is also a great piece. The game itself isn't bad, it just hasn't reached it fullest potential yet. 

What i mean by this is that there are plenty of additions the devs can make to the game. As of now there has not been a lot of updates. The big update with Quick Mode, Hard Mode, Creative Mode etc. was a great update adding a lot of new content. But that was mostly gamemodes and not features. I have some ideas I hope the devs will atleast take note of. 

1. Timelapse
A great way to showcase what you have accomplished after a you lose.

2. Different skins
Although I adore the style of this game, something they could add is different houses, different trains, etc. to make the world more customizable.

3. Hills
As I said before, the style of this game fits the premise, but it feels a bit flat. Whilst it doesnt need to be complicated, some hills would help out the feel of the world. The hills would also make for great for more diverse landscape, like if you were to have a water tile next to it, it would have a cliffside etc. 

4. More diversity
Although the houses work just fine. There are only a handful of different types of houses you get, the tower, watermill, windmill, and the other structure usually next to fields. What I would love to have is different buildings, for example a lighthouse if a full water-tile has one house on a side, or a trainstation where it would usually end, a lumberjacks house if a house is next to a large forest, a fishermans hut next to a little lake etc. This goes for boats and trains too, maybe have a slightly bigger boat, or a longer train. I truly think this would make the feel of this game even better. 

5. Scarecrow
Idk, the fields are kinda empty. just add some scarecrows

6. Boat and train view
I saw someone make a post on reddit of a mod they made where you could see the game from a boat or trains perspective. Personally i think this would be a fun way to take in what you have accomplished, kind of like the timelapse mode. 

I don't actually know if any devs are going to see this, but I truly hope so. I have loved playing the game ever since I got it, and will continue to play. But if any devs are reading this, please think about my suggestions.

Dorfromantik is like a digital zen garden for puzzle lovers. It's all about building a relaxing landscape with these cool hexagon tiles.  Think of it as Settlers of Catan's chill cousin –  super easy to learn, but way harder to master those perfect placements.  The best part? There's no way to lose, so you can just unwind and enjoy the flow.

Here's the thing: Dorfromantik can get a bit repetitive after a while. Placing hexagons to score points is fun, but it doesn't have a ton of variety.  Those fancy "biomes" they advertise? Honestly, they're just the same tiles with a different color coat. Not exactly groundbreaking.

Plus, for the price, I barely touched it.  5.8 hours in, and I already feel like I've seen most of what it has to offer. It's a great game for short bursts of relaxation, but I'm not sure it has the legs for a long-term commitment.

Overall: Dorfromantik is a calming puzzle experience with a unique concept. But if you're looking for a game with tons of depth and replayability, you might want to keep looking.  This one's more like a vacation for your brain – short, sweet, and relaxing, but maybe not a forever home.

Dorfromantik is a gorgeous and relaxing tile-placing game where you place tiles to build a map filled with plains, farmlands, forests, towns, rivers and railways. The music lulls you into a sense of timelessness, where nothing else really matters but placing the next tile. Do you want to complete challenges for extra points? Or create ‘perfect’ placements where all the edges match? Or just ignore all of that and go into creative mode to make /your/ perfect map?

Just looking at the waterfall of positive reviews on Steam is enough to encourage a try at this game. I personally found it well worth the investment of time and money, and still go back to it frequently. It’s not something I will play for hours every day, but that’s a good thing in my view - it scratches an itch that I didn’t realise was there, it lifts my mood, it sparks my creativity. At the same time, it lets me go and play other games and do other things, then come back and not suffer the annoying learning curve over and over. Once you know what you’re doing, then you know what you’re doing and can come and go as you please.

Admittedly, this  isn’t a game for everyone. I love it, my partner loves it, many people on Steam apparently love it. But this is not a city-builder, and I hesitate to call it a strategy game. As another Steam review commented, it’s more like hexagonal dominoes with a different skin. I find it incredibly relaxing and especially when I’m sick, this is a great game to just turn my brain off and focus on the pretties. When trying to get achievements or fulfill quests however, it can get annoying trying to make do with the random tiles you’re given. For some people, the annoyance can overrule the relaxation.

From a purely mechanical gameplay perspective, Dorfromantik is incredibly well made. I have yet to encounter any bugs, and Toukana Interactive are addressing those bugs which others have found. I have only played the PC version, not Switch, but I can see it being a really good portable game as it’s something you can pick up and put down as needed without worrying about losing out on anything. 

Toukana Interactive have yet to release other games onto Steam, but I for one am eagerly waiting for them to announce their next project.

it's a very cute game, but I couldn't find that much enjoyment:
1. Games tend be lost due to small mistakes accumulating, with limited options to solve your mistakes (without just unmaking tons of moves)
2. The game board feels unhappily lifeless. Only a couple of tiles creates any movement at all (train, boat...), but cities and other tiles have no activity at all going on. It would be so lovely to have little villagers interacting with the world you build. It would also be great if larger groupings of features took on new aesthetics - a large grouping of villages might become a city for example, build little walls and churches and so on
3. There is no difference between village, field and forest tiles. Mechanics-wise, they are interchangeable. Furthermore there is no reason to build tiles in proximity to each other: it's no problem if your fields are kilometres away from your villages, as no one seems to live there anyway
4. Quests are terribly repetitive
5. Most of the challenge come from balancing out "perfect tiles" and quests, which feels more like you are optimising some meta parameters rather than playing the game itself.

If there were some updates to introduce some life to the world, and create more interesting interactions between the feature, I'd absolutely play again and change the rating. Until then, it feels less like you are creating an amazing world and more like you are trying to avoid minor mistakes for ever

It's clearly meant to be a relaxing game... Unless you have OCD!

Simple enough game; 
~ Match the tiles given as best you can so that you can get more tiles in your tile stack by making perfect all round connections.. 
~ Complete the occasional quest tiles that may or may not show up in your tile stack in order to gain even more tiles in your stack, allowing you to progress further.. 
~ Tie in your tile sections after completing quests to gain additional tiles in your tile stack, IF the quest ask you to do such.
~ Branch out your tile set up as you progress to unlock secret tiles and quests on the map itself, so that again, you can get more tiles in your tile stack, as well as new tiles to work with..

This is all simple at first glance, and very relaxing with the music to match the atmosphere.. 
The problem comes with the tile stack, and the fact that you cannot shuffle it, or discard bad tiles that you cannot place at that moment... Combine that with the fact that the game loves giving you repeat tiles over and over and over again when you least need or expect it (Example: Needing to make a two 48 tiles lakes, and your stack keeps giving you twisting river tiles, houses, or forest tiles that each are a variations of the six sides from the previous ones)... The more you try to progress, the more you will realise that the entire game is just chance upon chance, upon more chance.. 

It's a chance that you will get tiles that match up perfectly, upon a chance that you will get diverse tiles, upon a chance that tiles will give you quests, upon a chance that you even placed the tiles provided in a way that forms the map you develop in a way that can branch out towards secondary bonus map objectives.. The game is legit 95% chance, 5% observation, 0% everything else. 

Again, there is no shuffling the stack of tiles, or discards, or even a tile save for later stack.. You are forced to place the tiles given.. And as such, you will quickly find out the hard way that more often than not, you will end up with a series of tiles that do not match up to anything you have going on, or are remotely useful towards the objectives in your game.. This becomes extremely frustrating when you branched out to a secret tile, unable to complete the objective to unlock it, because the last 20 tiles you were given to play with simply do no match up in any way that would complete the quest as required, OR EVEN any of the other numerous side quests you already have going, so that you can get more tiles to play chance with. And if you ruin that section by forcing a mismatch connection, you won't be able to collect tiles for perfect placement, let alone set yourself up for future expansion of that quest type (Which the game does throw you from time to time). 

You end up each game frustrated that you did not get the tiles needed to earn more tiles, to complete objectives that would earn you more tiles to complete other objectives... It's a self serving circle jerk of constantly needing the right tiles to earn more tiles to play, and not getting them.

This may just be my OCD's outlook on the game.. But yeah.. Relaxing to start a game.. Frustrating as it "develops", and inevitably ends when you just got attached to your map, and how it looks.. -.-

[h1] What is this game? [/h1]
[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is a tile-laying city-builder with a heavy board game feel. The previews and screenshots showcase the game-play loop perfectly, and everything is exactly what you expect. The micro-worlds you build as you play are beautiful, and this game excels in creating a cozy and relaxing atmosphere. There's no turn timer, and you can always undo your last move if you make a mistake, so it's stress-free and very forgiving.

A typical single session lasts an hour or two, with support to save and load whenever. You can also have multiple sessions saved at once, which is nice.

[h1] Setting Expectations for Strategy/Puzzle Enthusiasts [/h1]
While classified as a puzzle game, there are no actual puzzles with specific solutions. There are achievements to nudge you toward several different play styles, but you're ultimately free to do whatever you'd like, with the overall goal to get the highest possible score.

There are minor strategy elements, mostly around matching the edges of adjacent tiles for extra bonus points, but it's somewhat luck dependent and may feel a bit simplistic for those looking for something heavier or more involved. [i]Dorfromantik[/i] does offer several additional game modes, including a monthly challenge mode to keep things fresh and a "hard" mode, but it may still not be enough for a more hardcore audience.

Shifting gears completely, the developer included a "creative" mode for those interested; a great and thoughtful addition that provides that much more variety. Completing achievements also unlocks additional cosmetic options and tiles, so there's a small incentive to replay the game and complete these challenges.

[h1] My Personal Opinion (Recommendation Reflects This) [/h1]
I was looking for a light game to play between heavier sessions, and [i]Dorfromantik[/i] delivered brilliantly. What this game truly nails is a calming and [u]convenient[/u] player experience: something you can pick up and play for a little, drop and come back to later very easily.

This game probably won't satisfy a true puzzle-solving/brainteaser itch (check out [i]The Witness[/i], [i]The Talos Principle[/i] or [i]Baba is You[/i] for that), but there's just enough complexity to keep the brain stimulated while maintaining a casual and easy-going atmosphere. At $14 full price, it's not hard to recommend for those seeking this type of game.

[b]Dorfromantik[/b] is a relaxing tile-placement / puzzle game, where you place down hexagonal tiles to earn points and create beautiful landscapes, similar to games like "Islanders".
It is not a deep game, mind you. Aside from rotating and placing down tiles, there´s not much more to do. This is not a bad thing, however. The game was meant to have casual-friendly gameplay with just enough depth to keep the ones interested, that want a bit more strategy. But don´t expect difficult puzzles - you will get disappointed.

[h1]Pro:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Beautiful art; the dev´s found the perfect balance between unique, simpistic and beautiful.
    [*]Good sound design; the sounds used are, like the art, both simplistic and fitting.
    [*]RNG; the RNG makes every map look a bit different from the last one and forces you to adapt to the random tiles you´re given, which gives the game just enough depth.
    [*]Quests & Challenges; Quests and Challenges are yet another small addition to the game to give a bit more depth. If more than one quest is active it forces you to decide, which of those you want to finish first. Challenges are used to give you, well challenges and reward you with new tile-skins when completed.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*](bad) RNG; it can be frustating at times, when you get the n-th 1-wheat-tile instead of a much needed forest-tile to complete a corresponding forest-quest.
[/list]

I love this game.  There's a challenging puzzle mode, and I have gone quite a ways in it, but my current favorite is creative mode, where I can just place tiles to my heart's content.  It has different color schemes for different biomes and there have been seasonal terrain tiles in winter vs. summer, as well.  I love the little train engines and boats that travel the rails and waterways.  I really like the roundhouses where both boats and trains can turn around and set off on different paths.  After you've played the puzzle mode long enough you will unlock a wide variety of different terrain tiles, with different colored roundhouses, windmills, waterwheels, and deer meadows.  I like the quiet ambient sound effects, gentle and relaxing, and the music is cheerful and relaxing, too.  I especially like a couple features recently added: the ability to undo a move in puzzle mode,  and the ability to create a tile to fit a random space in creative mode.  Sometimes this leads to odd tiles like a waterway with three rail ends, but it fits.  I appreciate the way puzzle mode allows you to continue for a long time, if you manage to place tiles in ways that earn you more tiles, and it has bonus tiles spaced some distance away, so you can aim to reach them.  I like the windmills' movement and the flocks of birds that fly over.  Just a really good game, fun for puzzling and also fun for just relaxing and placing tiles.

I first played a pre-beta beta version of Dorfromantik as an add-on to something else I had gotten once and thought: "Hey, this is a super charming game, hope this goes somewhere". I then proceeded to pick up the full version of this when it released, opened it up, and the next time I looked up from the screen, the sun had gone down and 5 hours had passed. 
And so, Dorfromantik is an utterly captivating puzzle game in which you build your own little world with randomized tiles that you try to fit together to make cohesive areas (this includes fields, grassland, forests, railways, and rivery/water areas). The visuals are stunning and just so, so charming. It truly awakens that country-side feeling in you. What I especially liked was discovering that there are in fact skins you unlock upon completing challenges. Embrace the deer. Accept the deer into your heart. 
Add on the fact you actually work towards a point-highscore and you've got yourself an addictive little gem of a game. 
My one single gripe with the game is that the UI was a little bit complex to figure out, and that you kind of have to click around a bit to figure out how to change game modes. 
But in conclusion, if you want to have a relaxing, chill time just building a little aesthetic village and just throw lots of lakes and forests in there, this is your game. If you want a game where you do some strategizing in order to maximize a highscore or complete some fun challenges and watch numbers tick up, this is also the game for you. 
TLDR; place tiles to build an aesthetic village or have an actual think about what tiles you're placing, get swept up in incredibly charming and cute visuals, have fun. Final Score: 9.5/10 (Shoutout to the deer tile. Love that tile.)

After my first my hour of play, I would have described this game as a lovely little time-waster. After many more hours of play, it has grown to be one of my current favorite games.  The reason for this is that it is an elegant blend of engaging gameplay, simple mechanics, lovely visuals and replayability.  

While the gameplay is not complex, each tile placement requires you to be thoughtful, and be thinking about what combos and tasks you're building toward.  You get to see your current tile, the next tile and a tease of the following tiles, meaning you will be faced with difficult decisions about placement. For instance should I make a sub-optimal placement now to finish a current "quest", or do I hold out of the perfect tile later?  You can move at your own pace, but there is a "clock" of sorts in that you have a limited number of available tiles, which you can add to by completing combos and quests (specific goals set by the game, usually focused on placing a certain number of tile-types in chains).  Learning how to balance your near and long-term goals, while keeping one eye on the number of tiles you have, and will likely have as you complete goals is where the challenge comes in.  

The game also feeds that need in all of us for tangible rewards by letting you unlock new tiles and themes as you progress, which keeps the game engaging and adds additional variety.  In some ways, this makes it feel a bit like a very casual deck builder.

If you're like me and occasionally just want to build a cute little world, you can save any world you've built and continue it in a sandbox mode, without the pressure of a limited tile supply.

I don't have an major criticisms, though there are some quality of life improvements which would be welcome. Specifically, the soundtrack is very nice and suits the game well, however, it is limited to just a few tracks, which repeat often.  More tracks would be great.  In addition, unless I am just a fool and haven't figured it out yet, there is no way to abort a session.  If you quit, when you come back, your same session is waiting for you.  There are good reasons why you might want to restart, for instance if you're coming back to a game after a few days and have lost the thread of that session.  A way to reset would be good.

Overall then, I highly recommend this for anyone who enjoys world-building games, without the world-management and tile placement games.  It really scratches an itch I did not know I had!

This game seems to get recommended by Steam along with other "relaxing" and atmospheric games because it looks like it on the surface, but underneath it is a somewhat complex puzzle game.

You can still enjoy this game as a relaxing landscape creator, but if you decided to aim for high scores with the puzzle side of the game, it becomes mentally exhausting and fun puzzle game that can be replayed many times. This seems to be why we see some player reviews with playtime in the hundreds instead of few hours like other games of similar genre. So, if playtime and replay-value is a concern for you, this could satisfy that.

To explain the puzzle mechanic In short, the hexagonal pieces have a certain "sides", those being water, field, forest, town, rail, and farms. A piece can have any combination of types of sides, for example one can have 3 sides of forest and 3 sides of fields in a mix of order.

As you lay down the pieces, you must try to join the adjacent pieces with the same type of sides touching. This way you end up connecting things like the fields and forests into larger ones or create a lengthy river. And the game awards you points and extra pieces if you fit a piece with all 6 sixes touching the same type of zones.

The game also gives you "quests" to build a forest, town, rail, or river of certain sizes with points and more cards as a bonus.

You keep expanding your map until you run out of pieces at hand. If you continue to succeed in quests and lay down "perfect" tiles that meet conditions for all 6 sides, you get more pieces, or else you run out and the game is over.

All in all, much like other games that look at play similarly, this game has great art-style and relaxing music. If you want another relaxing game you play for a short few minutes at a time, this will do. Again, if you are looking for a challenging puzzle game, this can also meet that need.

I have watched four people, including myself, get frustrated and/or have their day ruined by this relaxing, chill, puzzle game. And it is a great little addictive puzzle game, for sure. But why do I despise it? Well all four of us made the exact same mistake of trying to earn achievements. This game was specifically designed to infuriate the player by not letting them earn achievements until they have "unlocked" them in game. So you can achieve the necessary steps to get an achievement, but not be rewarded with the achievement because you didn't progress to a point in the game where the developer is ready to allow you to start going for the achievement. Genuinely unforgivable game design.

Imagine spending an hour doing a task expecting a reward and not getting it. You start to doubt yourself and your intelligence. Am I wrong? Is this not what I'm supposed to do? That's what you ask yourself, but you don't get an answer until you scroll through the forums and find 1000 other people with the same problem. You have to unlock the ability to earn achievements. Wow. But surely the game tells you that, right? I don't know, maybe it does. But if it does it was looked over by all four of us. This system needs to be addressed in an upcoming patch for me to recommend this game.

It is a good game, it's a great puzzler beyond this issue. My only other gripe is that the play sessions tend to be too long. I'd prefer each level to be 15-30 minutes, but a high score run can take 90 mins plus. So if you're nearing the end and don't think you're going to beat your high score, it feels like a lot more time wasted than if it was only a 25 minute per round game. If you're looking for a city themed, object placement, puzzle game, definitely check out ISLANDERS. It is a lot like Dorf only without these issues.

Dorfromantik is a surprisingly good city builder/puzzle game. I did not expect to put in this much time, but its extremely smart about giving players different types of goals that require different approaches in order to reach them. It's a great game for podcasts, relaxing, or winding down after playing a competitive or difficult game.

You can expect to lay down six-sided tiles that contain different combinations of tile types which include, train tracks, water, plains, fields, homes, and trees. How you arrange them results in higher scores when successfully matching tile types or when completing quests which might, for example, ask you to create a forest with at least X amount or exactly X amount. Successful quests and perfect tiles (a match on all side sides) reward you with more tiles for your stack so that you can keep expanding and exploring.

Exploring for hidden special tiles and completing achievements results in tile unlocks that add to the visual variety such as beaver dam water tiles or a boar in the center of a forest tile. General themes that change the color palette and/or change the season can be unlocked as well. How you complete some of the achievements keep the game fresh via encouraging big forests, no mismatched tiles, no rotating tiles (insanity), and more. It's why I keep playing this game that punches above its weight class. Dorfromatik keeps me incentivized and stimulated with the different challenges.

As for modes, you can expect the normal Classic Mode that you play for the score and quests. There's no time limit; you just need to worry about balancing quests with expansion so that you don't run out of tiles. Every Classic game can be converted into a Creative one where you can lay tiles down and focus on the aesthetics instead.

Just keep in mind that the game has a much heavier emphasis on the puzzle aspect and the city building accidentally happens as you're playing. You end up with some really interesting layouts on some runs. I'd say give it a try and create your romanticized village today!

I love this game. 

Gameplay is surprisingly simple - you've got a pile of tiles with landscape bits on them. You build a landscape out of these tiles. For every tile you perfectly surround with matching borders to other tiles, you get a tile back. You get a bunch of tiles for doing quest objectives (making a farmland of a certain size, for example) or by closing off groups of tiles (indicated by little flags which you may earn from doing said quest objectives).

Correct and perfect play can lead to huge scores and huge maps. This tickles my brain in just the right way - I play it in the mornings, mostly, to see if my medication is working correctly, and this game helps a lot with that.

The devs have put a lot of love into this game since it was initially put on Steam, too. The release version has a Creative mode, where you can just make pretty landscape without pressure, ways to change your challenge with Hard mode, and a Quick mode for playing with a set maximum amount of tiles, challenging you to get a lot of points with only a few moves. It even has 'biomes', meaning groups of tiles may take on a themed look to bring variety to your maps. All of this at a fair price point - I am frugal and dislike spending more money on a game than it's worth, but even without a sale this game is absolutely worth it.

If you think you'd enjoy a game where you make a pretty landscape out of tiles, this game is worth your money. If you don't think that, it is also worth your money, because you're wrong; you'll love it. 

Buy it. Buy it now.

It's a strategy game with a city-builder theme. It's all very simplified and zen, but that doesn't mean it is brainless. It's actually a pretty solid strategy game.

You have to work with a randomly-sorted deck of hexagonal tiles. each side being of a particular type, whether that be city, forest, grassland, river/water, or train. Tiles will almost always have multiple terrain types, so placement and direction of the tile become key. There are also combos, so the more sides you correctly type-match in one tile placement, the higher the number of points. There are also bonus points up for grabs by completing missions like "place 35+ tree tiles" or "have 7 train tracks in a line." It's all very intuitive and with minimal amounts of text, which helps the game achieve the "zen" feeling. The game will go on forever until you run out of tiles, which can be extended by completing missions or creating large-enough tile combos. At the end of each game, the player gets a score that's auto-saved and compared to their high score. There are also opportunities to take screenshots of the completed map, and an available free-play mode.

The graphics are quite beautiful in their charming simplicity, which helps create the feeling of calm. The music is understated, but pleasant and chill enough. If I had to name a weak point, it's that the music is kind of forgettable, being more ambient than anything else. However, the sound design overall is quite good. Placing tiles feels tactile, the positive sound effects are cheery, and the negative sounds are never discouraging. The UI and UX are also fine enough. It works well for this game, even if it might not have as much character as everything else. It's hard to complain about functional and clear simplicity. 

Overall would recommend for a relaxing time that isn't brainless, especially if you love puzzle, strategy, or city builder games. (I fall into the 3rd category.)

DorfRomantik is a deceptively easy and straightforward puzzle game you play against yourself: can you get a higher score this time than you did last time? Can you manage a certain achievement you're aiming for? Can you play well enough to build the world you have envisioned?  

(And even if you got that achievement last time... muhahaha... good luck sucker on doing *that* again.)

You start with a limited number of tiles and will try to lay them in ways to optimise your score and fulfil quests that pop up along the way. If you manage certain things you'll be rewarded with more tiles and the game continues until you've run out. 

At one end of the scale, with the game in creative mode, you can just paint happy little pictures and create your perfect community of farms, quaint villages, sprawling cities, vast forests, and windswept meadows. You'll have endless tiles and undo actions to create your masterpiece. The art and music is lovely too.

OR... if you enjoy stress.... 

- you can try to balance conflicting quests for the highest possible score (This wants more, that wants less, oops, broke it. Make it bigger? Close it off? Now? Both? OMG what am I going to doooo!)

- set yourself against achievements that are difficult and focused and will require strategy and experience in the game.

- face the fact that there is an element of chance to the game, and you'll have to pay extreme attention to reach the higher scores and harder achievements and fail a lot anyway.

If you find the game too easy or too difficult (I've managed both), no worries, create your own rules and balances and face the exact challenge *you* want to face.

As you reach certain way points in the game you'll unlock new tiles and new biomes.

I tend to play "for just a few minutes" in the evening as a perfect "relaxing wind down" game. Then find that 2-3 hours later I'm up too late, squinting at the monitor, hunched over my keyboard hunting down that "perfect" placement of tiles that makes the points fly into happy places.  Just... one more... tile...

This game is like an advanced form of dominoes.  You match tile edges to other tiles to build your puzzle.  It reminds me of an old tile game called River, Roads, and Rails from my childhood.  This is more advanced in the sense that you are using hexes instead of squares, and that some of the edges have special rules (example - your rivers have to lead somewhere).  You have to match and chain hexes in order to complete quests and get more hexes in your deck.  Unless playing 'creative mode' the game ends when the deck expires.

It is a good game.  I like all the different modes and the ability to use a custom mode.  I am a big fan of being able to play games the way that fits you best.  It is super relaxing, like early levels of tetris zoning-out.  I think some of the cards appear too often.  Example: the five edge rails are hard to place and IMO show up way too often, I would think they should be a once a game thing if even that.  I also would like an option to leave quests on in creative because even though gaining more tiles is meaningless in that mode, it does help give some direction to the 'build'.

I am going to give this "overwhelmingly positively" rated game a big thumbs-down. Let me explain and start with the good:

+ The design is pretty
+ The music creates a pleasant atmosphere.

And now onto the bad:

- Insanely repetitive
- No content at all

I normally rather enjoy logic games, but this is just dumb. There is literally a single mechanic in the entire game: place a tile so its borders match the neighbouring tiles. There are also "quests" which require you to place a given numer of tiles of one type so they form a contiguous area.

[b]THAT IS IT. You just place tiles to get points and more tiles, NOTHING ELSE EVER HAPPENS.[/b]

I played for two hours hoping for... something - I don't know, towns developing an economy based on rail connections I made, or perhaps population wondering on the map and increasing based on the quality of fields... anything at all. But there is no content in this game. No economy, no population. Just tiles.

Final thoughts:
I deeply regret buying this game, even though it wasn't terribly expensive. Only consider it if you are in the market for a smartphone-timewaster kind of game but running on a PC. Or if you just [i]DESPERATELY[/i] love tiles.

Dorfromantik is a game that will suck you in with the simple task of matching hexagonal tiles, and before you know it you've invested three hours just building your little rural community. With no time limits or pressure on you to fulfill the tasks, the game is very relaxing and a nice way to spend some free time. You can leave a session for a while, come back another day, and carry on with no consequence. Different modes will appeal to different types of players, from those that seek to optimize to the highest possible scores on leader boards, to those who seek custom challenges, or those that just want to see their town grow, there's something for everyone here.

Very laid-back city builder.  It has more in common with a board game than a big daunting sim, with just enough complexity to be engaging but not overwhelm you with systems

You're dealt random tiles to place on a hexagonal grid, with each tile containing terrain that you can link together, like trees, houses, train tracks, etc. The focus is on short-term goals rather than something like balancing supply and demand or planning traffic flow. Sessions last until you run out of tiles. My sessions are typically an hour or so

It becomes a light puzzle game when you get a tile with a "quest" attached to it. The quests net you big points for linking a specified number of a terrain-type together, like a 25-house village or 200+ tree forest. Since tiles can have different resources on each side, this creates some decision-making for how to best arrange them when you have multiple quests in play and try to keep layouts open enough to accommodate tiles you might get in the future, especially if you also want things to look cohesive and make sense (not required for points, just for fashion)

[h1]A Charming and Creative City-Building Gem[/h1]

[b]Dorfromantik is a delightful and visually stunning city-building game that captivates players with its charm and engaging gameplay. While it might not be an entirely laid-back experience, it cleverly balances relaxation with strategic thinking, making it a thoroughly enjoyable journey.

One of the standout features is the variety of modes available. The ability to manually customize tile generation in different modes adds a layer of personalization, allowing players to tailor the game rules to their preferences. Monthly activities bring a competitive edge, offering a chance to compete with others and showcase your creativity.

The creative mode is a highlight, providing a blank canvas where you can generate any tile and construct your dream world. It's a testament to the game's versatility and the freedom it grants players to shape their unique landscapes.

Dorfromantik goes beyond the typical city-building experience by integrating Steam achievements seamlessly into the game. Completing in-game challenges not only unlocks in-game accomplishments but also mirrors as achievements on Steam. These tasks serve as dynamic objectives, prompting players to adapt their strategies—whether it's creating expansive waterways, intricate railway networks, or dense forests.

I highly recommend Dorfromantik to anyone seeking a refreshing and engaging city-building game. Kudos to the developers for crafting such an enjoyable experience that seamlessly blends creativity with strategy. Don't miss out on this gem![/b]

This feels a lot like the board game Carcassonne, but for one player and that's a good thing :)
With the people I play Carcassonne with, we often give tips to one another without helping too much and this is very similar to that style of playing.

Also: There is no real goal apart from solving tasks(ie. "Build a village with 20 houses" or "Create a forest with at least 5 tiles") which will give you more tiles to play, making your play last longer(and eventually give you a higher score)..    This (kind of) open-ended mechanism makes it easy to pick up the game for half an hour and not worry too much about making progress, there is no real way of "losing" the game, it's a very nice way to spend time.

I recommend this in general, because it does deliver that chilled out, laid back game experience that is being touted.

But that is not at all what the game is. It is actually a highly mentally stressful game that requires planning, memory, and precision to get past the early phase; you need to keep a vast and every-growing tree in your mind so you can know where to place tiles optimally. 

In other words, there is a fun and relaxing way to play the game and that is to simply find a nice spot for each new tile, such that your forests, towns, fields, rivers, and rail grow large or to the specific size required by the random quests that you uncover. 

But the game is balanced such that this type of gameplay only gets you so far, for me its 7000-10000 points. After a fairly short period of repeat gaming where you always top off at that certain point, it suddenly becomes very boring because you realize you are just playing the same game over and over. 

To REALLY play you need to do something entirely mentally different: you need to place tiles with an eye towards making "perfect" placements, where a tile winds up with each side touching and edge of the same type on it's neighbor. This is highly mentally taxing, as you need to keep a network of possibilities in your mind as you go. This is the opposite of the chill, relaxed gameplay that most people are coming to this game for. I totally get that there are people who are good at this type of braining, and people who love this type of challenge. The thing is, the game is really for them. If you don't like playing 5D chess, then you are likely to get quite bored with the early game phase and drop it after a few hours.

Dorfromantik, German for “romanticized town”, is a serene, relaxing tile placement game developed by Toukana Interactive. It follows on from their similarly causal previous games, like Townscaper.

In Dorfromantik, the player draws hexagonal tiles from a stack and places them adjacent to already played tiles. Each tile edge has a terrain type, such as buildings, forest, fields or plains. You gain points by aligning edges with identical terrain. Points track your progress and can add more tiles to the bottom of the stack. The game ends when the tile stack is exhausted, so the more points you accumulate, the longer you can play.

Besides passing the time and sense pleasure, Dorfromantik‘s enjoyment comes from having just enough of a challenge. Initially, the challenge comes from the randomized stack of tiles. Tiles with train tracks and water further restrict tile placement. Later, some tiles may give quests that give additional points for runs of identical terrain. Ghost tiles may appear that, when built on, reveal unique tiles with extra bonuses. 

Long term replayability comes from achievements, such as tracking tiles placed of each type or the longest continuous train tracks, and different play modes, such as “creative” with no stack limit.

Two design choices make Dorfromantik stand out. The first is its uplifting, relaxing visuals and sound. The graphics are stylized and colours oversaturated, featuring picturesque country towns, pine forests and golden wheat fields. You get subtle animations like birds flying overhead or boats steaming down gently flowing rivers as you build out the landscape. The soundtrack is also perfect, with soft dynamics in major keys. You cannot help but smile during the first few games.

The second design choice is the total lack of pressure. There are no time limits, no need to pause the game, and you can switch to another game or start a new one without losing progress. You can undo moves, but mistakes are hard to pin down with the randomized tile order and not individually costly. There is no AI or human opponent to outsmart you. You will not have moments where you want to punch the monitor.

Unfortunately, you see most of the game’s mechanics in your first game, taking about an hour. The lack of variety or progression may dissuade some people from purchasing the game for its undiscounted price. While there are strategies to maximize points, the randomized tile stack constrains you. There is no multiplayer option.

However, if you want something meditative to wind down or want to relax while enjoying a sensual but minimal challenge, Dorfromantik is your game. It is for the player who enjoys making a gorgeous landscape over intense strategy.

I love building games, I love puzzle games, and the combination of the two have produced some of my favorite experiences to relax with ever. That’s right where Dorfromantik falls, with its genius combination of challenging mechanics and practically no pressure to get them right. It’s rare to find a puzzler that lets you engage with it entirely on your own terms, but you’re really quite free here to go as light or as hard as you want. There’s even enough to work with here where you can play rounds with any number of goals in mind, from chasing high scores to unlocking new tiles to just making the prettiest landscape you can manage. Any part of that would make a fairly compelling game on its own, but here, you’ve got a lot to look forward to no matter how you approach it.

I’m not even going to hazard a guess at why this one’s called “Dorfromantik”, as there are clearly no dorfs and no romance that I could find. Each run of this puzzler hands you a stack of hexagonal tiles with different features on each edge. You may find grasslands, towns, forests, rivers, farms, railroads, or a mix of elements on each tile. Your job is to place those tiles to form a landscape, ideally with as many matching edges as possible. It sounds a bit like Carcassonne but it isn’t, really. Outside of water and rail features, there are no rules about where you put anything. However, you gain bonus points and extra tiles for making “perfect” hexes that match their surroundings on all sides. Also, matching edges makes everything look nicer, and in a game this pretty, you had better be playing for aesthetics.

Some tiles also come with missions, in the form of numbered tags. These tags tell you how many of the tagged feature (houses, trees, fields, etc.) need to be linked together to complete the mission. If there’s a plus sign, you just need to link up at least that many features, otherwise you have to hit the number exactly to get credit. Tags can also come with little flags that give you a follow-up mission to close off the linked features. Completing these missions give you plenty of points and a lot of extra tiles, which is your main way to keep going. After all, the game ends when you run out of tiles, so the more missions and perfect tiles you complete, the longer your run will last.

I think it’s really important to recognize that the game never really pushes you to do any of this. There’s no pressure to place tiles perfectly, no unpleasant effects or alerts when you fail to match edges. The indicator showing how many tiles are left doesn’t do anything other than turn a bit pink when you get to the last few tiles, and it’s so unobtrusive that I sometimes forget to even check it. You do, however, get a lovely bit of fanfare when you do complete missions and perfect tiles, so it’s really only positive reinforcement here. If you build things way out, you’ll also uncover hidden tiles with unique features on them. Linking these up and completing their mission unlocks new challenges that are tracked passively as you play, like making giant forests or placing consecutive matching pieces. These in turn unlock new colors of tiles and even new features that can show up in your deck, so the game experience grows as you get deeper and deeper into it.

This is the beauty of Dorfromantik, that it has all these missions and challenges and mechanics going on, and still never demands you to engage with any of it. You’re absolutely free to start a run and just place tiles wherever you feel like, matching or not, until you run out. Some of the challenges like placing tiles without rotating them even encourage this in a way, giving you unique twists on the gameplay that you can take or leave as you like. This extends to the many game modes that have made it in with the full release, including several challenge modes, a custom challenge mode where you define your own rules, a hard mode, and, of course, a creative sandbox mode. Perhaps most telling of how much the developers want you to chill and enjoy the game is that, whenever you run out of tiles in a regular run, you are offered the chance to continue playing in creative mode.

I’m not sure a game so relaxing and low-key would work without a suitable look and feel, but Dorfromantik hits all the right notes there, too. The simple 3D tiles and animated wildlife do so much to provide a sense of comfort and familiarity, and the way some features like water morph along the edges to make more natural-looking lakes and rivers is a lovely detail. I especially like how the color palette of your tiles changes as you go further and further from the start in different directions. The sound effects are rich and satisfying, and the music is just the right kind of subtle cheer that this game needs. If it seems like I’m gushing about this game, it’s because I want everyone to have a title like this to kick back and relax with whenever they want. Cozy experiences like Dorfromantik don’t come along every day, and they deserve to be celebrated when they do.

While the game does have a creative aspect and a specific mode for those inclined, the actual meat of the game is a sort of German board game / solitaire hybrid. Put the hexagons in their proper place next to the other hexagons, get points. You have a 'deck' full of these tiles that can be refilled through randomly generated quests, you lose when you fail to complete enough and run out of tiles. Simple but hard-to-master-if-you-wanna-hit-the-leaderboards kind of gameplay. 

If you don't care for competitive-ish things and are more into painting the map with pretty houses and such, the game does not limit you from doing so beyond having different 'biomes' (really just colour options for your tiles that can be freely changed) needing to be unlocked by simply playing classic mode.

I can see why others have described it as relaxing: the soundtrack is very good, the art is quite charming and nice to look at, everything about the game feels nice to play. The gameplay is nuanced and interesting enough to feel rewarding, yet flows smoothly in a way that never feels rushed or stressful. You can always press Undo.

That said, one of my few complaints with the game do stem from longevity issues. At the time of this review I have only played for a total of 10 hours, feel as though I have grasped the basic gameplay loop and... that's it. I know I said it is interesting, and it will keep you engaged at first, but it needs more personality to be something truly special. 

I understand the repetitive nature of this sort of game is obvious and do not think it necessarily needs a 'story' or little characters walking around as others have suggested, but maybe could benefit from more customizations and flavour additions like say, being able to name large cities, forests, etc. Perhaps a mode that adds random unmovable Mountain tiles. Puzzle mode? The game already has an array of options and by no means feels incomplete or less than a 1.0 release - it is worth the money and I highly recommend it. I am just hoping for more!

It's a really interesting concept. It's a puzzle within a puzzle. The game begins with a blank board with a single tile in the center, and you get a stack of 40 hexagonal tiles to be placed. Players select the top tile, like a deck of cards, and try to match them with other hexagonal tiles to score points. To match them up, the tiles are comprised of different entities such as fields, forests, houses, etc. Some will have 1 house or they can have 5 houses. These entities will represent one or more of the 6 sides of the hexagon. There are missions such as connecting 5 railroad tracks or 400 trees that'll reward you with more tiles. The game ends when you run out of tiles in the stack. It's a nice relaxing game but can be challenging if you try to aim for the high score on the leader board.

For those who may not be familiar with Carcassonne, it's a tile-based multiplayer board game where players take turns laying down and matching the borders of tiles which feature various terrain, scoring points by completing roads, cities, etc.  But, if you want to play it, you need at least one other person to play with which may not always be possible.

This game is pretty much Carcassonne solitaire, in the best way possible.  The challenge, instead of another player, are occasional quests that a tile to be placed presents (such as making a town with X number of connected houses); completing a quest grants the player bonus points to their score.

The best part?  Once your game ends, you can opt to switch to Creative Mode and continue playing with the map you just built; no more scoring takes place, but now you have free reign to place (and remove!) tiles in order to satisfy your aesthetic desire.

This is a game meant to be savored and enjoyed; there's no rush, no enemies to fight, and no other people to deal with.  Highly recommended!

Dorfromantik is a tile-based, placement planning, city builder puzzle game with challenges and unlocks - an intriguing mix between Concrete Jungle, Islanders, and Triple Town.  The basic concept is simple, and once you get it the challenge is to get your score as high as possible - thus the better you get, the longer your play session. The visuals and background music is very relaxing, almost like a virtual holiday. I can definitely see someone playing this while doing something else e.g. listening to a podcast. With the game's complete release, regional pricing and a nice discount, it's an easy recommend from me (edited for the Steam Awards badge).
Fun blend of stress-free gaming, puzzles, and city building. Combine it with a tetris-like block queue and you have rng-strategy, too.

At first glance, Dorfromantik seems pretty basic. You place tiny hexagons on an infinite board, and you can get more tiles to place by following the game's rule set. 
Though after just a few minutes of screwing around, you start to realize there is a lot of thought and organizing, that has to go into your playstyle, if you want to achieve a higher score. It's weirdly challenging and relaxing at the same time.
When putting every single tile perfectly, you can even go on without ever getting a game over. Here and there some small gaps start showing up, for which you haven't been getting the right tile yet, and I gotta say it's honestly so satisfying to get that specific one, you've been waiting for your entire run to finally fill in the gap.
Though even, if you don't put a lot of effort in, you can still have a great time, building a cute village. Alternatively, you're also free to just build tiny cities in creative mode to go full Zen, and just construct a beautiful landscape or play a quick round with a limited amount of tiles.
The soundtrack is just beautiful, perfect to relax or drift off for a little while.

This game is quick and easy to learn, and very relaxing to play. You don't need to perform mental gymnastics to slot pieces together, perfectly, but you'll still need to pay attention to what you're putting down, and where.

As the game tells you, each tile you place down has a variety of different biomes on it; some tiles will have nothing but trees, and other tiles might have houses on one side, trees on another side, and a railway going through the middle. Match the sides of tiles as you place them down to get points, and watch as your world slowly grows into a beautiful, very non-uniform, and surprisingly realistic looking landscape, with forests and wheat fields, and rivers running through the lot. It's like a giant jigsaw puzzle, except that there is no predetermined image you're trying to make. With each piece you add, you build your own, unique image.

As you play, you'll unlock more, different tiles. And, you can attempt different game modes, as well, including "creative" mode, or customise your own difficulty settings.

Dorf Romantik is the kind of game you can sit down, switch off, and just sink a few minutes into.  Or several hours.

For a bit more serious review: Dorfromantik is a relaxing tile placement game that feels like single player Carcassonne. Perfectly connecting all edges will give you a bonus and you need to  complete quests to keep getting new tiles. The highscore is your only goal, until the tiles run out, simple as that.

Now, I have some mixed feelings about how satisfying this game feels. Going for the highscore means you need to complete quests, which in turn means you need to branch out the tiles in several directions and place tiles that don't connect perfectly (a horror if you have OCD). This last point makes the actual resources on the tile feel a bit pointless, since it does not matter how you place them. That, and the fact that your game will end up looking like a Swiss cheese instead of a perfectly filled landscape (the trailer video is a bit misleading, imo). 

It does feel the game is designed to be played this way: just try to make the best out of the tiles you are given, without trying to perfectly connect the pieces. If that does not sound like fun, you could give the game "Islanders" a try.

Dorfromantik is a wonderful little puzzle game that's somewhat reminiscent of both the board game Carcassone and the Xbox Live Arcade game Hexic HD. Your job is to place tiles with matching edges onto a hexagonal grid and fill the board. Seems simple enough... but there's a good amount of depth to it.

To start, your tile stack isn't infinite and will deplete at a fairly steady rate unless you complete quests along the way. These quests come up fairly often and rely on you making a connection of either exactly X amount of a resource, or surpassing X amount in one group. Certain versions of those quests will drop a flag in their resource pool once completed. To grab the flag and accumulate even more tiles, you must close the entire resource pool. There's a nice amount of strategy in deciding when it's better to continue expanding a forest to complete quests that might require a large amount of trees, or starting a new forest and picking up more tiles so the round doesn't end. There's other ways to grab more tiles, such as making a "perfect" hex, by matching the patterns on every side of one hexagon piece. Managing both of these factors well will help you go far.

But, if you're not as concerned with the score there's a creative mode too. Upon finishing any round, you're able to continue playing and placing tiles as you wish with no pressure whatsoever.

At it's core, Dorfromantik is a puzzle game that's easy to learn, hard to master, and will have you fixated for hours. Whether you're looking to paint a scenic landscape with beautiful designs or seeking the challenge of making a perfectly aligned grid with nothing out of place, Dorfromantik is definitely worth your time.

A delightful, cozy, relaxing puzzle-sim game from Toukana. For the achievement hoarders, there is plenty to enjoy - whether it is the immediate numbers initiative (assimilate a pile of 500+ trees into a forest) that adds more tiles to your stack, the high score for each completed game, or the passive progress that carries over multiple games and unlocks new tile types and biomes, there is plenty to enjoy on varying levels. 

But when the numbers fall away, you are creating a little world for imaginary inhabitants to enjoy, and there is something cheerful about watching the subtle animations as trains and boats traverse the environment. 

The inevitable "is it on Switch" question will probably continue to plague Toukana Interactive over the next few months. Maybe they will embrace the challenge, or maybe they will just continue with small updates to the PC version for now. Either way, I'm curious to see what is next!

I feel they could make minor changes to the game for playability, such as more significant rewards for completing more difficult missions (like seven new tiles than the standard 5). Dorfromantik is a beautiful, slightly luck based, slightly strategic, challenging game. I only have good things to say about it, in all honesty.  This is not a game you will want to play if you are a person that goes for easy/fast achievements - I didn't get a score above 8k during my first 10 games.  The game has only become better as they have pushed updates, added content, and have made it even more of a challenge. I typically play this game once or twice every couple of months, casually. Its the type of game where you can put down and pick it back up without needing a refresher on how to play.

There are very challenging mechanics such as absolutely zero undo function for accidental/less ideal tile placement, and also no way of seeing exactly how to line up a tile for a perfect fit unless you really just have experience playing and have learned what the different pieces are. It forces you to take your time, to be patient, and to focus. These key components make up part of why I find it to be such an enjoyable game. If you're someone who doesn't like these types of challenging qualities in a game, then this game is not for you. If you get frustrated easily, do not buy this game - you won't enjoy it. But for everyone else, I absolutely recommend this game. Its just fantastic.

The game is evil and bogus. Problem #1, which is probably not apparent to the game's proud developer, is that the game has a broken tile generator. It repeatedly generates tiles within some finite set and goes rounds and rounds in it. You can play several dozens of games for several weeks, and you will never see some combinations of sides. So to play this game, you have to memorize that set of tiles; otherwise, you end up with never-covered gaps in your mesh. Problem #2: The game assumes that you must manually search for the correct tile position. That is stupid because it lacks fundamental usability and has nothing to do with gameplay. Forcing the user to search for the best tile placement manually is tedious and makes the gameplay boring. The game should highlight not only the best place, but it should indicate the direction on the border towards the best positions. Problem #3: It is near impossible to close flagged quests for two reasons, the required tiles never come, and the game constantly generates bigger and bigger quests, so it is impossible to start another small quest on the side and finish the previous one.  I give up. Bye bye

[b]How it feels to [strike]chew 5 gum[/strike] play Dorfromantik[/b]
Sure the game is pretty relaxing and zen-like played casually, however if you're trying to beat your high score and the fucking god damned pieces just wont fit the way you fucking need them to because you've gotten like a billion of those useless fucking train track junctions and the trees on all sides tile that would let you complete 3 quests at once seems to have gone to the other dimension and hang out with the line piece from tetris it can be a little frustrating as well.

[b]What actually is it?[/b]
For anyone wondering Dorfromantik is a weirdly named building / strategy game where you draw a tile from a pool and have to place and rotate it so it ideally matches on all 6 sides - trees to trees, houses to houses, water to water etc etc. Matching on one side only is 10 points, getting a perfect fit is 60 plus an added card to the pool so you can keep building bigger and bigger. This game is the definition of easy to learn, difficult to master. 

[b]What makes it compelling[/b]
Mixing up this formula are quests, either to build certain types of land bigger, or to close off segments that are already large. Completing a quest awards 5 cards so they're essential to progress, however quest requirements scale with what you've built already so it becomes a pretty interesting and in-depth balancing act between building well enough to score high points but keeping segments of your build contained and separated so the quest requirements don't blow out of proportion. 
It's an unusual and interesting deep layer mechanic that pairs beautifully to what goes on at the surface, making this game deceptively complicated. Cracking past 15k or so on the scoreboard requires big brain times.

This game is wonderful; relaxing yet challenging. It reminds me of a cross between Settlers of Catan and Carcassonne but in a single-player format where you are mostly in competition with just yourself. There is an inaccessible leaderboard, however, that shows your standing on the home screen.

Dorfromantik is like a giant, freestyle jigsaw puzzle with seemingly randomized puzzle pieces. Points are earned by placing tiles. Higher points can be earned by making good tile placements, like placing trees next to trees, houses next to houses, fields next to fields, etc. Additional tiles are earned through completing quests and perfect tile placements.

When I first started playing I didn't completely understand the rules surrounding perfect tile placements. I placed tiles to generally fit well together but didn't pay attention to each of the six tile sides. Sometimes it is better to wait for a tile placement to perfectly align on all six sides in order to score the largest amount of points and add to the stack of tiles in between completing quests.

Overall strategy can fit within your personal playstyle, though. Whether you just want to chill and play your way, rise up the ranks of the leaderboard or gather achievements, this game offers all of that. Designed to be relaxing, there's no time limit to make a move. Use this to your advantage whilst devising the perfect strategy to fit the way you want to play; planning ahead with chess-like precision or just trying to build the nicest-looking village landscape.

When it's time for me to wind down at night and I just kind of want to drink tea and occupy my mind while I listen to TV in the background, this is my go-to game. Previously I enjoyed things like Donut County and Unpacking, and while those are really good and relaxing games, Dorfromantik is the only one I can play over and over again because of its arcade style.

It's the best possible style of a "wind down" game. No story, no campaign, no time limit, save when you want to, and each round is unrelated to the one before it. You just connect the tiles to get a higher score and more tiles, and when you run out of tiles you get to see your score and your high score. It's nice to try to beat your high score, but I honestly find it just very soothing to see the little biomes that are created as a result of my gameplay. 

I don't think it's the game for everyone, but if you're just looking for something to let your brain relax a little, I'd highly recommend Dorfromantik.

Have you ever played Carcassonne? Hate board game implementations because of either a stupid or cheating AI? Are you annoyed that you have to wait for hours for every opponent's move? Do you love board games and you don't have anyone to play with?

Then you've come to the right place.

As the authors boast, this is a quiet and relaxing game where you play yourself, a game that is very similar to Carcassonne but with hexagonal fields. And if you get into it, you can play it literally endlessly.

I would highly recommend. Even if you're not in the habit of playing real-world board games, maybe Dorfromantik will convince you.

The sound and overall game design is a real pleasure. It's perfectly soothing, you can play as fast or slow as you like, and put as much or little effort/thinking into it as you want. 

Sometimes I'm just cruising along, placing tiles hap-hazardly and not caring so much if everything matches, mainly trying to make it look pretty. Other times, I might get really into it or try to beat my high score, and spend ages pondering over each tile, trying to find the optimum location to place it to get the high score and make everything match together perfectly.

The tiles and overall game are adorable, I really enjoy their design and unlocking new ones. The animations are not too distracting or in your face, but I like them as they make it feel a bit more dynamic and give me something more to discover.

It's become my go-to game when I just want something soothing, relaxing, feel-good. Often, I don't have the energy (or fast reflexes) for most games, since it can feel punishing and frustrating when you don't succeed. 
Not this game! This game is like a cup of hot chocolate or tea snuggled up on the sofa. Even on the days where I'm challenging myself, it doesn't feel stressful or like it punishes mistakes. 

In short: I love it.

Sometimes I want to play something but... idk. I go through my whole library of great games and nothing inspires me. Maybe I'll start a new book, play some GBA (GameBoy Advance) or browse new music on Bandcamp, but I can always simply default to Dorfromantik as well. The in-game music is nice, but I'm going on 100 hours playtime and really into the dungeon synth genre right now. I do leave the sound effects on though and it makes for some of the best and most relaxing gameplay on Steam.

That being said, this game isn't only good as a time-waster or when you don't feel like playing anything else. It is an excellent strategy game with depth. There has been a steady progression between high-scores for me. It took me a while to progress to the point where I can now score 35-45k per game most of the time and I think I can still improve and pass 50k soon. At times I have felt like I couldn't do anything else, "How can I get a higher score?" But you intuitively improve over time with pattern recognition and whatnot, and so I feel the game has been very well designed.

I should mention that I have been silently waiting for an update that adds what I thought would be common sense and highly requested, but maybe not. We need hotkeys quickly assignable to a camera position so that we can mark where our various quests or areas we are working on are. This way we can quickly hotkey through saved camera positions. It's just a lot of camera rotating and screen dragging back and forth between each piece, which (very rarely) causes me to misplace a piece and that sucks when you are trying really hard to be perfect. It would be so awesome to have this feature implemented soon to cut down on time spent rotating and dragging the screen around. I say this because an "undo move" option just doesn't feel right. I'm glad that hasn't been implemented because there are other ways to help that, such as by minimizing the amount of unnecessary clicks taking place on the board.

Anyway, this is an amazing game here that has been receiving a lot of developer support and engagement. This game is a must purchase and incredible deal at the current price.

Edit March 3 2022: I have some issues with the game sometimes from the updates and it seems to completely change things. I have deleted and reinstalled the game many times because it has felt broken from one update to the next. I was annoyed with this but then I realized the game is still in early access. It's worth a mention that you would completely forget this is an early access title. So it makes sense that there will be changes both good and bad throughout this period in the game's development and I should be supportive of that.

What can you say about Dorfromantik that hasn't been said. Who knew such a weird name for a game, would work. It feels and looks like a classic video game or board game, but Toukana Interactive hits it out of the park with its simplistic entry. 
PROS
Presentation: Beautiful animation that holds up in its simplicity and layout
Rules: My kids loved it, simple and easy on the surface that can get away from you super fast.
Control: Easy that a child can do it. 
Classic: This is as obsessive as any game I have seen in a while. 
Innovative: The simple rules are innovative as many card games struggle to do today.
Future: Interesting to see how the build on this entry. What can you add to make it better.
CONS
Rng: Can be frustrating in the necessity of getting what you need when you need it. 
Architect: My five year old knows how to build a lake better than I do. Ooi...
Careful: I am not sure if Adults will enjoy this more than kids in the long run of replay ability, but I sure did. The con here is they can add to something that I believe does not need it. 

OVERALL

Dorfromantik is what you get when you combine a landscape builder with a game of dominoes.

This game is a relaxing, casual world-building game with mini-quests, accompanied by calm music. 
You get a random set of tiles that you have to lay down. As you lay down tiles, some of these will give you a "quest" to fulfill (e.g. connect at least 14 more trees). Once quests are fulfilled, you receive additional tiles in your deck. 

The more tiles you lay down, and the more edge matches you get (grouping cities, forests, etc), the higher your score. 

Once you run out of tiles, you can opt to continue building out your world in creative mode, or start a new challenge. 

Highly recommended as a casual world building game to just chill out to.

The sound is pleasant enough but to be honest i quite often turned the music off so that i could listen to a book or the radio.
The game play is fairly simple, you have a stack of hex shaped landscape cards that you must lay in turn, you have a very limited view or what is coming next.
The session ends when you run out of cards and you gain points as you play, as mentioned before ive not really looked into how points are earned as i don't care but it seems to be linked to completing 'quests' or making well planned landscapes.
You get extra landscape cards in your stack by completing the 'quests' which ask you to link the different types of landscapes together in varying amounts. Houses, Farm fields, Water, Tree's and Train tracks.
The randomness of the next tile that you get means you should plan ahead trying to cater for the troublesome four way water tile or track tile, some quests as you to have exactly a certain amount of say houses or fields which can be a challenge if you current village already has more houses than required.
The big plus is that it never feels that much of a pain when the tricky tiles come up, yes it may 'ruin' your landscaping plans but i rarely care. Im having such a lovely relaxing time, I sometimes spend entirely too much time rotating and selecting where to put tiles that are essentially of not consequence to my sessions purely attempting to make my piece of landscaping art look more attractive.
A must try in my opinion, i think you will know if if a game you will enjoy well within the two hour refund time but I would recommend trying when you are in the mood for switching off your competitive mind and relaxing so that you can appreciate what this game has to offer.

Dorfromantik is a puzzle game: You are given a stack of 50 tiles (where each side can be forest, farmland, empty, buildings, water, or traintracks). Some tiles give you quests (i.e. link up 50 buildings to this hex) which give you 5 tiles when completed. Some quests also drop a flag when completed, which gives you 5 more tiles if you block off that quest type (i.e closing the forest region off). You also can get 1 tile if you place a hex perfectly (i.e. each side is touching another hexside with the same stuff in it).The goal of each game is to play until you run out of tiles. The game has objectives, some of which are always counting, some of which only count if it is one of the three objectives given at the start of each game. If you complete those objectives you unlock unique tiles (i.e. a windmill hex where all 6 sides are farmland). Each objective has multiple levels which grow in difficulty/time investment to complete. This is why the main gamemode is a puzzle game, not a city builder, you are trying to last as long as possible and get as many unlocks as you can in one run. There is a creative gamemode which gives you unlimited tiles and the ability to skip or delete tiles you don't want, but to get the unique tiles in the creative mode you must first unlock them in the base game. Overall, it is a very fun game, and can be pretty relaxing (so long as you aren't trying to complete one of the harder objectives, such as placing 200 tiles in a row without having any tile side touch a hex whose side is different).

It amazes me how such an uncomplicated game can be so not boring. The gameplay is very easy to learn and is rewarding very quickly. As straightforward as it is - there's a great variety in which it can be played... achievement hunting, casual quest completing, fun 'exploration', high score, town/landscape sculpturing, etc. And the beautiful part is that you don't have to 'pick' a method/goal each time you go to play it. The goal is enjoying the game - and how you get to that destination is completely fluid, based on your mood and choices, and you can swap your strategy around several times within a single gameplay. It's really all about having a good time. 
My other comment is on the graphics and music... I can't say thank you enough to the devs for giving us such a peaceful, charming and pleasing environment. It's hard finding an honest to goodness 'relax and enjoy' kind of game (esp for a strategist) - but finding a game where the graphics are not painful or offensive is... breathtakingly refreshing. 
In a word, I have found Dorfromantik to be a sweet, simple, priceless gem of a game that is very endearing. God bless all the devs for providing the community with such a treasure!
P.S. I haven't' fiddled much yet with the 'creative' option (maybe only in early access as of this review) - but it looks like a really nice outlet for those unrequited needs to build and create! A definite plus for those with that inclination.
P.P.S. Despite my logged hours - I've played this game with family on a sibling's account for well over 100 hours! So I speak from the heart and some experience ;)
P.P.P.S. Thanks for the updates & new lovely biomes!

Dorfromantik is like a puzzle with dominoes: you grab a tile and try to find the best spot to place it. It's relaxing, yet there are still a few tiles to unlock to enhance the gameplay. There is no rush, your only goal is to reach the highest score by forming groups of tiles that match. The better you place them, the more tiles you'll earn. Sometimes you need to create patches of land as big as possible, sometimes you have a specific number of elements to stick together, but either way there is absolutely no pressure when playing this game. There is a sandbox mode although I don't play it, the regular game mode is enough as far as I'm concerned to justify buying the game. It's the perfect game for these little gaps when you don't know what to do (in transports, waiting for someone, etc...), but beware: you can easily spend hours trying to beat your high score! The only thing I didn't like was the UI: it's so simplistic that, at first, you'll struggle a bit to find how to navigate through games modes. The music is very nice though, the world coming to live (boats in rivers, windmills etc.) is a nice touch. It's truly a game for everyone.

Relaxing, at times quite challenging and very, very addictive. When this game first came out I was instantly obsessed. The mechanics are simple enough... Match up the tiles with field to field, house to house, forest to forest and so on, but even in your first round you will notice that this task is harder than it seems. You have to plan ahead and watch your pile of tiles, because before you know it, you have none left. To make sure you keep the game going you complete build-quests attached to tiles in your pile or found in the surrounding area as your landscape grows bigger. They require a certain amount of connecting tiles, either asking for a very specific number or anything above. You can also get tiles back when you perfectly match all the sides of a tile. The thrill of the hunt for a new high score keeps me up most nights.
I would recommend this game to anyone who loves strategy and board games, but also for the people who just need something to play for shorter periods of time.
