I'm very grateful for Dorf Romantik! The visual style of puzzle is very appealing. I don't do so well with classic 'puzzle games' & this game allows me to experience that satisfaction in a way I can actually wrap my mind around. 

Also, it being such a visually focused game, I appreciate how beautiful the developers created the graphics. Staring at something akin to hideous to progress through a game I can find rather grating. In Dorf, I find myself sometimes sitting back and watching the train puff by in the lovely landscape I've just obliviously laid out. 

I also like that with Dorf, I don't have to set aside at least 1 hour to make any appreciable progress. It's really freeing to be able to simply hop in, knowing I'll only play for 15 minutes and it's still a rewarding experience. 

The quests, short term and especially challenge based, are a ingenious way to keep a repetitious game play brand new. With the particular focus of the 3 challenges per game, it can really change the viewpoint of that play-through, allowing you to discover different creative strategies you'd never used before! 

I've really enjoyed watching the development of the game. I've never been part of an 'early access' before, but this one certainly has been rewarding. The updates always add enhancements to the game and I feel like I just received a brand new bundle for free! (Especially the creation of a whole new bunch of tiles - that was an exciting update!) 

The music is also great. It's a very soothing background, with enough variety to not drive you crazy (especially if you are playing for hours at a time :D) I've done sound effects work professionally and theirs add a very nice touch of creating a gentle, easy-going environment. I was very impressed. 

Lastly, and mostly, I really like Dorf Romantik because it's such a genuine game. It doesn't have to compete and be cutting edge, mature themed, excessively mature themed, or horrifying. It treats people as people - and not an enhanced human of superiorly attuned reflexes with skills of a veteran soldier or an ex-zombie, thief, assassin, or prostitute. It's just a really simple game, that's peaceful with an attractive environment, that people can relax & enjoy being in (with a little bit of challenge) as we all struggle to navigate through our own day-to-day. I really appreciate what the devs at Dorf Romantik are doing in providing such a game and I wish there were more like this. I'm very, very grateful to them. Thanks so much!

The game is very simple. You have a stack of hexagonal tiles. Each tile can have one or more features on it, e.g. houses, woods, or train tracks. Tiles can be rotated and by placing your tiles correctly, you can build large villages or create lush forests. This is important as certain tiles will have quests on them, e.g. build a village with 25 houses. The reward for fulfilling a quest are a few more tiles. This is the primary way to extend the game. You can unlock special tiles by building for example a long train track or river system. And that's it. 

Pure and simple.

Dorfromantik is the pinnacle of "sit back and relax" play style. There are no timers ticking down, no pop-ups vying for your attention. It's just you and your stack of tiles. So sit back with a nice cup of tea and find the perfect place to put down your tiles.
I normally dislike games like this, but really enjoy the peacefulness.

It's a fun puzzle-type game with resource (well, card/tile) management. Amazing how quickly time can fly by while playing it. There is definitely a point at which it can become frustrating, but that's the fun of the challenge.
This game is one of my favorite ways to relax in an almost meditative state.

You might want to check the "Serene City-Builder Bundle", as it features quite a few quality products. Islanders has been a favorite of mine for some time, and while Dorfromantik doesn't reach the same great heights, it's nevertheless a really, really nice rogue-like tile-building game. 

You like the board game Carcassonne? Well, this could be the solo video game version. The art style, the chill vibe, the *fantastic* soundtrack, I can picture myself coming back to this once in a while. 

Highly recommended.

Relaxed solo puzzler that seems to draw some inspiration from tabletop game Carcasonne.
Basically you lay tiles to form or connect fields, cities, rivers and even train tracks.
The game will give you challenges, such as making a 12-tile long railroad or a town counting 67 houses.

Completing a challenge will give you a few extra tiles to place, but when you eventually run out the game is over.

Dorfromantik has some other challenges integrated into it's system, that will let you unlock new tiles or buildings for more variety. Some places tiles have add life or movement to the board, such as a train driving back and forth, a deer in the forest or a boat on the river. These little diorama's can be chill to watch, as the game does not include a time limit.

Extremely relaxing and nice game, especially for Carcassonne fans, either kids or adults. Although there’s no competition, the scoring is somewhat limited, and the tile edges do not have to match, the general principle is similar. While listening to very soothing music, the player composes a “map” of tiles containing fields, meadows, rivers, forests, towns/houses, rail tracks, railway stations, lakes – all of these nicely animated with details such as deers, locomotives, boats, and so on. In the normal game mode, the number of tiles is limited, but you receive bonus tiles for completing simple “quests”, such as creating a forest with a given number of trees or a railway with the requested length. Points are awarded for matching tile edges, completing the missions etc. There is also a creative mode, where the player creates maps from any tiles contained in the game, and there are competitions for creating best maps with a specific theme, for instance lake or city.
A good game for short sessions during breaks in work, however it is absorbing, and you can play on and on for a long time without noticing. This a beautifully designed product bringing much joy in these uneasy times.

The core of the game consists of placing hexagonal tiles to form the world mostly as you see fit. The catch? Dorfromantik suffers from a bit of misleading advertising: there are no dwarves to be seen, and romance seems to be completely absent,

Other than that, it's more or less a hex-based single player version of Carcassonne. You're given a limited amount of tiles to place, the occasional objectives tied to specific tiles (have this railway tile be part of a railway network that spreads across exactly/at least X tiles) and are rewarded for completing said objectives with more tiles to place. When you run out of tiles, the game's over, and you'll have to start again. There's no time limit, you can quit at any time and pick it back up right where you left it.

The game is fairly easy to learn, helped in no small part by the comfy, relaxing atmosphere it builds. But tile placement has much more to it than you'd first think. Dunno if it's hard to master or if I'm just gifted with a particularly thick skull. I'll go with both.

Very relaxing but not mindless.  I love to put on some music and unwind to this game, it's perfect for it.  The game gives you some goals to work towards for future runs as well, which I appreciate when I'm in the mood to spend more time thinking about the task at hand, rather than just making a pretty landscape (which is a lot of fun in it's own right).

Sometimes you need a game that lets you sit down, relax, and listen to some peaceful music. Dorfromantik nails those points but also has high scores for people who want a little more competitiveness in their games. You receive more points for matching tiles perfectly together, for example a tile has a blank side, a forest side, and a town side. You then are rewarded for placing a new tile that matches the side it is connected to. This quickly becomes complicated because each tile has 6 sides and you are trying to perfectly fit together hundreds of tiles.

This game has a limited amount of tiles you place and you complete quests to add more tiles to your stack, for example a quest might ask to have 50 trees in a forest. You would then combine your tiles with trees into a long chain to make a forest and complete the quest. You can also receive 1 extra tile for making a "perfect" tile, this is a tile that is surrounded by 6 other tiles and all sides match each other. 

One of the nicer additions to come out of early access for me was the option to play without the limited tiles in creative mode. This truly makes the game one of the most relaxing I have played with no worries about the puzzle aspect, you are just combining tiles to make a neat little map.

Sure you could just throw them in willy nilly  but  eventually you will run out of tiles and be unable to complete higher tiers of the achievement.  Your extra tiles and game score are from completing quests and perfect placement scores ( not as easy as it would seem).  I love that you can make something very visually pleasing by accident. This is a fun easy to play game that gets trickier as you play.

You have a stack of tiles in the lower right of the screen. The object is to place as many tiles as you can before running out of new tiles.

They have grasslands, farmlands, woodlands, bodies of water- rivers, railroads or even towns and more. All are animated on each tile.

You match one side of the tile with another tile with the same thing on it and win points and more tiles. If you can not make a match you don't loose anything you just won't get new added tiles.

Some tiles have a required matches you need to complete like a set number of houses or a fixed amount of trees linked together. If you do this you get extra points and more tiles.

It is a fun and relaxing game with a simple game play loop that becomes a- "One more tile, then I will go to bed."- addiction.

Dorfromantik is a relaxing little puzzle game.  I tried out the demo during the steam demo...event?...last year and quite enjoyed it, so I picked it up.  From the music to the basic tiling laying gameplay (you can put anything except rivers and train tracks anywhere, but you need to keep in mind that you need to finish the mini missions attached to tiles to get more tiles to keep playing) the game is satisfying.  However, as given by the price point, it is also a relatively simplistic game.  A little closer to Tetris (randomized pieces that you need to slot in to get points) than a logic puzzle, y'know?  

Being basic isn't a bad thing though.  It is what I was looking for in a game at the time, and my did I get what I paid for.  It is something to just open up sometimes and play 2-3 games, only to realize you played 6.  Definitely suggest it!

One thing to note: if you are obsessed with getting all the achievements, this game will not let you scratch that itch. As far as I can tell, for each game you start you get assigned three random achievement categories, and no matter how awesome you do in that particular game, you can only unlock achievements in those categories (other than some broad ones like total points, etc).

For example, I know that I've built a village larger than 50 houses loads of times, and that I've built forests larger than 750 trees most games I've played, but since those two achievement categories were not active in those games, I have not yet earned those achievements.

The achievements bit is annoying to me, but considering how insanely difficult the top tier of achievements is in this game, I doubt I would ever 100% this game.

This game is described as a relaxing tile laying city builder, but the inclusion of quests (various tasks to complete before you run out of tiles) takes all serenity out of the game and makes it a stressful mess.  The tiles that you get in your stack seem to be inversely linked to the quests that you have, especially if you find one of the rare tiles to unlock.  Find a rare tile that requires you to build a long railroad?  You will see fewer railroad tiles.  Need a particular tile to complete a long river?  You won't get that particular tile.  Decided to build the river in a way where any possible water tile will complete it?  You won't see another water tile for the entirety of your game.  This is not an exaggeration - as soon as I needed ANY water tile, I went 70+ tiles without getting one.  I saw that behavior every round where I found a rare tile, so I don't think it is random chance.  I can't understand why a game like this would include mechanics with the sole purpose of annoying the player - this isn't supposed to be Dark Souls the city builder.

Fortunately, the game was only $8 when I bought it so I don't feel like I got screwed too badly for the price.  If you want a little tile laying city builder game and are capable of ignoring the quests, challenges, and rare tiles then this game might be OK for you.  They even include a creative mode for just that situation.  The graphics are fine and the music is relaxing.  If you are a completionist then avoid this at all costs unless you want to set a new blood pressure high score.

Edit: Corrected usage of quest vs challenge vs rare tile

This is the MOST peaceful and relaxing puzzle game that I've ever played. Dorfromantik is a peaceful building strategy puzzle game (try saying that phraze a few times in-a-row). It has such a zen vibe with the music that it feels like I'm in such a sweet relam that I can have a nap in. However as I said, this is a peaceful building strategy puzzle game, so there is definitely things you can do while sleeping in this relam. 

The objective is to get as much points as you can by placing hexagon tiles, each with varying objects on it. The goal is to keep building until you either run out of hexagon tiles or you decided to have enough. I like how there is also pieces that have quests which rewards you with more hexagon tiles to keep the game going. There is even some that requires you to have an exact number of things and also an additional one where you need to close off the region to get bonus points. I did have times where I ran out of tiles right before I was close to completing some quests. The game also encourages you to ever-expand your building with unique pieces and objectives appearing outside your current build area which you need to build up to for that to unlock, and there is biomes aswell which changes the colours when you're looking and building in that biome.

What I talked about before is basically Classic Mode. This mode feels very balanced with plenty of room for creativity while also strategizing on where you place the tiles with the sense of stress when you have limited tiles and the slight annoyance when the piece that you want isn't appearing in your batch of tiles to place. The unlocks for this game is decent with either the addition of a new type of piece to place, or a new biome. You get these by either expanding and exploring the map and a greyed out piece shows up that you would need to reach to see what it is about. The other is also completing overall challenges above the tile batch on the right side of the screen which the progress continues on in multiple sessions.

I have not tried Creative Mode yet which gives you endless freedom and the lack of tile limits. The challenges and unlocks that you get from Classic Mode can be used in Creative Mode. I haven't played through the game enough to get every unlock, but I'm hoping that one of them is a snow biome. As much as I like seeing the summer greens and the spring purples or violets, I actually don't like summer but I do love winter. I do see heaps of potential and these updates so far have been pretty darn good. The art style for this game is perfect and unique. This game would be really good to appear on consoles like the Nintendo Switch, both Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S, PS4 and PS5. Of course this is up to the developer.

So yeah, Dorfromantik is the most peaceful building strategy puzzle game that I ever played, and I solely recommend you play this game along with other games that are similar that I recommend especially Mini Metro and Mini Motorways.

A low-key, very relaxing flavor of puzzle game that also manages to be surprisingly compelling for how simple the core loop is.

The premise is simple: 
-You have a finite stack of hexagons to put onto a grid next to one another.
-The more edges match, the more points you get for the placement.
-If all six of a tile's edges match after a placement, you get bonus points and an additional tile.
-As you play, you get challenged to compete certain specific objectives for more tiles.
-Once you run out of tiles, the game ends.

There really isn't much else to say; everything works appropriately, the music is pleasant and fits the pastoral quality of the scenery you'll be constructing, the sound design is unobtrusive...  If this looks like the kind of puzzle you'd like to put together I can only recommend.

Dorfromantik has been a joy to play this past year. 

The formula is perfect for whatever you want to get out of it. If you want a relaxing domino-style town builder, you've got it. If you want an intense, puzzle-forward game where you race for that highscore, you've got it. If you want a neat little tool to design settlements and experiment with making beautiful landscapes, you've got it. Toukana seriously thought of everything.

All of the biomes are stunning -- my favourites have to be the Enchanted and Sakura ones. The music never fails to blow me away, and the sound design is supremely satisfying. 

I have high hopes for Toukana going forward, and for this game with the Steam Awards coming soon. It deserves recognition for everything it has achieved. Definitely worth the purchase, at full price or otherwise

Not sure if relaxing is the proper way to describe it, maybe meditative? At least when you're in classic mode, which gives you limited tiles. Creative mode is fully relaxing, but unless you're really into landscaping from a blank canvas, or are particularly attached to a particular map you've just lost in classic mode, you won't have as much incentive to dwell into it.

Classic mode is a mix between pensive thought, creativity and stress intermixing as your tile number goes down, since you have to find ways to clear missions (usually connection a certain amount of pieces, i.e: trees, houses, wheat fields, etc.) to prevent it reaching 0, but still get pulled by your aesthetic sense, or your chasing of a high score if you figure out how the scoring system works, so that you have to spend a few tiles on places there are no missions to clear. 

More than a few times I've been trying to get a mission clear with 9 tiles left praying that I get enough to clear an additional mission somewhere, while noticing a tile I placed a few dozen tiles before would've helped if I had given it a bit more forethought, but still wasn't able to completely feel it was a mistake since it looked pretty or looked like it'd help more where I placed it back then. 

It's a bit complicated like that, but it isn't really frustrating when it happens, and more often than not it helps you learn the game better and think more about what you're doing while enjoying the act of building a nice...village? city? region? in the middle of nowhere.

Don’t let the simplicity of this game fool you. You start out thinking it’s simply point, spin a tile and place it. Think again…. because with every tile you place, you take a step deeper into committing what you’re going to build next! Hidden behind the clean interface, and ease of use is a great little “thinking” game. 

The four students who created this game should be commended for identifying and building a game that hits a niche market. That is, a game that makes you think, gives room for creativity and best of all stays true to wholesome gaming, bypassing the insanity of constant combat, starving people or racing against the clock. Bravo!

The game has goals, which are actually attainable and achievements come at a satisfying rate. Even better, there is “creative” mode (think sandbox) that lets you just go at it and build out a map larger than you would think possible. Is this game going to be for everyone? No. But, for those who want a game that’s challenging yet relaxing, you should give it a try. I look forward to the developers continuing to add on to this game, while staying true to its theme.

Dorfromantik is a perfect game for relaxation. 
Sure, you can figure out exactly how the game works, all the little details and try to get the highest score possible, but that, to me, is not the real strength of the game. 
The thing it does best is to challenge your mind just enough to keep you invested in the game, while also keeping it real simple. 
All you do is rotate tiles and fit them into ideal places to either satisfy your sense of asthetics or to earn higher points by combining alot of forest tiles for example (or housetiles, watertiles and so on). 
Combine that with relaxing music and overall great rural sounddesign and you have this game, which doesn't do a lot, but what it sets out to do it does very well.

This was a blind purchase for me, so I didn't really know what to expect, but what I got was a puzzle game that feels deceptively relaxing at first but gets quite nail-biting as it progresses.  There's never any time pressure, though, so if you mess up, that's entirely your fault!  (unless you are the type of person who blames RNG for your own shortcomings)

The idea is simple:  You are given a finite stack of randomly-generated hexagonal tiles, each with bits of landscape features such as meadow, houses, trees, or bits of train track.  You need to arrange them on a gently expanding grid, with the goal of matching like features together.  Over time, a lovely landscape will emerge.  It's basically Cities: Skylines meets dominoes.  The more matches you are able to make, the higher your score will be, and when you place your final tile, it's game over.

However, you can extend your run as well.  Making a "perfect" match on all six sides of a tile grants 1 additional move, and some tiles may spawn with "quests", which have secondary goals like "make a neighborhood of exactly 57 houses" or "make a river at least 12 tiles long", which also grant extra moves when completed.

The game also offers a number of long-term goals which can be worked on over multiple playthroughs, and completing these goals may unlock extra "skins" and visual elements that lend your future landscapes more visual variety.

This game feels like a single player Carcassonne with missions. There are currently two modes: High score and creative. In high score mode, you earn tiles by completing missions (link over 30 houses together, create a forest with over 200 trees, close off a set of fields, etc). Your score depends on the placement of these tiles (10 points for each edge matched, for instance. There is no time limit so you can take it easy, placing the tiles until you eventually run out giving a score at the end. As you progress you also unlock more tile types to add variation the better you get.

Creative mode has unlimited tiles and you can change which ones are most likely to appear next. 

Both modes are relaxing, unless you get obsessed about beating your high score :D

Reminiscent of the sims, it's based on world building, and connecting pieces to make the world work, so if you like that, then this is a game for you. 

It's one that surely won't be for everyone, but personally, I'm enjoying this a lot more a lot of games in my Steam library. I think why I love it so much is that it arouses some feelings of self-awareness, in a very odd way, where time can be reflective of the kind of metronome like sounds of the music, or in the different shades of colour that pervade the background in different sections of the world you've built. It feels existential, in it's own way, and arouses feelings of sadness and loneliness (but not in a bad way, but perhaps a way that tells me I've been playing games for too long which may be why I love it so much). 

As a whole, the game reminds me of a sort of puzzle waiting to be unraveled, and reminds me of a childhood game I can't quite place. 

It doesn't hold your hand at any point, and you can lose but losing doesn't feel like failure here. In each instance, you're creating a relaxing world that looks like something straight out of Fantastic Mr. Fox or one of those dutch paintings while being accompanied with fantastic sounds that encourage you to keep building in a world you know you can return to anytime you're looking for something therapeutic, and maybe a bit nostalgic. Just beautiful all around. 

I urge this studio to keep creating as I'm eager to see what they do next.

A casual tile-placing puzzle game where the objective is to go for the high score and optional challenges. The player gets a stack of random hexagonal tiles and is asked to place them on the map. You get points based off placing tiles next to other tiles with matching edges, and for completing some in-game quests to, for example, create a contiguous group of farms with 14 fields. Completing the quest will reward points and additional five tiles. Perfect tile placements (where all six sides match adjacent tiles) will also reward one additional tile. Closing off certain groups of completed quests will also award five additional tiles.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
+ Easy to pick up, but still has some depth if you want to go for the high scores.
+ The quests keep gameplay engaging.
+ There's a creative mode.
+ Calming soundscape.
+ Mobile controls

[h1]Cons[/h1]
- Placed a few hexagonal tiles, placed them all. Don't expect anything more complex than tile placing.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Ultimately, you just need to ask yourself: "do I want to play a hex-tile-placer puzzle game?" Boy, did I. Placed those tiles real good. Got a bunch of perfect placements. Made a big looping railroad track that went nowhere. And a big forest. 

Yeah, this game's alright.  [i]Recommended[/i].

The game looks relaxing. It sounds relaxing. But it actually isn't.

The game only counts as relaxing, if you don't play for score or achievements, but just for the visuals, and don't care about how far you come. I imagine that the creative mode will actually be quite relaxing - but not really a game, since there's nothing to gain or to lose.

Because if you play for score and achievements, you will inevitably become frustrated. No matter how well you plan your moves, 90% the time it is impossible to reach the achievement goals. 
It doesn't matter if you see to it that you fulfill every quest to get more tiles, while also having an eye on the achievements, which, once completed, also give you tiles.

Of quests, there are those types: 
1. Group tiles of a certain type together, which is parted in:
1a. AT LEAST that many tiles or
1b. EXACTLY that many tiles. 
2. Close off a group. Those groups get marked by a flag. The flags are usually earned through 1b. quests.
3. Find hidden tiles on the map and fulfill their quest.

Achievements come in different versions. Some are global, meaning you can finish them over several games and some have to be completed in one run.
1. Group at least that many tiles together (e.g. form a forest that consists of at least 800 trees) Usually one run.
2. Score perfect placement (means that all edges have to be aligned with an edge of the same likelihood) Come in both versions.
3. Close off tile-groups. (e.g. form at least 50 closed-off field groups having at least 10 tiles) Usually global.

Example: I just finished a run (which prompted me to write this review) in which I planned everything perfectly. In the 30 mins I played, I managed to complete every quest, while still lining up achievement requirements. I connected every train and water tile I could connect (as I had achievements going that prompted me to form a train track of 50 tiles and a body of water with 60 tiles) and in the end, the run ended, with me falling short of 3 train tiles and 4 water tiles. Tiles I could have added to the train track, while adding them to the water body, would not have made any difference (there are tiles that can be used for both).

There was NOTHING I could have done better. Yet, the RNG did not even PROVIDE me with the tiles needed. It was simply impossible to get the achievements!

I see two major problems here:
1. The (badly designed) RNG has complete power over the game.
2. More complicated quests to complete don't gain you higher rewards.

ad 1.) If the RNG decides to only give you tiles you can't use and no achievement tiles, then that's that. If the RNG decides you not even get enough tiles to finish your achievement, then that's that too. Also, the tiles you get get worse the longer you play, making them unusable at a certain point. This isn't fun.
I would suggest adding a mechanic like in "Islanders", in which you get to choose which type of tiles you get next when you reach certain score points. 
To explain for "Dorfromantik": Let's say you have 3 quests for a forest open, and you hit 2000 points, you should be able to choose to get a certain amount / more forest tiles for the next 20 tiles. This way, you could influence the game a bit, without killing its gameplay.

ad 2.) The longer the game runs, the higher the requirement for the quests are. E.g. in the beginning, you need to connect 20 houses to finish a quest and get more tiles, later you need 200. Problem is, you only get 5 tiles as a reward, and it does not matter how many you needed to complete the quest. Which means, ultimaltey, that it is impossible to keep going. I get that this game is not meant to go on indefinitely (in classic mode), but it is frustrating to not get higher rewards for harder quests. That is one of the basic principles of quests, which should be adhered to. Otherwise, why even bother with the harder quests? Oh right: because you don't get easier ones later on.

TL;DR: The RNG, on whose mercy you have to cast yourself, and not getting higher rewards for more complicated quests and achievements kills the game.

Dorfromantik straddles the line between casual and hardcore with aplomb. You can happily play it with no care in the world, plonking hexes down to make a beautiful little world that looks fine on an old machine and vibrant on a modern one. Every one of those hexes going down is a considered move - do you look to build a new cluster? Plan for how to join your railway or rivers? Reach for an expansion task? And yet, even though you're making truly tactical and strategic choices every single turn, you never feel pressure to get it right. You can understand that you're going to run out of tiles but it's not something that hurts even if you know where you messed up and how you could do better next time to reach a higher score.

This game is special. I cannot recommend it highly enough.

it's a simple game, or, rather, a toy. After 4 runs I put it back in the box and slid it under the bed: it gave me no sense of satisfaction but rather a slight disappointment of failure.
I imagine if there were some challenge like connecting to a railway station tile to run a train or building a city of certain population in a designated space would give me that satisfaction that I missed, and without it there is no real motivation to play it again

Short Version: Chill Game, No Real Point, Music Is nice but repetitive, Purchase while on sale.

Long Version:

Pros: It's a relaxing tile puzzle game. It is easy to understand the concepts and difficult to get good at. As you can see by the hours I've played it, I've put a lot of time into it, but frankly I'm not trying to be good at the game. It has a lot to offer for those who want to be able to take their time with choices they make. There's not a rush to get it done, and as such, I've accidentally left it on for an hour or two before realizing it once already. If you quit, you can simply pick it back up where you left off, or start up a new game. This is not a graphically intense game, so you should be able to play on lower end machines as well. 

Cons: If you want a game with a story, this is not for you. That I recall, there isn't even a semblance of a story to be had. The music also tends to get repetitive after a bit, and there isn't really any winning to it. While I don't mind this type of game, some people do seem to enjoy a more driven experience, so I felt it useful to put that here.

Conclusion: Frankly, if there was a "maybe" for recommendations, that's what I would have put. It really depends on the factors I laid out in the cons section, but if you do get it, I recommend waiting on a sale, as there isn't a whole lot to the game to warrant full price purchasing. If you do buy at full price, it's okay, but it's better if you don't.

If you have played carcassonne (the table top city building game), you already know how to play this game. You get a stack of hexagonal cards that have trees, houses, fields, rivers and railways on them, you will just set them on a board and try to match these elements together to form forests, villages and so on.

There's no clock or timers in play, so you can relax and play as slow you like, actually you can just quit the game any time and continue when you got the time. There is, however, a goal: to meet the needs for the sizes of forests, villages etc. Reaching goals is rewarded by getting more tiles to play with.

Graphics are nice and relaxed, sounds are minimal but informative, and there's a soothing background music. I do hope they'll extend the background music selection, that one track may get old soon.

The only downside is, there's no undo. I am a bit trigger happy with my very sensitive mouse, and I have often clicked on a wrong position and played a tile in a totally wrong place.

To start off with a warning: Anyone going into this expecting a city building game is going to be disappointed. This isn't SimCity or Cities: Skylines. At it's core, this is a tile-based puzzle game.

So what is Dorfromantik? Well, you get a stack of tiles to place anywhere you want and when the stack is gone, it's game over. To get more tiles, you need to complete tasks (things like "make a city with 25 house" or "make a railroad with 14 tracks"). You can also get additional tiles by making perfect placements (when all 6 edges of a tile match). And that's pretty much it. If it sounds simple, it's because it is. The fun comes from trying to complete the objectives and achievements and trying to beat your high score.
This game is so calming. It's perfect for casually playing while I half watch a show and drink a cup of coffee.

You've gotta come in to the game expecting a different, less deep experience than some of the other popular map building games out there.

Treating it like a score competition will both delight and frustrate you. The quests that you need to keep going can be difficult to complete, and sometimes impossible with the random tiles that you have left in your stack. Getting "perfect" tiles is key for having enough reserve tiles, but sometimes you're just going to have to give up on some carefully planned placements.

I'm looking forward to creative mode as it will make it a fantastic game for kids as they love making new landscapes. It's fun to play with a little backseat driver telling you where things need to go.

What I liked: it's quite relaxing. Good controls. Soothing music.

What I think could be improved: A) the graphics are OK, but could be a little more detailed, forests and fields in particular look very stylized. B) The game tends to starve you of tiles. You get one extra tile for a perfect placement and five for a quest, but perfect placements are not so common, and completing a quest will take you more than five tiles on average once you've progressed beyond a certain stage. Watching your stack of tiles slowly run out and being unable to do much about it is frustrating, not relaxing. C) Clearer indication of open borders for "close group borders" quests, they're difficult to see right now.

What the game is missing: A) a creative mode. That's promised. B) An undo button. Sometimes you misplace a tile and want to undo that. Would be nice to have an "Allow undo" option, at least. C) An "Add extra tiles" button would be nice - one that, when clicked, will give you an extra five, for free. Think of it as taking a mulligan. (And again, this could be an option.)

Overall: a good effort that I don't regret picking up. It'll be interesting to follow this game's further developments.

Think of it like a procedurally generated jigsaw puzzle.

If you're looking for an adrenaline rush, look elsewhere. This is a slow game that makes you calm down.

You get a stack of hex tiles that you have to place down one at a time. On each of the side is a type of landscape (river, railway, forest, field, town, grassland). The more sides you match at once, the more points you get. If you can match all 6, you get an additional tile. And when you run out of tiles, the game ends.

You will also get tasks where you group up large quantities of the same type, rewarding you with 5 tiles at once. 

Planning is hard and sometimes you just won't get the tile that you need. So if you're easily frustrated or impatient, stay away. If you want a game to sit and sleep to while playing, this might be what you're looking for.

Overview:

	Dorf Romantik is a tile based puzzle game where you get a set of randomly generated tiles to place down on a flat plane.  Every once in a while you'll get a tile with a quest on it.  As of right now those quests are just to match a certain number of like tiles together.  Once complete you get a few tiles in your deck.  The main object of the game is to complete as many quests as possible in order to get more tiles so you can keep the game going for as long as possible.

Pro(s):

	Keep it Simple, Stupid:  Ever heard that term?  It's an excellent design philosophy and the makers of Dorf Romantik did a superb job executing it.  The game is incredibly simply yet challenging.  The challenge mainly comes from the randomness but as you play you'll find ways to mitigate problems that arise from unfavorable tiles.  There's subtle techniques you'll learn to extend the playtime.  
	Atmosphere: This a really peaceful game to play.  The music is soothing and it's nice to look at the world as you play.  Watch the trains and boats traveling down the railroad tracks and rivers and rotate the world around to see what you've created.  It's different every time.

Con(s):

	There could be more types of tiles.  It's early access so maybe over time we'll see more variety.  Quests could be expanded as well.  Maybe people from the villages could traverse the world and offer up new quests.  Tons of potential for this game.

Conclusion:

	Dorf Romantik is an excellent gem of a puzzle game.  It's simple yet addictive and you'll find yourself trying to beat your best score as you develop new techniques to extend the game.  Each playthrough is unique, so you won't bore easily.  This would be a great game to have on your phone if they ever make it available.

Dorfromantik is a deceptively simple and relaxing puzzle game with a card deck hook. You expand your territory by placing tiles from your hand, building connections between the different land types. Rivers and rails will pose a specific problem when they can only connect to tiles containing the same type of land. Some tiles will request to be connected to a number of tiles with the same objects; trees, houses, farmlands, river, or rails. As you expand you will encounter challenge tiles that request far more than the average. Each time you complete a task additional cards are added back into your deck. It is a race between your diminishing deck and completing tasks to keep your round going to an ever increasing score. 

Relaxing yet challenging, Dorfromantik is absolutely a worthy way to spend your time.

This review comes in three parts:

[h1] The Good [/h1]

If you're in the same position I was a few weeks ago, you've just clicked on the page for this game you've never heard of because you thought the game looked pretty. I cannot overstate the importance of the beautiful design in this game, though I suspect is speaks for itself. Every little world you build will be absolutely adorable, to the point where you'll want to spend a few minutes looking at it from every angle when you lose before you move onto the next game. I have friends who were content to just sit in my room and watch me play even before they learned the rules. Even if you don't want to go all in on trying to get the highest score possible, you can always treat Dorfromantik like a mobile game you just play brainlessly while you listen to music or a podcast or something (not to discount the beautiful soundtrack!). Quite delightfully, the game incentivizes you to do things that look nice anyway, so playing to make a nice looking village doesn't ultimately feel that far removed from playing optimally anyway!

But what if you really do want to aim for the highest score? Admittedly, I'm not the most skilled village builder (my current high score is around ~20k), but I do feel like I'm getting a hang of the strategies. I won't try to explain my approach to the game here because I'm sure other people have already posted much better ideas, but I will say that the process of trial and error to improve my score really has felt rewarding. I've intentionally avoided reading strategy guides/watching other people play the game, because I've really enjoyed figuring everything out for myself. The game only takes a few minutes to learn, but thirty hours later, I'm still finding ways to raise my score, bit by bit. I've yet to play more than two or three rounds in a row without breaking my high score, so I never really feel like I'm getting stuck.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

While this game definitely challenges you, part of it's draw is that it can be so mindless. If you're putting 100% of your brain power into getting a high score and optimizing your play, you're going to be less than 100% satisfied, because that's not the point. You can focus in really hard and spend minutes on every tile if you want to, but if you do that, you'll probably end up getting a high score in the hundreds of thousands without ever appreciating the beautiful world you've made. Of course it's a little ironic for me to get on my high horse and talk about how the game isn't the most strategically interesting it could be while I'm stuck around #15,000 on the leaderboard, but my point isn't necessarily that the game is easy, more that I find that the game is significantly less fun if you're really trying to play optimally. Obviously your mileage might vary, but I'm a person who usually likes to optimize every game and play perfectly in any way I can, but I feel like I just don't have as much fun in this game when my only focus is winning. I can spend five minutes on each tile and I play a lot better than I normally do, but I get so bored.

That said, if you're not playing optimally but you still want to get a high score, the randomness can occasionally feel a little frustrating. Every round that I get down towards the bottom of my stack, but I also have a lot of quests I'm close to finishing. All I need is for that last tile to have some trees, a house, even just an empty side so I can place it next to this other tile to get a perfect placement and... it's a railroad. Of course I understand that it's my own fault, it's not like I played perfectly, or even like I got particularly unlucky, but it's just a fact of how the game is set up that once you get a hang of the rules, nearly every game ends not because you made a bad decision on your last move, but because you drew a bad tile on your last turn. 

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

The devs have already said they plan to add some of these, and I am not a game designer by any means, but I still feel like there's some small changes that could improve the game a lot for me. I should take a moment to say that while I do think there are some features that are glaringly missing, this game feels surprisingly polished for a game in early access. I've found no glitches, and there's already a lot in the game to make every round feel different. That said, there's more I would like to see:

-Undo button! In my opinion, this is an absolute must for the game. It feels like every other round that I mess up my village because I've accidentally placed a tile in an awkward spot. Every way I've thought to implement the undo button does feel clunky to me, but that's why I don't make video games. I'll take the undo button no matter how weirdly it needs to be implemented—it's just too painful to feel like I've screwed myself every time my finger slips.

-Some indicator of perfect placement. If you're unaware, surrounding a tile on all sides by matching tiles awards a new tile in your stack, and these "perfect" tiles are really helpful (if not absolutely necessary) for improving your high score. The problem is, it's not always obvious when you're about to score a perfect placement. There are some completely unintuitive mechanics that I've still yet to figure out (I think lakes next to empty edges count as perfect, but only if the tile with the empty edge has no water on it, but water train stations absolutely need to be connected to rivers/railroads to count as perfect? Correct me if I'm wrong—I genuinely can't tell). It would be nice to have some explanation of these rules somewhere, but it would be even more helpful to just have some simple visual indicator like a little glow around a tile if you're about to perfectly surround it.

-More "classic" (i.e. not creative mode, but I'm also excited for that) game modes. I would really like to see some twists on the game, even if they're really simple. Something like a mode where there are only rivers and railroads, or a mode where you can't gain new tiles but you try to get the highest score possible with what you have. I'm not sure exactly what I want (my ideas are probably terrible, but I feel like there must be some small edits that could add a new challenge), but it just feels like there must be lots of subtle variations on the main game mode that could add a lot of new life to the game. I don't expect this any time soon, but I think it would be really great to have a few small spinoff modes.

[h1] In conclusion... [/h1]

Don't let my long, rambling negative sections alarm you: this game is amazing, and it already feels like a finished product even though there's so much more to come. Even for all my frustrations about how I feel like I can't enjoy this game quite as much when I really try for the highest score, I've still found my own very satisfying middle ground between completely ignoring my score and agonizing over every move, and I'm sure you could too.

Created and published by Toukana Interactive, Dorfromantik is a casual strategy puzzle game that allows players to build their own picturesque countryside one piece at a time. Based in Germany, Toukana Interactive was founded in early 2020 by four game design students attending HTW Berlin. Their second venture, Dorfromantik, showcases their whimsical disposition and talent for crafting games that keep the player coming back for more.

GRAPHICS 8.5/10
Dorfromantik draws you in with tranquil landscapes and keeps you hooked with tricky gameplay. 

Quaint and colorful, this game has a cute, cel-shaded style that instantly catches the eye. Red-shingled houses and trees have a hand-drawn quality, and natural features like plains and lakes are filled in with rough strokes of color, giving the appearance of an oil painting. Changing seasons are represented by gradual variegation across the board, fields of green and purple slowly bleeding into warmer hues of russet and gold. Deer wander through woodland meadows, windmills turn in a gentle breeze, and plumes of white smoke drift up from chimneys, adding movement and life to an otherwise stationary landscape. As a gamer drawn first and foremost to visuals, I find the art direction of Dorfromantik one of many shrewd moves in Toukana Interactive’s already blossoming career.

SOUND QUALITY 9.5/10
Drift along on a current of calming music as you expand your world. 

Dorfromantik’s soundtrack is curated by Laryssa Okada and Pygoscelis. Only a handful of musical tracks provide a backdrop for the game, but their relaxing atmosphere pairs perfectly with its leisurely pace. One particular track bears an uncanny resemblance to Yoko Kanno’s song “Green Bird” from the anime Cowboy Bebop; another employs the ethereal notes of a piano à la film composer Thomas Newman. The additional sounds of roosters, cows, and horses accentuate the game’s country vibes, while boats and trains chug along their highways and birdsong trickles up from the treetops. There’s also an adorable little pop whenever you lay down a tile (and what sounds like a low note on a glass jug when your placement is invalid). Altogether, the combination of music and sound effects is soothing and transportive.

GAMEPLAY 9.5/10
Although one could literally play this game single-handed (a fact I relish when my cat falls asleep in my arms), that doesn’t mean it’s mindless.

Like any good tabletop sim worth its salt, Dorfromantik is easy to learn but difficult to master. Even after watching the tutorial, it took a few sessions to really wrap my head around how to get the most out of each turn. However, once I finally understood how my actions either promoted or kiboshed a biome’s ability to expand, my high score began to increase by leaps and bounds. The goal of Dorfromantik is deceptively simple: build outward from a central tile and connect matching biomes to earn as many points as possible before you run out of tiles. Each tile is a hexagon that contains one or more natural or manmade features: village, plain, farm, water, railroad, and forest. Each turn can net you between ten and sixty points depending on how well you align your current tile’s edges with the existing board. The more landscape types you match up, the more points you earn. This wasn’t specifically pointed out in the game’s tutorial for some reason; I discovered it by accident through a combination of trial and error (emphasis on the error part) and online research. The main focus of Dorfromantik is the quest tiles, which require linking a prescribed number of matching biomes to complete. Fulfilling a quest tile rewards you with bonus points and—more importantly—extra tiles, which are essential to the continuation of your game. Biomes light up when connected to each other, giving you a nice little visual hint about the effectiveness of your placement. Much like chess, surveying the whole board before making your next move is essential. The number of linking biomes required to complete new quest tiles increases the longer you play, so leaving large stretches of farms, rivers, or towns open-ended is definitely a wise move. However, you may choose to ignore a new quest if it means completing another when you’re short on tiles. One tile is drawn from the stack with each turn, and once you run out, it’s game over. See how long you can keep your session going—the longer you play, the higher your score!

OVERALL 9/10
Toukana Interactive’s Dorfromantik ticks all the right boxes for a peaceful yet engaging game. 

The beautiful landscapes, clever mechanics, and constant desire to beat your high score will have you saying ‘Just one more game!’ like it's nine o’clock on a school night. Every session is unique and culminates in a new map that’s just as beautiful and organic as the last, resulting in a very high replay value. The combination of strategic puzzle solving and creative worldbuilding is also downright addictive. It’s just the right amount of challenging and relaxing, and when mixed with a bird’s-eye view of the halcyon world emerging almost as an afterthought of your game, it evokes a satisfying sense of productivity and serenity. I can already tell that Dorfromantik is one of those games I’ll be coming back to again and again for years to come.

While it's playable in the current early access form, I'd wait to pick it up until it is closer to completion. I played it a bit and got bored with its repetitiveness. Some of the tiles you get feel strange for certain terrain (what sort of river branches in 5 directions?), and playing the game to achieve a high score turns into a sprawling strategy that conflicts with how you'd lay out terrain naturally. I'd like to see the way tiles are randomly generated adjusted to give more useful tiles. The way the first tiles are initially seeded shows there is some programmed bias in how they get picked, I just feel the bias they have settled on is not ideal. Certain types of tile layouts also are statistically unfavorable. Too many times I get a tile I need but mirrored in the wrong way so it won't fit. It would be nice if you could not only rotate tiles, but also flip them for this reason. Overall, I'd say the game needs some better tuning under the hood along with options for users to also adjust parameters like tile frequency in the game setup, and more depth to hold your attention for more than a single week of gameplay. I would be happy to see it grow into something more in the future, but lost my interest pretty quickly as it currently stands.

I usually don't review Early Access games, but this has been such a gem that I want to help spread the word on it. You know when people ask those questions like "What's your downtime/chillaxing game?" This is another one to add to your list.

Dorfromantik is a puzzle game in the guise of a citybuilder. You start with 40 tiles and have to strategically place them on the board to get the highest score you can. You get points by connecting things together like buildings, trees, and rivers. 
But 40 tiles can go by pretty quickly. Luckily you can earn more tiles to make your world and score bigger. One of the easiest ways to do this is to complete quests. Some of your tiles will have a number hovering above it. These are quests you can complete and they start off simple like "connect 5 houses together" and upon completing them, you get more tiles. As your world grows, so do the quests so you'll have to develop your own strategy to maximize your points and size.

While there is a global leaderboard for competitive players, I personally just enjoy the calming nature of the game. The music is beautiful to listen to, the tiles and pieces look great as you build, and the overall feel of the game is perfect for when you need some downtime. You earn new tiles as you play, so there's always something to look forward to as you get better and better at the game.

I think my only gripe I have with the game so far and many other players is the lack of an "undo" button. As you world gets bigger and bigger, it gets a lil harder to move around the screen and sometimes you accidentally place a tile down that you didn't mean to and now your whole run can be ruined (this has happened to me a couple of times). An undo button would be a nice addition for when this happens. Being that it is Early Access, this can be added later and I hope the devs consider it.

Final Verdict? If you are looking for a nice, relaxing, and charming puzzle game, then you need this in your library. I look forward to getting better and better at the game and making more bigger and better worlds as I play. This game is a gem and definitely deserves to be your next downtime game. Thanks for reading!

tl;dr: Want a chill low-stakes tile-laying game? This is a great one. Want to play score attack? Be prepared to pull your hair out.

Like a lot of other negative reviews, this isn't THAT negative. Dorfromantik is a relaxing tile-laying game in the vein of boardgames like Carcassonne, where you create a landscape one tile at a time, gaining more points for matching the edges of tiles appropriately, and gaining more tiles into your draw pile by completing 'quests' that are all some variation of 'have a terrain feature that is at least/exactly X tiles long / contains at least/exactly X many terrain elements'. The first few playthroughs were quite nice, building a nice little rural region, maybe focusing on quests now and then but not worrying too much. If you think 'oh, that sounds nice,' then stop reading and pick up the game. It's cheap - you'll have a lovely time with it. If you're like me and have more of a competitive, optimization streak, read on.

The game comes with a scoring system - 10 points for every matching edge placed, with a 100-point bonus (and a free extra tile) for completing a 'perfect' tile surrounded on all sides with matching edges. Playing the game to try to maximize score - which overwhelmingly requires generating perfect tiles for the points - is [i]exhausting[/i]. After about ten-fifteen minutes of play, each tile placement becomes a nightmare as you comb the map for the exact right place to lay each and every tile. And if you screw up and accidentially place a tile where you shouldn't (surprisingly easy), there's no undo option, ruining potentially several perfect tiles and hundreds of points. And this isn't even to mention rivers and railroads, which must be connected logically, making it nearly impossible to integrate either map element with your perfect placements. And getting perfect placements at the start is really difficult as well, since you simply lack the correct locations for most kinds of tiles, leading to chains of restarts until you get the sequence of 4-5 tiles in a row that actually let you chain them together.

Overall? It's fine! I enjoyed my first few hours with it, but mostly didn't enjoy my last few. If you're the kind of person looking for a chill tile-placement game to zone out to, you could do a lot worse (maybe check out Islanders too, which I hear is also good, although I haven't played it myself). If you've got the same brainworms I do and can't help but optimizing... maybe pass on it.

Hi. I don't usually write reviews but just thought I'd share my views on this game. It's in Early Access presently.
The game is very very simple- place tiles connecting either grain fields, buildings, or trees (and railroads and rivers occasionally) endlessly expanding. Along the way you'll receive "quests" which are either, expand said village/forest/grainfield to a certain number or above, or expand to a certain number exactly. There is very little nuance or skill in the game. For example, you might receive a quest to create a village of ten buildings, but your current huge village is already up to 20 buildings. It doesn't take a genius to work out that you can create a second village of ten buildings, then later connect it back to your main village if you have a quest demanding,say 30 buildings or above. 

You continue building until you run out of tiles, then you lose.

That's about as complex and "efficient" as the game gets, and therefore while it is fun to start with, it becomes pretty mindless pretty quickly. There is very little in the way of smart or good moves you can do to maximise success. You might have a tile that has some buildings on one side and trees on the other, and place the tile so it connects to both a village and a forest, and as such expand both, for maximum efficiency. But this won't have a huge impact on your game really, the efficiency is not really rewarded. 

At a certain point, the demands of the quests just become unwinnable. You might have connected practically every house on your map together, but the game will demand hundreds of house, and given you only get at a maximum 7 houses per tile, it simply becomes impossible to complete the quests and you naturally run out of tiles. You rarely feel like you've made a mistake when you lose, just the game has eventually worn you down.

Thoughts on how to improve the game:
- More nuanced "quests" that provide much more variety.. for example creating a village in a certain shape, or having to complete a quest in a certain amount of moves or it disappears.
- Quests demanding a number of trees/houses etc don't ramp up so fast as to become impossible to win.
- Other tiles that may reward you with extra tiles in other interesting ways. for example, place two artefacts next to each other to score a bonus ten tiles.
- difficult and meaningful choices for example, having to choose one quest or another, or tiles that act as a "wild card" of say ten buildings, 30 trees, 7 grain fields, and you have to choose which one you want out of the three.
- some tiles on the map, that if you build to them reward you with bonus point or tiles for your stack.

Some might say I'm missing the point, the game is supposed to be "zen" and I do agree with this, however zen becomes pretty boring when there is very little skill or choice involved.

I don't know. I want to like this game, but I can't like it very much. It's Entanglement, Tiny Town, and maybe Frost, mixed up into mush and then sort of ruined by something I can't quite put my finger on.

I think my dissatisfaction centers on the absence of any way to set aside tiles I'd rather use later. Combine this with never having a choice between multiple tiles, no option to shuffle them or peek ahead, and so far as I can tell no way to build or even examine your deck between games - it amounts to a nightmare feeling where the more tiles I collect, the less my familiarity with the deck becomes and the greater my chance of being stuck with something I can't use yet but would have liked to use later.

I can't imagine this never being addressed, but then again I can. Watch a few playthroughs and make sure you understand what you're getting yourself into. If you don't imagine it driving you up the wall, go ahead and buy the game anyway because it's cute as a button and might even be fun. And, my comparisons notwithstanding, there isn't really anything else like it.

A very simple, relaxing, and deceptively addictive game - and a delightfully small install size. If you've played the table top game Carcassonne, Dorfromantik will feel very familiar. Like Carcassonne, you lay tiles (in the case of Dorfromantik, they are hexagonal) one at a time to build a countryside that includes towns, fields, trains, boats and forests. Unlike Carcassonne, this game is a single player venture where you instead can try to beat your own score while trying working to complete small quest-like goals and overall gameplay achievements which, respectively, extend your play by adding more tiles to your hand and adding new types of tiles to your deck. I've played this for about a week now and thoroughly enjoy it. I'm looking forward to seeing what I can unlock next. The main menu also contains an as-yet unavailable "Creative Mode" which it says is coming soon, so that should help to extend the mileage of this title. For the price, if I get another week out of playtime I'll be more than satisfied with this purchase.

Do you like puzzles?

Do yourself a favor and get this game. It's an incredibly relaxing single-player puzzle game with dead simple rules. Match stuff up and make big cities, dense forest, vast farmlands, and long river and rail lines. To top it off, listen to some calming ambient music while you play.

Fun little game, and pretty addictive. Similar to ISLANDERS which I also enjoyed, but not as dependent on pixel-perfect placement, as everything is contained on hex tiles. The soundtrack is great too!

I unlocked all tiles after about 20 hours of play, and I felt done afterwards. The quests/achievements are overall pretty okay, if somewhat bland. The 'close off decently sized territories' and 'get x perfectly placed tiles' definitely stick out as they help you learn about perfect placements (you get 1 tile back) and avoiding impossibly large quests (something that I still greed for far too often).

The 'Place perfectly fitting tiles consecutively' quest is fun, but seems a bit too luck dependent, as you sometimes need to compromise and place a tile imperfectly to finish a quest and get enough tiles to continue, but losing your entire streak in the process. It'd be great if you (had a gamemode where you) could hold 1 or 2 tiles, like in tetris. 

Saving a tile or two would also help with the very annoying rails crossroads. Rivers are fine, because you can end them with both the pond and the water-rail station that don't care about adjacency as much, and can always serve as ending point for a few more rivers. The rail only has a single-end tile besides the rail station, which is non-expandable and has other adjacent-tile edges you need to take care of.

Additionally, it could use a single undo level, maybe with a 3-use limit or so for when you accidentally place a tile while trying to drag the camera. I've resorted to using WASD for now, but little features like these are keeping the zen-feeling back a bit.

"The perfect is the enemy of the good."  -Some guy in a wig

But that sort of sums up the crux of this game.  Do you spend the time to slot each hex perfectly or just click away to try to unlock the tasks presented as fast as possible? Which one will keep you alive longer or could you do both?

Here we have a casual puzzle game. Crafting a model train (and boat) world one terrain hex at a time. Each hex is some combination of fields, fallow land, forest, or town. Some hexes have water or a railroad section. place them to have all their sides match and you get a "perfect" and another tile. Make contiguous spaces to meet challenges and you get five tiles. Expand and find hidden challenges that give you more ways to score. Don't spend more tiles then you earn or you lose.

I BARELY recommend.. It lacks a LOT in the point/reward/unlock system to keep me wanting to play over and over again. Even when taking the time to make perfect matches every single time to maximize "Perfect" placement, you are at the mercy of the random tile generator to keep the game going without depleting your moves, which isn't very long at all. Skill should keep the game going, not random chance of the tile generator stealing away my dopamine kick and leaving me feeling disappointed in the gameplay mechanics. There is no point in trying to beat a previous score if it doesn't rely at least MOSTLY on skill to get the score!

I like the game.... It has potential to be something really good!.... but right now it's a "Fun At First" game that loses it's replay appeal a little too quickly.

Skill based unlockables for score multipliers or other bonuses would be a nice added feature.... Maybe "Natural Disasters" that negatively affect your score and multipliers which could also reduce the number of tiles on the screen making it more skill-based to increase the size of your kingdom and gain more points. Your "Enemy" could be the elements causing the disaster. Something to outwit skillfully to keep the game going. 

More modes!... a "Beat the clock" mode would be cool, Multi player for competition, Creative mode is okay, but meh.... 

I know some of my ideas kill the "Relaxing" humdrum type feel that is hyped as a core feature of the gameplay.... But casually placing little tiles until the random tile generator has decided you are entitled to go no further gets super old super fast!

UPDATE.... Never mind... I see the developers are satisfied and consider the game complete... So I had to change my vote from recommend to NOT recommend. This game will most likely remain a "Fun at first" novelty that quickly devolves into a "Why am I doing this" task.

This game just didn't do it for me. It isn't a builder game, for sure. The game's description is quite literally correct: it's a "village landscape" builder. The gameplay consists of dropping tiles that have fields, trees and/or houses on them. The tile either lights up or doesn't but nothing prevents you from placing it. If it lights up, it means the features on the tiles connect to similar features on adjacent tiles. Creating these lit-up connections are how you complete "quests" in the game.

Imagine a jigsaw puzzle where each piece can fit against other pieces in multiple ways and the puzzle has no real end state. That's essentially what this game is. It didn't have to be villages or trees, it could've been hexagons and triangles. It could've been light bulbs or drawings of banana bread. It's a tile connector game with simple gameplay.

I understand how other players find it relaxing and addictive, but for me it was just boring and unrewarding. I'll stick with building sims where I can interact with the game world more deeply.

Easy to learn, a lifetime to master is a saying that applies to this Carcassonne-like puzzle game.

A number of the reviews focus on the aesthetics, and though it is an element, it's not the core of this game. You can build a board to be beautiful if you want, but it has little to do with the scoring system.

The mechanical core of this game lies in the infinite complexity that comes with the fact that if you want to play to score big, every single tile is a source for hefty deliberation and the potential joy or alternatively dismay, when you find that it does or doesn't fit the board you're making. And not only do you want it to fit on all the sides you connect, but you also want future tiles to fit on ALL sides without really knowing exactly what tiles will come. Jeez! On top of that you also have to consider all your quests, which ones you want to pursue and how, and which ones to ditch and how. The result of these considerations determine how many tiles you get to play with and how much you'll score with each tile. Once you get into this (perfect placement) you're going to get hooked, IF you have the patience for this kind of thing. These are not all the elements in the game, but it's the essential ones.

I recommend you start by reading an external explanation of the scoring system and some general strategy. It's not complicated, you'll learn these mechanics and guidelines in 5-10 minutes. Once that's done you're ready to make your choices (which IS complicated) and puzzle your creation, potentially until you die of old age because the replayability is through the roof here.

Needless to say, it's a thing of beauty for patient people who enjoy deliberation. Highly recommended.

Without comparing this game to any other, it's a friendly little game that gives easy to achieve landmarks, with constantly running achievements over the life of all your games, so that you can receive special tiles. Build "perfect" tiles by making all edges connect to a similar piece to earn more points.  The number of remaining tiles lives in the bottom right corner. The more goals you complete, the more tiles you receive. When you run out of tiles, your game ends. I prefer knowing there is an end to the game, rather than having to make the decision on my own of when to quit playing.

The high score leaderboard is also helpful to maintaining interest in a game without any enemies. It's a friendly competition if you choose to pursue a strategic approach.  But, if you just want to play a cute tile building game, you can do that, too!

I enjoyed my first hour or two with Dorfromantik, but after that I found it to be repetitive and irritating. 

You are given a set of randomly generated tiles with rivers, trees, houses and fields on them. In order to keep gaining new tiles and avoid a game over, you need to make bigger and bigger sets of matching tiles (a line of 20 river tiles, or a group of 30 houses etc). 

The problem is that the game wants to be both a relaxing casual game and an addictive puzzle game, but doesn't really excel at either. You can't just relax and make a beautiful countryside scene because you are forced to constantly hit your goals, i.e. you might want to put a cute little forest next to your hamlet, but you have a goal to make a group of 400 trees, so you are forced to just keep expanding this one great big forest you have. If you don't hit these goals you won't get any new tiles and will get a game over. 

You also can't play it solely as a puzzle game because there's not enough substance. You are literally just making big groups of matching tiles - there's not really much strategy to it. A few times I tried to plan ahead and just never got the right tiles I needed to create the design I wanted. You are at the mercy of RNG - if you need 10 more trees to hit your next goal and you just get 10 field tiles that are useless to you, you're just out of luck.

Dorfromantik stikes a great balance between being simple enough that it's not stressful, and complex enough that it allows for strategic play and constant room for improvement. The crux of the gameplay is placing tiles on the board in order to form groups of similar objects, such as houses, trees and fields. The tiles you get are random, as are the quests attached to some of them. There are only two types of quests: "make a group of X or more objects", and "make a group of exactly X objects". If you complete a quest, you get a few more tiles to place, but eventually you will run out of them and the session will end. 

Dorfromantik is pretty much perfect for when you want something simple and engaging, but not mindless. It's easy to learn but very hard to master, and the aforementioned randomness makes every session unique in its own right. Moreover, the game looks beautiful - the color scheme is superb, and the artstyle makes it feel almost like you're playing a board game with cardboard pieces. Definitely recommend, especially for its price.

edited review written 02 may 2022

i am changing my previously negative review to a positive one.


general description of the game :
-----------------------------------

Dorfromantik is first & foremost a puzzle game. not a city builder & not a world builder. what you see in screenshots is all cosmetics, no function. the function of the game is similar to domino, placing same "biome" sides of tiles adjacent to each other, trees to trees, houses to houses & so on, grants the player score points. there are quests, where a certain number of adjacent tiles has to be placed, accomplishing quests increases not only the score points but also grants additional tiles to the stack, which keep the player longer in game. the session ends when the stack is depleted.
in the current release version of the game there are several modes. the Classic & Hard mode work more or less the same, where the game starts with a certain number of tiles in a stack & the more quests a player is able to finish, the longer the run can last. the Quick mode has a finite stack of 75 tiles, the game ends when tiles run out. the Custom mode gives the player the freedom to tweak the game to the player's liking, where probability of biomes can be adjusted, number & quality of quests, number & quality of tiles in the stack. the Monthly mode is based on the Custom mode & offers a changing set of rules. & the Creative mode is a sandbox mode where a player can "paint" pretty pictures of no other consequence. there are also Rewards, additional options for building, which are unlocked when certain in game goals are met & are available for the other modes only after they are unlocked in the Classic mode, btw some of those goals are extremely steep so that only a tiny number of players will ever unlock them.


now a bit more in depth analysis.
-----------------------------------

so has the game changed now to my full satisfaction ? - no it hasn't.
was the game improved since my original review ? yes, a little.

the most significant improvement is that the Perfect Placement was nerfed. now placing a hexagonal tile with all sides matching doesn't grant additional tiles to the stack as it was previously, it just provides score points. that change removed Perfect Placement from its central role in Dorfromantik.
the second, small but important improvement was the addition of the Undo button.
the third is the inclusion of the different play modes, which are not that great but ok enough.

the game has still nearly no strategy options, the few things that can be called strategy are the Undo button & for the player to know how the game & the tiles work & to try not to place them where a later tiles won't fit as needed.

on the plus side, the game became easier & more stressfree.

though in the long run the game is a bit dull due to the described lack of strategy options, but if taken as a relaxing experience it can provide some fun with nicely designed optics & quite soothing music.

but on the other hand, if you play it relaxed you will be punished because the in game progress is linked to the goals/Rewards, which are reached only when you don't play relaxed but concentrated, focused, patient, observant, restrained, which is in the end nothing but stressful & not relaxing.


so my resume is - the game is ok, better than it was in Early Access but still rather just a nice puzzle game garnished with some questionable decisions.
Not sure what you call it, building, puzzle, either way, relaxing with enough challenge to keep you playing for hours

This is a pretty relaxing game, hours of chill fun (I had no idea I'd already played so many hours of this game). It's easy to play, challenging when you're ready to be challenged, but never tense. Just peaceful. The best part is settling into the "flow state", getting in The Zone, and just laying down tiles and building endlessly. The worst part is running out of tiles and having to stop. I hope there will be additional features to make it easier to keep going and going.

Some possible examples:
1. A game mode where you just don't run out of tiles (but maybe then you can't unlock any new secret tiles - or the game mode is unlocked after you have unlocked all the secret tiles). Maybe this is what the proposed "Creative Mode" will be?
2. UNDO. A single undo, or even destroy a tile would be great for those mis-click moments where you put something down where you didn't want to.
3. The ability to set aside one or more tiles to use later (or draw multiple tiles like a "hand" and choose which order to lay them down), because sometimes you get a piece you don't need NOW but will need SOON.
4. Or, the ability to trash or reshuffle the current tile.
5. The ability to mulligan/reshuffle the entire stack, when just nothing is looking good.
6. The ability to buy a specific tile you need - maybe chosen from a few specific ones rather than selecting ALL possible tiles (like, a station, a full water tile, a full forest, full field, and so on).

Features like that would be nice amenities, but aren't necessities. To be clear, I'm having plenty of fun with the game exactly as it is! After all, my suggestions are all ways to continue playing the game, specifically to prolong the flow state.

Even if it stays as it is, it's a work of art! Absolutely worth it. Thumbs up!
