Dorfromantik is a casual tile-based landscape building puzzler with soothing music and pleasing visuals.  You place hexagonal tiles from a randomized "deck" of tiles and try to match up elements (farmland, houses, trees, waterways, and railways) to satisfy size requirements that are associated with random tiles in the deck.  When you meet a requirement, you get more tiles added to your deck, and when the deck is empty the game ends.  The trailer on Steam explains the game perfectly and after watching it you pretty much know what to expect from the game.  By the end of the run, the rules of the game cause a pleasantly complex landscape to emerge, with towns, railways, farms, and rivers with boats.  

This game has a lot in common with the also very excellent casual city-building game "Islanders", to the point where I'm almost certain the two games share developers in common - although the publisher of this game on Steam is different.  The music, scoring system, progression, and even the voice narrating the trailer are so similar that I'm convinced it's the same people.  

Despite being simple, learning how to progress in the game can get fairly complex, as you learn more about how the different kinds of tiles fit together and the "meta" of the game (best practices for where to put certain types of tiles to prevent blocking yourself later).  Like Islanders, the game is simple but not easy.  Accessible without being shallow. 

This is a solid full-price purchase if you appreciate a chilled-out puzzle experience with consistent and pleasing aesthetics, or if you enjoyed the game "Islanders".  If you're looking for more of a management simulation city-builder, the complexity is not there in this game but it's still worth playing for the novel puzzling aspects, clean design, and excellent music and visuals.

TL;DR - Not a bad game, but even for a lightweight city builder, it feels lacking in depth. 

After having fallen into an obsession with the similar lightweight city-builder Islanders, I thought this would be a great companion game. However, DorfRomantic feels inferior to it in most respects. This isn't to say that the game is bad in and of itself, but it feels underwhelming in comparison. As a lightweight, low-stress, affordable, visually appealing game, it's perfectly serviceable. But Islanders does all that and provides interesting gameplay, which DorfRomantic doesn't quite deliver on. Specific pain points are listed below. 
[list]

[*] The terrain features don't really interact in any interesting ways - in fact, most of the goals provided incentivize lumping all the similar features together in big blobs, which gets pretty boring. There's no incentive to place farms near towns, or woods next to rail lines, or any interesting buildings except the Rail Station (a hybrid Water/Rail tile with very lenient placement requirements).

[*] Besides the aforementioned Rail Station, pretty much all the unlocks are cosmetic only. The Windmill is just a reskinned farm tile, boats and trains are just kinda there but don't do anything, and the different biomes don't impact gameplay. This isn't bad in and of itself, but the lack of interesting mechanics means that there's not much incentive to actually push for achievements or challenges.

[*] The hex grid is very limiting in terms of placement. New tiles have to be placed adjacent to existing ones. There's many times where you'll get a tile that doesn't really do anything for your current plans. So instead of throwing a useless tile to the side or putting it in storage, you are forced to slap it down someplace random and just hope it works out and doesn't screw you somewhere down the line. 

[*] Water and Rail tiles have restrictions on where they can be placed and what can connect to them, meaning you start to dread seeing those tiles show up in your stack. There's been times where water or rail has blocked otherwise good plays. Instead of giving an opportunity to adjust your strategy or try something new, you instead feel screwed over when forced to place them. When I start actively disliking 2 out of the game's 5 terrain features, I feel like that's a problem. 

[*] Numerous times I've placed a tile and realized it didn't connect in the way I wanted or there was a better placement/rotation somewhere else, but there's no undo option and I just have to live with my failure or torpedo the town entirely.
[/list]
I understand that this is an Early Access game, and additional content is slated for the game. If content comes down that addresses some of these issues, this game will be great, especially at this price point. But for now, Islanders does more for me than DorfRomantic.

[h1] Highly original stress-free indie game. [/h1]

Up until recently, I had no idea Dorfromantik existed. I just discovered it by chance from a curator and I am very happy since it's very rare that you see an indie game made by a team of beginners which is both good and original. 

It is an easy to enjoy, beautiful game where you just build/create a village canvas continuously.

You begin the game with a set number of random cards that you can place. You can only see the top 2. Every few cards you get a quest to match a certain type of tile like forest,house or tree in a minimum or exact number. Completing quests earns you more cards so the more skilled you get at the game, the bigger your map will be.

If you get to have a big enough map, you will discover hidden points which generate prestige quests, similar to the normal ones but you get skins and achievements for them.

All in all this game is pretty, fun, relaxing, has progression and is very easy to install and play. On top of that, the price is fine and it only takes up a few hundred MB.

This is the reason why I am happy that Steam exists so that once every few years I can discover a simple and original gem made by a small team. I recommend this game and I hope the team behind this game will continue to make more good games, they really have talent.

The Bad: Keep in mind that this game is still in Early Access, so it may not represent a complete product. This includes bugs. Luckily, I have not seen any so far but I generally shy away from Early Access for that reason. The game also feels a little repetitive and there only seem to be three different soundtracks that all sound the same. Dorfromantik answers a question that nobody knew they needed to ask - what happens when you take the stress and worry out of strategy?

Taking notes from tabletop classic Carcassonne, the tile-based gameplay revolves around building a wonderfully well-matched group of forests, fields, houses, rivers, rails and more to increase your score and gain more tiles. While not overtly complicated, there is a degree of challenge here that keeps the game engaging.

While the game suffers from a lack of variety in terms of modes (something which is already on the roadmap for the future development) it offers near-infinite replayability thanks to the ever expanding tile sets and placement combinations - no two games will be the same!

PROS:
+ Replayability
+ Relaxing, engaging gameplay
+ A great stress reliever

CONS:
- Limited variety in gameplay
- Biome and skin unlocks don't add much to the game

Ultimately, a pretty fun and peaceful game that you can really just chill out and play.  However, the game starts to reveal itself as a little too simple after time.  The only changes in the game are "skins" for some of the tiles.  While these are mildly cute, they aren't anything exciting, and don't change the play of the game at all.  On top of this, once you develop a play-style, it's really really hard to build any larger.  Oftentimes, the randomness of the tiles can kind of screw you over, which can be frustrating.

I keep coming back to this game when I just need to occupy myself and/or calm myself down a little. Soothing music, zen gameplay- but plenty challenging if you choose to go after those achievements. The visuals are very pleasing too, especially as you unlock more biomes and can see them transition into one another as your map grows.
Also the sound design is really, really satisfying.

Fair warning though- it can be super addictive.

Dorfromantik is a fun little puzzle game in which you are given hexes with different elements on them (trees, houses, train tracks) and have to build a city while also trying to fulfill certain goals - some tiles want to be around no more than a set number of similar tiles, while others want to be around as many as possible. All in all, it's a pretty easy game to learn... except for one mechanic that's not fully explained.

The idea is that you lose if you run out of tiles, and get more tiles for meeting goals - except that's actually not enough to keep you in the game, as the requirements get higher and higher the longer you play. What you're supposed to do is clear a goal and then watch for flags to spawn, which give you more tiles if you "close off" (prevent any more tiles from linking) the area you just used to meet the goal. My only problem with this is that it can become borderline impossible to both meet the goals and also do the close-off afterward - you simply don't have enough tiles to do it.

In particular, the goals revolving around trees are the worst, as many of the tiles with trees on them are arranged so that they're hard to link, and tree-related goals typically require the highest number of linked tiles in the game - sometimes numbering into hundreds of tiles containing thousands of trees. 

There's also a problem with the way you unlock things. You mostly unlock things through achievements, but some tile types are locked behind having to build your tile stack out to them and then complete a goal once you reach them. The problem is that you can get very unlucky and have the hidden goal tiles spawn in such a way that their goal automatically fails when they're uncovered. 

I also had a bit of an issue with the game's logic when it comes to tile linking. There are cases where you'll close off your tile set not knowing that you did - this usually happens around railroad tracks and rivers - and render a goal unwinnable. There's no way to manually cancel goals either, so if this happens to you it's probably going to be a reset.

And I understand that, for a leaderboard system to work, you need to have some sort of scheme for players to lose but at the expense of limiting players creative freedom?

[b]In Conclusion[/b]
It's a chill game to play with stunning aesthetic landscapes and the ambience and music bring it all together to make a charming peaceful village builder. Perhaps when creative mode update releases, I'll have a different opinion on this game but currently, gameplay wise, I don't recommend it.

TLDR;  A puzzle game for (non-puzzle) gamers.  Why are you reading reviews?  Just try the demo.

Wordy Review

The biggest reason I don't like puzzle games is frustration resulting from having no idea what I'm supposed to do.  I've tried other puzzle games and very quickly ended up looking up guides and/or quitting after getting stuck.  Always seems like there's one specific solution and, unless you programmed the game yourself, it's almost never intuitive.

Dorfromantik is completely the opposite.  It's obvious what the player is meant to do.  It's really simple.  Match the same type of tiles for bonus points.  Match larger groups of tiles together as the quests indicate for more turns resulting in higher scores.  Couldn't be any more straightforward.  Now, what's the best way to maximize that?  There's the puzzle and appropriately added strategy tag to this title.  All fun so far.

The music is kinda meh.  Plays as much as its off.  Maybe going for a zen sorta feel?  Gave it a few rounds then went back to *insert preferred music steaming service.

Wouldn't really call it a "city builder" either.  It's nice to look at and I enjoy the atmosphere, but the game would be mechanically the same if each tile just had a number you had to match.

It's also pretty rng.  Not necessarily bad, the strategy comes with giving yourself the best chance to use the random tiles for maximum points. 

All in all, its $10.  Less than the cost of a movie ticket.  Had fun for a few hours.  I'll probably play some more but if not... Interesting experience worth the cost of admission.

Dorf Romantik (eng. Village Romance) is a very cute and adorable little puzzle game that will be able to hold your attention for quite a while if you are interested in such games. With its detailed world and wonderful art it is a unique style and absolutely wonderful to play. Do you focus more on expansion? Are you focusing more on the details of making everything fit together as best as possible? Welcome to this game where it can either be quite therapeutical or frustrating. ;)

You begin a game with 40 tiles, each tile being hexagonal in shape. There are different types of biomes, like villages, forests, farms, plains and even rivers, ponds and train tracks. Every tile can be divided in subtiles, like a card that is mainly forest biome can also have a small house on its border or a farm plot. Your goal is to gain as much points and finish expansion quests as best as possible. The more borders you correctly align with the already placed tiles, the more points you get and your highscore will update. 

Personally I find it a quirky little game with much of love and potential for more and I am looking forward to see what more is to come!

I personally can't recommend this game, although that doesn't mean you won't like it. The appeal of the game is obvious -- it recreates the calming feeling of maneuvering physical blocks and putting them into place, while mesmerizing us to a nice soundtrack, pleasant sounds, and pastel colors. It feels like playing with children's blocks, the kind that are fun at any age.

So why won't I recommend it? Well, the game itself is a fairly empty experience, to the point where it interfered with my ability to maintain the emotional state the game was pushing for. While it feels rude to talk about gameplay in this sort of game, let's talk about gameplay.

The first issue has to do with the core gameplay, which is just a simple 'color matching' mechanic. You could replace the trees, houses, plains, fields, and so on with just colored edges, and the game would play exactly the same. Just match the edges. In fact, the countryside aesthetic interferes with this cores gameplay element by disguising misplaced edges -- an aesthetic of a microchip would have been more appropriate by making 'wrong' placements more visibly readable, if billions of times less charming.

So the aesthetic setting doesn't matter at all. This leads to a tension while playing the game between what you're seeing (countryside landscapes) with what's actually there -- nothing. Usually, even in minimalist games, there's [i]some[/i] relation to what the game is showing -- the harbor goes near the water and the rails have to connect to rail stations and so on. That's not the case in this game. It makes the game feel empty -- it's not a dreamy utopia, it's just a reskin of dominoes. 

Which wouldn't be so bad, except that the puzzle element isn't all that good in this game. There isn't the indication that the 'puzzle' element has been meaningfully created at all. Sure, you can get a bit more skill in matching edges over bigger and bigger areas, but the randomly generated tiles don't feel like they're responsive to either an intentional challenge or to what's on your board. That's a bit frustrating. (And there's no other mechanic -- you can't peek ahead at future tiles, or discard them, or insert a specific tile, or any other agency that would layer depth. As for placement, you don't get bonus points the bigger cities are, or for keeping fields within 10 units, or for having a rail or river nearby. Again, it's just like simplified hexagonal dominoes, with the tiles pulled from a big bag.)

So there you go. This game bills itself as a strategy and puzzle game, but ultimately falls short at both of those genres. For me, I can't get over these things to really relax to this game. (Finally, I really like landscapes and cities, and was disappointed there wasn't even a single thing, other than aesthetics, that related this game to them. It's so abstracted, you can't even name your save file (or the 'world').

- For people who like genuine puzzles ('find the best move'), I'd recommend [i]Into the Breach[/i]
- For people who like relaxing minimalist peaceful city builder games, I'd recommend [i]Islanders[/i]
- For people who like interesting relaxing puzzle games, I'd recommend [i]Gorogoa[/i]
- For people who like the aesthetic of cities and don't need gameplay, I'd recommend [i]Townscaper[/i]
- For people who just want to relax, I'd recommend watching gameplay of [i]Gris[/i] on YouTube

The idea of this game, i think is based on the board game "Carcasonne". The difference here is, Carcasonne is played with square tiles, "Dorfromantik" is played with hexagon tiles. 

you have tiles for
train, crop, house, forest, waterways, gras

You try to combine the tile borders to achieve greater connected areas of the same tile type. So every time the game is played, the map you build looks different.

During the time of the release and a some time afterwards, i improved my placing skills of the tiles and at some point not only unlocked some special tiles, i also reached a high score of 10k. At this time i looked forward to increase my highscore but the downside, was i never again since the patching of game started. in other words, when the patching of the game started, the score dropped to 50% at best.

So i observed and tried to identify what changed:

reason #1:
currently for me, their are two starting conditions. one is, that at start i have all special tiles with numbers on it. which is a pain to start with. yes, the starting special tiles, do not have high conditions to met, but all 6 of them at the start, well not my favorite situation to start with.

reason #2:
the total opposite of getting any special tiles. up to 4 straight waterways or 4 crop fields in a row. this maybe sound easy but when you get 4 straight waterways and the suddenly 4 curved or 4 intersections of waterways in a row, this can ruin quickly every attempt to even make some nice layout. the worst round i had so far, was when i got 12 crop tiles in a row.

To put it simple, the shuffle system was altered in an unknown way, which puts the player, me at a disadvantage from the very beginning or at some point during the game, were the end is clearly at hand.

Sometimes also the fact, you get a special tile, for example to build a forest and the rest of the cards you receive are only crop tile fields. so you have no chance to finish the task without a fair chance.

To put in numbers, you have for example 25 tiles left, you place a tile which requires 48 crop tiles connected and 50% of the left tiles represent anything else, but not enough crop tiles. 

Before the patching of the game startet, i was able to reach one time a highscore of 10k points, took my some time, but now if i am lucky, i reach a score about 4-5k at best. so the shuffling and some game mechanics appear to be altered to totally disadvantage situation for the player.

So what did i change, i now play the game in the morning, 1-2 rounds and the evening 1-2 rounds, nothing more. even when i try currently i cannot reach the point, where i would say "that was a close one".

Not casual in my book. A look at the game mechanics tells us that the odds of finding the correct tile for a 'perfect placement' (which is essential for keeping the tile flow going, but not even covered in the tutorial), is too low to make achieving perfect placement pay for the tiles you'll need to wade through to get to that perfect tile. This could become a good game, but the developer's attitude in the forums suggests that it will not.

Dorfromantik is a casual city builder puzzle game where the player must strategically place hexagonal tiles from a limited inventory in order to gain additional tiles whilst also gaining points. The game ends when the player's stack of tiles is depleted.
With many objectives to meet, several achievements to unlock, a beautiful visual style, and a relaxing sound track, Dorfromantik is a highly addicting game with very high replay value. Having a high variety of tiles (which continues to grow as achievements are met) that generate in random order, no two cities ever look the same and no two sessions ever play out the same way. There is no rush to place tiles, allowing the player to take his/her time.
I highly recommend this game for those who enjoy a relaxing game that offers a little bit of challenge.

Dorfromantik may be one of the most peaceful and relaxing games I have played in a very long time. The art style and the music blend well and help aid to its overall atmosphere.

In terms of gameplay, it is very simple and easy to pickup/understand. You start each game with a procedurally generated set of hexagonal tiles and you earn points each time one is placed. Once you run out of tiles, the game will end.

Each edge of these hexagonal tiles are tied to a specific biome: Forest, farm, field, town, river, or railway. Matching the edges of these biomes to other biomes of the same type will earn you more points.

As you draw tiles, some may have large numbers on them that indicate they are a quest tile. These quests are tied to specific biomes and requires that you connect them to other related biome tiles. The number on the quest tile indicates how many connecting biome tiles are required to complete the quest. Successfully completing the quest will generate more tiles into your stack allowing you to continue to play longer and gain more points in the long run.

I don't see myself playing this game super often as I usually find myself playing longform RPG's and grand strategy games but this is one I will always keep in my favorites list if I am ever in the need of something short and sweet to wind down or relax to.

I really love this game. It's peaceful while at the same time a real puzzle. You can't go for perfecting every tile, as you just won't get the right tiles. You also can't only make 1 forest/town/river/rail/field, as some challenge tiles require a certain size. Losing isn't even that much of a downside, as you get to take a moment and just enjoy the world you created.

Now, with all of this being said, I do think there is room for improvement. There have been times where I've placed a tile, either on accident or just without thinking, and wished I could have picked it up. There have been other times where I saw the third tile available and wished I could have stored the top one for just a few turns. The ability to pick up a tile directly after placing it and the ability to store 1 tile for future use would, in my opinion, give the player just a touch more freedom while playing. 
I would also love to see my old worlds, something that documents my journey. I could take screenshots and all that, but it would be nice if the game, at the moment you lose, just took a small screenshot that you could go back to in menu and see your past adventures.
The last thing I would really like to see is a small change to movement. You have it so scroll is both zoom in and out, and also tile rotation, not the most elegant solution. In addition, sometimes the rotation of the world through right click sometimes feels off, and I wonder if it would be possible to allow camera rotation in not just the horizontal, but also the vertical - instead of locking camera at 45 degrees, allowing for 40 - 50 would be nice - maybe a setting.

I hope everyone else enjoys this game as much as me, and I hope the game only continues to improve :) ♥

Ill be completely honest. When I first started this game, it was after an impulse purchase of no real reason, and I was thinking of refunding it. The game was good, but didn't really hold my interest. Had a 1 hour session and got bored and closed it. 

However, something drew me back. I wasn't sure what it was, but I felt this strange desire to keep going. Unlocking more and more tiles, building massive cities, all to the tune of relaxing music just hit an itch I didn't know I had. I easily blasted through another 2 and half hours straight without a single regret. I enjoyed my time building a massive moving world.

Another thing that kind of goes unnoticed is the degree of freedom you have over how you move the camera. A very subtle thing to add, but I can tell that it definitely makes a difference. You can drag the screen around. You can move the camera regularly with WASD. You can hold SHIFT to move it faster like you're sprinting, and even rotate the screen around. Little things like that make the game feel just that much more fluid to play and make it very enjoyable.

TL;DR 
If you're looking for a relaxing and enjoyable puzzle game to pass some spare time, this is definitely the game for you. I definitely enjoyed it. Even losing by running out of tiles felt strangely enjoyable, a charm not shared by many other puzzle games.

Dorfromantik in german means "romance for the countryside", which refers to the sensation you get when you finally immerse yourself in the simplicity of a village after living in the city.
It is one of those small games that make lightness its strong point.
We face a very simple puzzle game in terms of mechanics, with a gameplay structured in levels of challenge to score, which introduces new elements of the game from time to time (for example the special tiles that require the use of specific adjacent tiles) and greater difficulty in the strategy to be operated.
In other words, it is a great game if you just want to relax and enjoy the construction of this colorful bucolic landscape (which so much recalls the maps of some old board games), but just as challenging if you want to reach the highest scores.
It is part of that category of "another turn and I'll stop" games, thanks also to its high replayability: you will hardly have a run similar to another.

Recommended to people like me, that keep a title in library for those days when they don't want to try their hand at too demanding games.

Fun little puzzle game with a simple UI.  Scoring is not clear at first, but becomes understandable after your first few rounds.  Experience will help you as some bonus pieces are impossible unless you have planned ahead.  The randomness of the pieces can sometimes cause frustration when trying to manage separate biomes (rail and river on the same piece).

SUMMARY: A relaxing, beautiful, and surprisingly challenging puzzle game about building a countryside.  A great game if you love those kind of build-as-long-as-you-can games.  Even for Early Access, the game is fully playable, merely lacking extras.

Dorfromantik is NOT about romancing Tim Conway's famous character Dorf.  Sorry.

The game's core loop is simple.
1) you have a pile of procedural tiles with grassland, train tracks, rivers, forests, houses, etc.
2) Line them up to match as many sides as possible to get points.
3) Some tiles provide quests to connect as many lands types, perhaps with limits or to be "closed" off.
4) These quests provide points and more tiles.
5) You may find quests you can connect to to trigger them.
6) Quests grant more points and tiles.
7) You unlock various tiles and achievements.

That's it.  But the game is deceptively simple when it's often complex - more than it may seem, and for some more than may seem relaxing.

As you  play, you start discovering a variety of possible strategies and complex situations.  Do you take a quick win on a quest to create a space you can't fill later?  Do you line up as many ideal connections to gain a few points or complete quests?  Will that river tile interfere where your railroad tile may go?  If you obsess over the game, you can obsess a lot.

The game is also well-presented.  Lovely graphics, relaxing music, easy controls, a pleasant attitude.

It's easy to compare this game to Islanders - another lovely puzzle game - but it has a different feel.  This is more puzzle-like alignment than zoning.  But if Islanders scratched an itch, you should buy this.

So who's it for?
* If you like alignment-puzzle games and path-building you'll almost certainly like it.
* Did you like games of build-your-own lands?  This might be for you - it's that in puzzle form!
* If you like puzzle games in general, it may be for you, though the random nature might frustrate you.

Overall a great game and it's hard to believe it's Early Access.  Mostly what it's missing is some extra features, but the core game is solid.

I love the game's art style and visuals, but this game is fundamentally lacking in too many ways for me to want to play it any more.  I fell into and out of love with this game over the space of a couple of hours.

It's so pretty and calming, but there is no undo, so an accidental click while dragging the map will wreck your perfect work, leading to annoyance.  There is very little indication of which faces are matching correctly or not, and precious little explanation of mechanics like the perfect tile bonus you should presumably be targeting.

Worse still, my play felt very RNG controlled.  Why did one town build into a picturesque mostly connected beauty and the next a spider work of rail lines and rivers when my care and method of placement was unchanged?  It could be me, but it didn't feel that way, it felt like the tiles I was dealt planned for me to create a mess of lines that wasn't calming at all.

There is no advancement that I can see, beyond unlocking tiles, and there are no options for me to tune it (e.g. no difficulty mode adjustment, no "this isn't zen enough for you, turn on even-more-zen mode").

This game is incredibly well made.
It is a relatively simple puzzle/strategy game with a lot of depth.

[b][u]Difficulty[/u][/b]
+ Very easy to learn
+ Intuitive controls
+ Very smooth learning curve to reach mastery. By the time you master one element of the game, the next element is ready for you as soon as you feel ready to make the jump
[b][u]Atmosphere[/u][/b]
+ Very player friendly. Someone at the door? Answer it, you don't even have to pause your game. Baby crying? Go clean that diaper. The game will wait.
+ Relaxing sound track
[b][u]Depth[/u][/b]
+ There is a strong strategic element that adds a lot of excitement. Playing as perfectly and balanced as possible; finishing small quests, making perfect plays and trying to unlock new tiles by reaching and completing bigger quests.

So I think this game is pretty much as good as perfect, but there is still room for:

[b][u]Possible (minor) improvements[/u][/b]
- There's not a lot of music in the soundtrack, I haven't reached to point yet where the soundtrack annoys me because the tracks are very relaxing and subtle. But some extra tracks won't hurt.
- In some cases it hard to figure out which part of a tile is which type of landscape (especially with forests) you will eventually figure this out with experience and by that time it is no longer an issue, but here's some room for minor improvement here. Mainly aimed at new players.
- I'm nitpicking here, but sometimes zooming in out out can be a bit of a hassle because the controls are very similar to the controls that turn a tile. It's nice and intuitive to have these controls so similar, it makes the gameplay simpler. But sometimes I wish there was a key (like ctrl) I could use to zoom in situations where otherwise I'd be turning a tile (and the other way around).

I think the game delevopers may have spent 27 years watching me, tracking me, documenting my every move and analyzing my habits and choices in life. Because this video game is EXACTLY WHAT I WANT FROM A GAME. I am scared and intimidated by the eerie precision of how well this game gets me... I adore city builder games, I'm into puzzle games and strategic choices, and trying to cram things efficiently into a tiny space is like CRACK for me.

Dorfromantik is phenomenal. Its minimalist design choices are extremely effective, and the art style and colors that come along with it are nothing short of stunning. Though in its current state the game has very few mechanics and concepts implemented, this serves it well in its pre-release period -- it's easy to quickly learn how much fun the core game is without the learning curve that comes with more bells and whistles.

That said, the simplicity of the base game is PRIME for being added to; the design space is vast, and there are numerous ways that new and engaging content can be incorporated to bring more to the experience without disrupting the magic that's already there. More buildings? Unique missions? Totally doable. A system of resource harvesting that uses the landscape you've built to generate food/productivity/etc? Completely plausible, if that's part of the developers' vision. The potential is almost dizzying.

Dorf Romantik rewards your patience for perfection, so much that each tile placed that has all 6 sides matched up with adjacent tiles awards you with another piece, ensuring a chance that you can maybe get a perfect tile to finish off that "other" mega-zone you were working on. You get many tiles to start with and easy early missions to make themed environments which reward you with more tiles upon completion. They get progressively harder, particularly ones that focus on exact numbers instead of minimum required. But keep in mind that your patience and attention to detail will help you, especially when the play field really expands.
The gradually shifting colors of the biomes you see as you expand along with the relaxing music make for an appealing, all-ages game. There is no rush and progress is saved automatically so it's easy to pick up where you left off or if you only have a short time. The arcade-style scoring system with global rankings as well as the unlockable biomes, hybrid pieces and their skins will keep you replaying again and again.

You place down hexagons that have trees, houses, rivers, fields or rail tracks on them (most tiles have a mix of those). Each hexagon is bit different though and your stack of tiles is limited. You can find special buildings with their own tasks by expanding up to certain tiles which gives you some extra motivation and objective. This is one of those games that has one simple, easy idea, that is done very well and allows for different styles of play. You place tiles, if possible joining up edges to match adjacent tiles. Completing missions (by creating towns, forests, etc of certain sizes) or getting 'perfect' placement where all 6 edges of a tile match up with those of its neighbour, earn you points but more crucially extra tiles. When you run out of tiles, its game over.

That's pretty much it, but its incredibly addictive. You can just go for mission completion, not really caring where the other tiles go, or if like me you are a perfectionist, you can make things really complicated for yourself by trying to make every tile perfect. It can be frustrating when the game just isn't giving you the tiles you need to close off areas, but when you finally get the one you need its a real buzz!
 You can also unlock new tiles by spreading your world out far enough, or completing certain challenges.

More content is on the way, and I'm looking forward to the 'creative' mode as it would be nice to focus on building a world without the pressure of running out of tiles. But its a lovely little game as it is. Clearly a labour of love from this small team, and I'm really glad that they are deliberately focusing on doing just a few things, but doing them well. 

As a casual tile placing world creation game, it is ticking all the right buttons for me. I'm slowly learning the tactics to extend my games, getting close to the 20,000 points mark, but to be honest whether my games last 10 minutes or 10 hours, its just a lovely soothing experience after a busy day :-)

When you take strategy, luck and puzzle elements into building a landscape, the result turns out to be something like this!

Dorfromantik is a game that might remind a mixture of some simpler games in terms of managing a city or a small population, with those of some board games where your progression is based in a mixture of strategy and some form of luck. 

Rather than money, resources, worrying with traffic, population, you simply lay down the pieces to build a landscape constituted of a few different elements like houses, trees, landfarm, water or railways. These do not give you anything, other than more pieces to extend the puzzle so long as you fulfill certain quests. 

You work on an hexagonal board where you start from a pre-placed center piece, and from there, starting with a stack of 40 pieces, you lay down tiles which expand the surrounding area where you can deploy more tiles. From time to time, one of these tiles will have a quest attached: Either you must string together at least X number of these, or put together precisely Y number of something, or after the latter, make sure the area can be expanded no more. 
From there it's down to the luck of the draw and your forethought into how you organize your tiles. Maybe you aim to expand the map with houses in a direction, and farmland in another, while maybe in the middle you try to squeeze trees should a forest be requested -- Or perhaps every step is improvisation. The freedom is yours.

Simple aesthetics, but pleasing to look at as you might to a simpler train set construction kit with a few moving pieces like trains and boats (as you unlock them), and a gentle sounding soundtrack make out of this a game perfect for relaxation if still allowing the gears in your brain to keep working. 
The game is saved at every tile so it's easy to take a break for 5 minutes, look over your world, and decide where to place a few tiles and carry it on later. However It's also a game I'm seeing myself returning to for what's intended as a short bit but extending into a whole map at a time, which almost reminds of Civilization as you want to put down Just. One. More. Tile!

Eventually, like perhaps a game of solitaire, it becomes a game where you'll know all the rules and understand that it's intent is limited, but rather than completely opening its hand right from the get go you do have challenges to fulfill in order to unlock new pieces for the tile deck which will make the game a bit more complex as you start new games from scratch, but never becoming overwhelming. 

For those that might even end up enjoying the looks more than the gameplay and would just appreciate being able to build the landscape to their delight, a creative mode is also going to be available somewhere down along the line, even if clearly the board game aspect is the core of the fun.

I want to preface this review with the statement that I came to my decision primarily because steam reviews have no 'mixed' option. 

Dorfromantik is a very simple puzzle game, on the surface. You are tasked with building a rolling village countryside, placing hexagonal tiles and trying to earn a high score. There's no city management or anything like that, you simply score points for every side that matches an adjacent tile. 'Fields', 'trees', and 'houses' to name a few. It's intended to be a relaxing sort of game, helped along by a wonderfully soothing asthetic and gentle music.

However, for me it kind of falls apart and becomes a bit frustrating thanks to a few design decisions. So, you are given tiles in order, you don't get to pick which of your tiles you put down, and the 'deck' is hidden save for the next two after your current tile. A big part of earning enough points to keep going is 'perfect' bonuses, when every side on a completely surrounded tile matches. With only one tile at a time this can be a hassle on its own, not helped by the way river and rail tiles work. You can only end a rail line with a designated end piece, and a similar rule applies to water with rivers and lakes. And because of the aforementioned perfect bonus and tile mechanics, it can be very difficult to make rivers and rail lines without shunting a random single piece of rail or river off to the side, or force you to throw away bonuses because you have no idea when the next time you'll be handed another piece will be.

There's another mechanic where certain tiles will have 'challenges' on them, where you need to make continuous fields of tiles, like a forest with however many trees for example. Some of these challenges however, are failed if there's too many of whatever it asks for. For instance, if you connect something asking for ten houses to your group of eleven, it will just fail so you must put the tile somewhere else and start over. I understand why these tiles exist, otherwise you'd just have one mega forest, one mega town, and so on, but it's still not so fun to get a bunch of them in a row. Thankfully the limits aren't retroactive so once you complete it there's no worry of ruining it.

Randomized tiles also cause their share of headaches. I had a single game with hundreds of tiles and not one single train to put on the rail lines, and I had unlocked the train, yet I got like seven boats. All these little quibbles really make it feel like kind of a chore at times, when I simply wanted to build a cute little village. A little change that would go a long way would be some sort of 'hand' of a few tiles, so there's some kind of determinism in what tiles you can place, though some might appreciate the challenge of getting as high a score as they can with the current mechanics.

That said, this game is still in early access so I suspect that things might turn around for me. Until then, if you just want to make something pretty I'd wait until the creative mode releases. This is a frankly adorable game, and I expect I'll be changing this to recommended sometime in the future.

The aim of this game is placing hexagonal tiles next to each other, in such a way that they make a beautiful landscape. The landscape created will include forests, villages, fields, rivers, railways... Occasionally, you'll be given a quest to place a certain number of structures adjacent to each other for a score bonus. There are also quests that track your score over several games and unlock new types of tile. As of the time of this review, the sandbox mode has not been implemented yet, so the number of tiles you can place is finite.

This is one of those games where I wish Steam had a star scoring system. This way, I could have given Dorfromantik 4 stars. Dorfromantik is a pleasant and relaxing game with clean and clear presentation. It reminiscent of Civilization and jigsaw puzzles having a baby. The games I have played (which are 3 playthroughs on twitch) lasted anywhere from 1.5 hours to 4 hours. It's fun and easy to learn and the very few complaints I have may just be related to the way I play, but I also wish they were explained a little more thoroughly in some capacity through the game. One is that at some points when connecting pieces, you can sometimes run into a problem where connecting the common pieces will block you off from getting the achievement, but it never explains why or when this is going to happen, and with what pieces because they are so varied and only certain tiles have this feature. So, sometimes you have to start a new section even though you have the opening to put the tile down, it will cancel your achievement out. Now, I haven't found any explanation as to why this happens or what the reason behind this is. The other issue I have is the last game I played had Flags you have to block off, and I believe my game glitched to where I could not close off those tiles, because I surrounded the tiles with my last few of the game, and where you are supposed to block off these tiles is usually lit up. Well, there was no light indicating where to block these two flags off, and I lost because you gain tiles by gaining these achievements. Other than these two issues, this game is a solid, fun, casual, strategy game, again with very clean, clear, simple presentation. This is a very access-able game for any isometric/strategy and/or puzzle fan.

This is NOT a city builder/sim/resource management game.  It IS a STRATEGY game.

For those of you who have played Carcassonne, it is very similar but it is play alone and, from what I have read, they do not plan to make it multiplayer.  Which is fine by me; it doesn't need to be.  Caveat here that it would be a good game for two or more people to sit down together to plan a strategy.

For those of you who have not played Carcassonne, it is a tile game with different landscape elements:  Forests, villages (houses), grasslands, rock fields, railroad lines and water/river/oceans.  (More biomes are promised.)  

The basic premise is laying down the tiles in such a way as to build on those areas.  But that's not all . . . each play through (session) has different "quests" and/or rewards so you are doing something different and changing your strategy each time you play.  Example of a quest may be that you must match tiles with a certain number of houses exactly, or sometimes at least that number and sometimes you must close off an area of houses so the area cannot be made bigger.

Very addictive game.  Devs are hands on and listening to the players.   I've played for 10 hours at this writing and I'm not bored yet.

Highly recommend this game.

This game is not calm!
 Okay, what I mean is that when first getting into it "Dorf Romanitk" it will lull you into thinking that its just a peaceful game right? But slowly, bit by bit, you will notice that it is not what it seems. The simple mechanics of "Dorf Romantik" get gradually more and more challenging the longer the game goes. It is incredibly rewarding when you are successfully able to complete a quest or fully connect train tracks and rivers together!

When I bought this, it was tagged as a city builder; I wouldn't have bought it if I'd known it was a puzzle game instead.

It's great at what it is, don't get me wrong. If you're looking for a tile-placing puzzle game, it's nicely executed and very pleasing. Just... don't be misled by the description of it being a "building strategy and puzzle game"; there's no building elements involved (at least, not as building fans would expect.) That's not the game's fault, though, and I wish I'd been able to come to it without disappointed expectations tainting my view of it. 

That said, I'm giving this a "not recommended" because I feel like the replayability isn't there. Once I got over my expectations and got stuck in, I did actually enjoy the gameplay loop quite a lot. But I feel no real desire to fire up another game of it. It's so incredibly random that your strategy options are fairly limited; I feel like it would increase the replayability and interest if there were some elements of choice beyond simple tile placement - for example, some ability to influence what was coming up next in the stack, by swapping the order of them or expending some kind of powerup to lean towards a certain kind of tile. It's not really any more engagingthan Townscaper, and a lot less relaxing (and twice the price.) 

Edit: after having played a few more games of it, I've put my finger on the other main gameplay quirk that spoils the game for me: you have to complete "quests" and perfect tile placement (where all six sides match the adjacent tiles) to earn extra tiles to place, but generally quests and perfects cost you more tiles to achieve than you earn back. So unless you're very lucky with tile order _and_ extremely good at placing them, the last 20% (ish) of the game is an inexorable (and perceptible, and disappointing) slide towards the rather hostile "game over" screen. That means every game ends on a sour note, and I could feel myself losing interest at the end of each game because I knew there was nothing I could do to stave off failure. 

It's only early access though, and I'll be keeping an eye on it to see how it develops, and I'm looking forward to creative mode - and I look forward to seeing what else comes from these devs, because they've clearly got talent.

This is an extremely addictive but also very chill tile placement game.  It has hints of Carcassonne solitaire to it, but operates on a hex placement system vs square tiles, and it has more different placement options and less 'punishment' baked in to its scoring system.  

There are a number of different biomes (grasslands, fields, forests, cities, water, and trains) and you generally score when placing tiles for all of the matching surrounding tile edges, while getting bonuses for any now 'completed' tiles that perfectly match all 6 of their edges.  

On its own this would already be a pretty well tuned game system, but what takes this one to the next level is the game duration is controlled by completing mini 'quests' that occasionally come up attached to new tiles.  In this case its generally asking you to connect a certain number of elements of a specific biome to that tile (number of houses, number of trees, number of fields, etc) and when you complete those quests it adds more new tiles to your placement stack.

The more quests you can complete, the more tiles you get, and the longer and more high scoring the game becomes.  When everything is lining up well you can create absolutely enormous play maps with huge scoring bonuses and complete even larger quests to unlock newer tile types.  

The final game-play element is that after completing some quests, they leave a little 'flag' in that biome, which acts like its own separate mini-quest and grants even more tiles when you completely close off that biome to complete it.  This often puts you in a situation where you need to both expand a biome to complete some open tile quests, but also need to close off that biome to complete all those flags and is very engaging as a balancing act encouraging serious strategic thinking.

Overall this is absolutely one of, if not the best solitaire tile-placement game I have ever seen and even though it is still in early access as of the time I'm writing this review, it is essentially already a completed game that is more than worth its asking price, and hopefully will only get better still as its further developed.

The objective tiles run out too soon, but I also can't close groups soon enough before another objective comes along requiring that I make an unachievable addition to an already bloated, hard-to-close group. 

What began as a relaxing and beautiful puzzle experience has turned into a brain-melting, jaw-clenching battle for perfection against a system that allows for either relaxation or success—not both—and where beauty is just a happy accident.

Old review:
It's Carcassonne meets Islanders: a puzzle of proper placement of a handful of map elements. Planning ahead becomes possible once you've learned how and when certain pieces might appear (tempered by a good dose of faith/luck), and is essential if you're going to progress very far. 

The only major problem right now is there is no one-step undo button. I've had LOT of maps end early (or I have ragequit) because I misclicked or slightly moved my scroll wheel before placing a critical tile, which ruined my playthrough.

For being a simplistic game (as most puzzle games are), this is a very enjoyable time sink. At the time of this review, I have already put in 15 hours after and am far from done playing this game. The game is not that deep which is exactly what I look for in a game when I want to wind down. You basically match up hexagonal tiles to create a rural landscape while aiming for a high score. Here are a few pros and cons:

Pros:
- Love the art style
- love the calm and relaxing soundtrack
- Some of the tiles animate (which in of itself is neat) and are not too distracting
- Relatively easy to pick up on the puzzle mechanics (admittedly, it took me a couple of sessions to figure out how tiles actually match up)

Cons:
- There could be a greater variety of tiles (i.e. buildings/farmhouses/stores/etc) - granted some tiles can be unlocked through achievements
- Wish there was an undo function that would me to go back one move to account for times I misplaced tiles. This happened a couple of times for me when I would pan the screen using the mouse.
- Apparent v-sync issues - I personally haven't had this issue but have seen other have this complaint, so I figure it's worth mentioning.

With all that said, the developers seem to be reading feedback and addressing issues as well as working on additional content such as a freestyle mode. The game does not cost a lot, so I definitely recommend picking this game up.

Dorkromantik is a single player tile laying game where you build a beautiful countryside. Think of Carcassone if it was single player or Islanders if it had a board game aesthetic. 

You start with a single six sided tile on the board and add to it from a randomly drawn stack. You get points based on how many edges you match to their correct features (houses, grassland, fields, tress, etc). Randomly you will also get tiles with quests on them that want a certain number of that feature which will grant you 100 bonus points as well as add more tiles to your stack. The game ends when your stack of tiles runs out. 

The music and art are both beautiful and relaxing. The animal noises and use of instruments mixed in are a nice touch. It is an easy game to play for 20 minutes and stop or hit "try again" and play for hours. The game is an absolute steal for the price the developers are asking and it feels like a complete game already so Early Access can only bring us more features. 

I highly recommend it.

A nice tile game where you have a deck of tiles that you have to place and group specific types together when indicated. It is game over when you run out of tiles. 
The idea is to earn more tiles to keep going.

Example: You place a tile with a forest and it has a 37 number bubble above it, this is like an objective tile that if you meat the requirements you get more tiles added to the pile. So you need 37 trees (not tiles) to complete that little objective. There is also 3 main objectives, eg. place 500 tiles (not sure if this is during a single run or across your games). But you also unlock new tiles along the way.  

You also want to group specific tiles together, they light up a little when its place correctly as you anticipant what new objective tiles come along, eg. 14 houses. You place that objective tile next to a group of houses already on the map and that requirement reduces by that number of houses. So now you might have 5 to go and you wait for a 5 house tile.  You also have to think about way ways and train tracks so they won't become cut off. 

There is a creative mode coming which it sounds like this will just be for creating your own rural map as you see fit. Perhaps it might have some other aspects to it but it's being worked on at present and not available at the time of this review. But it is coming. In the same vein as Islanders, this game takes a singular mechanic (tile placement) and creates a game and a world around it. As you organically create the map by placing hexagonal tiles, you enact a balancing act between achieving strategic objectives (e.g., quests, creating linear rivers and rail lines, etc.) and achieving perfect placement of individual tiles. Both offer points that allow you to continue creating your world. A good strategy lies somewhere in between, with a further layer of complexity in trying to make your hexes compact, multi-use, and carefully deciding when it is best to continue a terrain pattern (e.g., a forest, city, or farm fields), and when it is best to close off that pattern with other terrain (which can give a closure bonus). In the end, you will eventually run out of tiles and your world will be wiped away like grains of sand in a mandala, but from beginning to end of each world is a journey of discovery, joy, frustration, and ultimately, fulfillment. It is a game that is fun to play for a few minutes, or for hours - it is very much a 'just another turn' type of game. Also, while the game mechanics do suggest there is a 'right' way to play, by placing tiles in the 'proper' orientation, I find there is no way to create ugly worlds in this game. So whether you care about high scores or not, this game has something to offer. An easy recommendation for a really neat game.

Dorfromantik calls itself "relaxing" and "meditative" but is so restrictive in its puzzle elements that all your games will be cut painfully short unless you stress over every single tile placement from the start. The only two ways to receive additional tiles are to get "perfect placements" where all 6 of a tile's sides are compatible with their respective adjacent tiles and to complete quests, which require varying amounts of a specific kind of tile or object (like houses) to be connected, and both are structured to not encourage but [b]require[/b] careful play just to sustain your tile income and stay in the game.

Presenting a challenge like this is fine, but requiring the player to to weigh the potential location of every tile on [b]every[/b] spot on the board at [b]every[/b] available angle of rotation against 1) their surroundings 2) your next few tiles 3) the many, many little permutations of each individual possible future tile and 4) water and rail tiles which place hard restrictions from the start is not relaxing. It's exhausting, and not in a good way.

To the devs: in my opinion, relaxing quest requirements substantially for the first 10-15k points would be a good starting point to allow for much longer sessions without stressing over much before the 380+ forest and 17+ rails quests show up while still not allowing infinite games. Either that or a separate mode (NOT creative) with relaxed quest requirements and increased tile rewards to smooth out the challenge over a much longer session.

Sometimes, you just want to kick back and relax. To just enjoy some sweet music, a relaxing atmosphere and puzzles that don't punish you for failing because it just looks too pretty to really care about said failure.

That is what Dorfromantik gives you. If you're a hardcore puzzler who wants to minmax every tile you use in order to get the high score, you'll find an oddly challenging little game, that keeps expanding itself slowly as you work your way to greatness, making every run different.

If you prefer to just enjoy the scenery, this game's got you covered too. You'll still unlock new things from time to time just from playing the game, and you can still enjoy everything it offers you.

The gameplay itself is very simple. You have tiles which on each of its side feature a "connection", which can be forests, houses, farmlands, rivers, train tracks and several others. Connecting the right pieces together will grant bonuses, but sometimes you want to end chains because you get a challenge requiring you to fit together an exact number of tiles together, or to actually enclose an area.

Each time you get a challenge and clear it your stack of tiles increases, letting you play on a bit longer. The game hints at a neverending mode but it's not present as of yet - part of why it's still in early access.

But even in early access, it's easy to lose a few hours to this. A single round will easily take about 30 minutes, but fortunately the game autosaves so you can jump in and out as needed.

Definitely worth a buy, and once endless mode is available, it'd be absolutely perfect.

Possibly the 'nicest' game I've ever played, with some time spent both in this release and the previously available playtesting demo. The game doesn't hide much from you; its a simple European village landscape builder with a wonderfully relaxing soundtrack. It effortlessly invokes a great feeling of nostalgia for my childhood which was partially spent in a village setting. You learn to love and accept each world you make then peacefully move to the next once it reaches its conclusion, with each game not typically lasting very long, though potentially endless. 

If I had to truly comb through the game for what I see as faults or problems, then I'd say that tiles involving rivers can end up being awkward to place sometimes and you end up creating what feels like long and complicated canal systems rather than rivers. Also, when you use your last tile and the game ends, a little game over sound effect plays that insinuates that you 'lost' which feels ill-suited to the game - in Dorfromantik there isn't really any winning or losing despite a score system, and even the smallest worlds can be pleasing and rewarding to have made.

Ultimately, Dorfromantik is wonderfully charming and lovely to play. I think it's very fairly priced would recommend it to anyone with an interest in it.

Whilst the game play is relaxing, it's never dull. Between the visual joy from building your landscape, through the building quests and even the jigsaw like element of matching edge types for more points, the game keeps you hooked.
To keep it fresh you unlock skins, tiles and biomes through game play. Reaching a milestone will give you a new element that either alters the way you can get tile elements to interact or just a new cool looking feel to tiles.
Whilst the game is still in Early Access and only one game mode is available, it seems like a finished game. I'm excited to see what future releases will bring. Freeplay is already teased in the game's menu. Also the design style is open to a whole host of different themes, tile elements and tiles that can interrupt or progress your village landscape.

It comes across as a quaint builder whereas in fact it is a surprisingly sophisticated puzzle game which rewards you for thinking about your placements, however with the placements being at random you really have to think; Should I place this tile there and it looks aesthetically pleasing? or do I place it where i can best make use of the space an earn more tiles and thus achieve a higher score (Really looking forward to creative mode).

My hat off the developers who have built something unique and special here, would love to see how they progress in their development journey.

I first discovered this game when its demo was included in the itch.io social justice bundle, and again during the spring festival, and enjoyed it immensely both times. The challenge is simple: place tiles on a grid to build a landscape; connecting sides with similar elements nets you more points, and completing the occasional quest grants you more tiles. This basic gameplay is incredibly satisfying, scratching that creative itch in your brain in a similar way to games like Islanders or Townscaper, and it is helped along by the beautiful graphics and soundtrack.

This early access release greatly improves upon the experience, providing much more content and challenge while still keeping the core gameplay loop very satisfying. 

I had some nits before, but most of them have since been addressed. All in all a great job and a great game!

Do you just want to shut off your brain for a couple of hours? Do you like to just vibe? Do you like puzzles? Do you like calming music? This game is for you if you answered yes to any of these. This game is so peaceful, relaxing, and addictive! It's very easy to pick up!
This is a beautiful little game. It's very relaxing, and it's easy to lose track of time just placing tiles.

As others have mentioned this is an early access title so if you don't want bugs, random crashes and other things that come with an early access game then wait until this has been released properly, because oh boy will it be worth the wait. 

At its core, its such a simple concept.  You just have to try your best to match tiles with another similar tile, whilst thinking about how you can expand it and best build a chain of tiles that are the same type. But couple this with relaxing music and a beautiful aesthetic, and you have got yourself one of those games that I feel like I can spend hours in and still feel like I want to come back for more. 

Sure there are some annoying things, like how it's not always clear why I can't put a river or a train track in a certain location, and it why it wouldn't loop back to the surrounding tiles. Though that might be down to the my still small play time and the fact that I am still learning the ropes. 

In terms of bugs, I haven't come across anything major as of yet. The only one was when I booted the game for the first time and picked to play the tutorial, it asked me if I wanted to restart the tutorial, insinuating that I had played it before. However, this didn't stop me from progressing further so it wasn't a big deal in the grand scheme of things. 

In terms of what I would love to see in the distant future, I would love for it to get ported to the Nintendo Switch or Mobile platforms, because it suits the 'pick up and play' mindset that comes with those platforms. E.g. it would be great if I could get on a long flight/train journey and bust out my switch to play this and easily pass the time. It's a no brainier in my opinion! 

Overall I would recommend the game in its current state, I can't wait to see what future updates bring.

Dorfromantik is a super peaceful village building puzzle game that that has you placing tiles next to each other to try to get as many points as possible and build up a super nice looking village.

In the game you start out with a blank slate and a pile of tiles in the bottom right of your screen.

And your job is to place down the tiles in hopes of matching certain objects together. So you want to try and connect forests with other forests, houses with other houses, railroads with other railroads, and on and on. 

And the more you get together the more points you get and overall the main objective of the game besides just being a completely relaxing experience is to get as high of a score as you can.

Now every now and then the tiles you place down will give you a quest. And these are pretty much like you need to have 30 houses touching, or have 100 trees touching and if you complete the quests you get more tiles added to your pile.

And these are important to complete because if you run out of tiles then the game is over. Also every now and then you might find a special tile in the middle of an area with a quest that you can complete to unlock brand new types of tiles and buildings. 

And there are also challenges you can complete to try and unlock more content for your future runs which is nice because it gives the game just a little bit more to work towards which is very helpful.

So overall you are just putting tile after tile down to try and get as many points as possible by completing as many challenges as you can and in the process you end up making some absolutely stunning looking towns. 

It is really fun and rewarding to feel like you are the city planner or something of a village and you can kind of do cool things like okay I want a forest to be on the right side of the village and we will start constructing a neighborhood over here and we will have a railroad run through the area here and stuff like that.

And so the game is super awesome because not only is it just so fun and relaxing to watch this village get built up but the puzzle and strategy mechanics really make the game interesting to play for points as well.

You really need to plan out your areas and optimize your adjacency bonuses if you want to get far but it's nothing crazy stressful and obviously you can play the game however you want. You don’t need to stress out about getting as many points in the world but if you do want a challenge you can definitely try really hard in this game.

And the game is presented in such a relaxing way. First of all the graphics are absolutely stunning and the colors really pop and it kind of has a pastel color pallet in terms of the background which is really relaxing.

There is also really calming music that plays along with ambient sounds like wind blowing, birds chirping, dogs barking, that really just completely put you in such a zen place its absolutely amazing.

And the game did launch in early access but overall they could have launched officially and I wouldn’t have blinked an eye. The core gameplay is there but they are going to be adding more things like a creative mode that allows you to build freely without tile limits and quests, along with just adding more content like new and unique tiles.

So if you guys are interested in a super relaxing village builder with some awesome puzzle mechanics I would absolutely recommend picking up Dorfromantik. Even if it never got updated again I would still say it’s worth it so I am super excited to see what type of stuff the devs add to this game.

And if you love small little experiences like this as much as me then follow my [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/37595085-TimeToGrindGaming/] Steam Curator Page [/url] for more reviews and videos about them.

Chill Hexagonal Tilings
No rush, just relax and enjoy the potentially infinite mosaic of villages.

You start with a couple handfuls of tiles and earn more by completing tile objectives such as "connect 12 field tiles" or "forest with 117+ trees"

Tiles have seven distinct zones which can be any combination of City, Forest, Plain, Field, Water and Rail.
Water and Rail tiles have connectivity requirements that no other tiles require.
A few special tiles exist such as the lake tile and the "on-the-water train station" which allows both  river and rail tiles to terminate with them.
The score is calculated based on the number of matching zones the tile has with its neighbors with a bonus for each "perfect" hexagon surrounded by all sides by matching zones.

Dorfromantik is a puzzle game based on a simple premise: Match the edges of hexagonal tiles. The more edges match, the more points you get when placing a tile.

Sounds quite simple, but the game comes with a twist: Your stack of (randomly picked) tiles is limited, and if you run out of tiles the game is over. To get more tiles you need to fulfill objectives, like creating continuous areas of certain sizes, closing off existing shapes or creating "perfect" tiles where all adjacencies match.

Right now challenge mode is the only available way to play the game, but the developers are working on a sandbox mode.

The game graphics are unspectacular, but the art style is quite charming. The different biomes create a nice and varied look as you expand into different directions. Combine that with the peaceful sound track and you get a relaxing, but quite challenging puzzle game.

I did not run into any technical issues during my play time. In terms of QOL my only complain is the lack of a scroll speed setting, as moving around in the later stages of the game to check potential tile placement can be a bit tedious.


All in all Dorfromantik is a great example for taking a simple premise and turning it into a well developed, fun game. If you like relaxing puzzle games - give this one a try.

This game just feels right. I don't know how else to sum up how I feel about this game! I love puzzle games but only if they are FUN to play! So many games pull off the puzzle bit but feel more like a chore than something you want to continue playing. Among all of the many games I have, this is the one that seems to make time melt away inside the little ever expanding map. This game made me late for errands but I still didn't mind.

The music is relaxing and you can definitely zone out plunking down little tiles. It can also be intense - carefully planning each move to maximize space. The plunking sound is just right and the mechanic of placement is satisfying. When you get in the zone and you're nailing the short term goals one after the other, this game becomes truly enjoyable. It took me around 10 hours to fully grasp more efficient placement and how to do things like, for example, start a new run of rivers one tile from the other run so if a short term goals pops up with a specific number goal you can use the separated run until that number is accomplished then a number+ goal comes up next to be connected on that single open tile onto the original run. (Those are a lot of words to explain a relatively simple concept.)

Now, the only input I have for adjustment are the goals that are on the outlier of your starting points. If you can't tell what they are until you get that close to them, they should either change to the format that you have extended all the way to them (forest, towns, railroads, fields, or water) or they should be visible as soon as the round starts. It's a bit frustrating to make your way all the way to one of those goals only to realize it's the format on the opposite side of your map that will connect!

Anyway, I HIGHLY recommend this game. I am a bit concerned I won't tire of this game and it will continue to disappear some of my waking hours. In the meantime, I will enjoy plunking my little world together!

This game is so much fun its crazy. So very relaxing and chilling its worth every penny.

PROs: 
- the idea is very refreshing.
- the design is really beautiful.
- the price is low.

CONs:
- the game has basically 0 content.
- the entire play time of this game is roughly 20 minutes (0.3 hours). So with 2 hours, I played the game basically 6 times.
- understanding the combination bonusses is high end science. In the last game I placed two villages next to each other and the little houses of the icons above turned red with a cross, telling me: "You ain't get a bonus and no, we won't tell you why!".
- the tiles you are getting are completely random. 
- you can not store or save a tile or swap the incoming next 2, so you are forced to place them even without ANY possible position.
- you can not replace any tiles (not 1, not a even a fixed amount of 3).
- you can not even undo the LAST tile.
- if one of the last 3 cons occure: You can basically start over.
- some tiles (extremely sharp train racks, extremely sharp river curves) do not make it challinging, it makes everything simply much more annoying.
- you must have an extremely high frustration tolerance.

SUGGESTIONS:
+ make tiles come in pairs and make them swappable whenever you like
+ let players replace tiles - for the cost of 2 tiles?
+ let players turn tiles - for the cost 1 tiles?
+ improve bonusses visually.

CONCLUSION:
The game is beautiful and has an astonishingly relaxing atmosphere. I would not confirm statements of other critics saying the game is lame, boring or not relaxing. But if you take a closer look, you can read quite a lot "this game lacks some functions" - simply because it does. At the time of review, I have put 6.5 hours into Drofromantik, and I didn't notice that that much time had passed whatsoever.  The game has beautiful artwork, the music is relaxing and catchy, and the ambient noises (such as a dog barking) is pleasant.  Each world is a puzzle, ready for you to solve.  As well, there are objectives towards the edges of the maps, so that even if you feel directionless, the game will nudge you and reward you towards those goals.  If you don't get it the first time, well, there's always another!

Dorfromantik has been on my mind since it launched in Early Access, and let me tell you, it’s hands down my favourite time-killer in my massive library of games.

It’s super easy to jump into, doesn’t bombard you with a million things to do, relaxed to the max – but here’s the kicker: It’s surprisingly deep. I mean, it depends on what you’re expecting, but bear with me.

Dorfromantik doesn’t have fancy gimmicks or make use of confusing elements. Nope, it keeps it simple and sweet, hooking you with gameplay that’s consistently enjoyable. Just place your tiles on the board and try to score as many points as you can – and here’s the deep part, I suppose: Points vary based on placement, like, what you placed it next to, how many of the same tiles are connected, how many of the tiles next to this one has matching corners. And on top of that, you got little mini-quests that need fulfilling in order to bring in more tiles for you to place, and more tiles = higher score. As a bonus, you unlock new types of tiles by finishing achievements.

But even with all that, it’s the kind of game that lets you genuinely relax – from the relaxed gameplay loop, to the pretty visuals, and the soothing musical score. Honestly. While the game can be considerably more involved if you want to chase score, at no point does it force you to do this. It even helps you along with where to place tiles.  

Oh, yeah, the friggin’ music! Let me tell you, it’s like the musical equivalent of, well, whatever truly satisfying thing you prefer. For me, a hot cup of instant coffee with a splash of milk and an episode of The Wire. What? I’m a simple man.

In the world of casual games, Dorfromantik is the one that shines the brightest. It’s got an undeniable charm. It’s a bit like Civilization, not in terms of gameplay, mind you, but in that ‘just one more turn’ kind of way. You’ll find yourself stuck in it for way longer than you intended. If you’re in the mood for a casual/puzzle game that’s the absolute chilliest something can be, do yourself a favour and dive into Dorfromantik.

Trust me, you won’t regret it.

What I'd love to see in the future would be completely new tiles apart from the current base tiles (forest, field, town, water, train tracks) like mountains, power lines, roads, swamps etc.

The fundamental game concept is great though and I'm eager to see what the devs come up with going forward!
