[h1][b]Okay! Time to eat my own foot. It's also a city builder now, but not quite.[/b][/h1]

Yes. This is a puzzle game. Not quite a city builder like everyone else has claimed, but the Creative Mode update has changed that, and I think that is an interesting thing to look into, hence the update. This is no Sims and it sure as hell doesn't need to be. For a small group of german game design students, this game definitely shows their skill at game design. It's exactly as advertized. Relaxing, fun and surprisingly challenging. I still haven't gotten to 10,000 points bare minimum yet, and there are people who have hit 24K, which is impressive in its own right.

[h1][b]I CAN'T AVERT MY EYES! OH GOD![/b][/h1]

Yeah... This game is uh... It's addicting. DAMNED addicting. Like, you actually lose your sense of time while playing it which is impressive, and I have unfortunately caught myself dreaming of detailed hexagons thanks to the game because I'm clearly in need of another clinical cure to my sanity. I'll let that, again, be its own indictment of how good this game is. It's a fun game, but I definitely recommend short play times with a maximum of two-hour intervals so you don't burn yourself out or end up playing until the dawn has come to burn your vampiric, ghost-white flesh from your sorry bones.

[h1][b]So, uhh... HOW DO YOU PLAY IT!?[/b][/h1]

Answer: The pieces.

You have puzzle pieces with six sides that can have all sorts of items placed on them. The side types are as follows:

Plains
Wheat Field
Household
River/Ocean
Railroad

You basically put the pieces together while fulfilling challenges to keep the fun going. The further you get, the higher your score and the more of a colossal bird's-eye continent you have that you can just examine at your leisure. This game DOES NOT rush you. You can take as long as you like to place a single piece. You also get bonus points for matching the pieces together like you building the continent of Mata Nui from the Bionicle board game (Look it up).

[h1][b]YOU SAID IT WASN'T A CITY BUILDER! WHAT CHANGED, YOU CHUNGUS???[/b][/h1]

Well, the Creative Update fully released, and as such I only thought it would be fair to update my review to reflect that and clean up errors people had brought up in my review to reflect that. Creative Mode adds a lot of new shit to the game that makes it more fun for people wanting a more free-form experience. Again, it's not QUITE a city-builder, but Creative Mode lets you play around  with the game's tile generation settings to get more results that you'd like for use in making an endlessly large map. I spent about an hour playing around with it and had some fun. For once, I finally got to make an ocean, so that foot in my mouth is tasting at least something like a toes-and-philly-steak sandwich. I got a real [b]kick[/b] out of the little boost of playtime the new mode provided to say nothing else more concise.

[h1][b]HOW BIG IS IT!? WHAT IS THE NOISE IT'S MAKING!?[/b][/h1]

So... This game is currently a piddly little 396 megabytes in size. Yeah, it's about half the size of Diablo II. Which is fucking impressive. Being fair, it's not exactly consuming any real resources so the size is to be expected. The music is a recent addition, and it helps with the relaxation. The colors are bright, but don't assault your eyes. In short, it's a joy to play,

[h1][b]THE VERDICT?[/b][/h1]

Gameplay: 8/10
Music: 6/10 (Relaxing, but not outstanding/doesn't need to be)
Graphical Fidelity: 6/10

OVERALL RATING: 7/10

In short, it's a very fun, relaxing game. IT doesn't set out to do more than it desires to achieve, and in an age of indie games that always over-promise and in cases more often than not, under-deliver or don't deliver at all, Dorfromantik is a fresh breath of air in a vein similar to Slime Rancher for me.

The graphics aren't impressive and don't need to be. They're good enough to be enjoyed and the simplicity of how everything appears is perfect. The music, while relaxing, kind of makes me think of Minecraft... which hilariously makes sense, given the kind of direction this game was aimed at. Minecraft on peaceful has very relaxing music you can build and mine to. If that is the goal, it has been reached.

In short, I definitely recommend Dorfromantik. Buy this game while it's still 10 dollars, or get it on sale. It's surprisingly good. Seriously.

So far, it is a four-dollar game, which is pretty good for a ten-dollar game in the first days of Early Access. 

There are some major quality-of-life fixes needed, like, perhaps, an undo button. (Somehow, every fortieth time or so I click to place the tile, I rotate it at the same time, which causes problems.) It would also be nice to get some more documentation on how to get a high score. What determines perfect placement? It would also be nice to be able to turn off some of the unlocked biomes---one of them is pretty ugly, to my eye, all grey and red and yellow. 

It's also fairly empty, still. At a certain point, you run out of things to do. What do you expect? It's Early Access. 

Islanders is the better game, and the prettier one, but I definitely don't regret my purchase. This is a fun concept which could stand even more TLC. At the very least, keep an eye on this one.

This indie game is more like a puzzle activity. You have hex tiles with meadow, fields, forests, and houses. You quickly unlock rivers and rails which increases the difficulty. Tiles can have "quests" which ask you to connect multiple tiles of the same kind. If you complete a quest (or finish of flagged areas) you will get more tiles to play with. Your play is limited by the remaining tiles you have.

As you play you will get little notifications (easy to miss) to "grow" your tiles out towards. If you do, these become quests tiles for that session. If you complete that quest you get a challenge. Challenges cannot be selected, but you are given three to work on each game, from what you've unlocked. The challenges, when met, will give you powerful tiles that will always request a quest. 

Example: you may need to grow out to a white hex, reveals itself to be a tower in a city. That city then wants X houses around it. If completed you get a challenge. The towers want you to get perfect placements in a row (where common edges match other common edges). If you do this challenge in a game, you will get tower tiles added to your pool. Towers always ask for more houses around them, so they become a great tile to get bigger cities.

Between the random tiles you are dealt, the challenges you aim to meet each session, and the charming aesthetic this game is a delight and will entertain you for blissful hours. Enjoy!

Dorfromantik is a small puzzle indie game, that can provide dozens of hours of enterntainment.
The premise is simple - player gets a bunch of hexes, and one-by-one has to stack them together on the game field, to make towns, fields, forests, rivers, train tracks and so on. The better hexes' sides fit together (i.e. forest to forest, field to field, etc.) the more points player gets. When all the available hexes are placed, and there's none left in the stack, the game is over. Player can get more hexes by completing quests, like getting a town of 23+ buildings, or a field of exactly 12 pieces, or "close" the borders of a forest, etc..
I would thoroughly recommend for everyone to give Dorfromantik a go. Whether you want to think about maximizing efficiency, "survive" as long as possible and get high scores, or just chill and stack some hexes into beautiful ladscapes.

Dorf Romantik is "romantic village" in German, and that's exactly what the game delivers - a lovely little village in the country, with pine forests, rivers, fields of grain and lavender, the occasional windmill, a bear or two, and tons of relaxing. 

OK, look, it is TECHNICALLY a puzzle game. You can try to complete quests and achievements, build out to "special" tiles for unlocks, and max out your points. And that is really fun, for us completionists! 

Or you can just put tiles down while listening to the soothing music, taking a mental vacation from the pandemic and your city life and place some hexagonal tiles to build your dream German village in the country. Unlike the country villages near where I live, you will not encounter anyone with a firearm, no one will ask what you are doing there and threaten to call the police, and there's no traffic. I mean, there are not even roads in Dorf Romantik. You have to take the train or a boat to get there.

Dorfromantik is, despite my better judgment, not actually a game about dwarf romance.
Instead, it is perhaps best described as a puzzler. You are given a stack of hexagonal tiles to place down across a landscape, somewhat haphazardly at best. These tiles have features on them (Houses, trees, railways...things along those lines) and you are periodically given objectives to create connected features of a certain type and size. Doing so will give you a wonderful sound effect and a few more tiles to continue placing. You'll wind up making a wonderfully quaint little village or countryside and maybe as a side bonus score some points to get a new high score. For me, I quite enjoy this puzzle-minded gameplay, but if you're just looking to place tiles around and make a map look pretty, there is a creative mode available for you.

There has been a renaissance of city builders recently. I suppose in this case it’s more of a “world builder,” but the result is similar. Of course, this is just as much a mild puzzle/strategy game as well. While the premise, design, music, and overall goal is to mellow out and enjoy the ride, there’s still an underlying level of challenge to keep you coming back for more even when it’s 4:00 AM. That’s what makes this early access title worth checking out even before the full launch.

Abbreviated Review: https://youtu.be/bm0l_Ol9LIs

[h1]Hexagonal Happiness[/h1]
Dorfromantik is a simple game at its surface. All you really do is place hexagonal tiles beside one another and collect points. However, there’s a bit more going on underneath the hood. The tiles you place are limited and if you run out, it’s game over. You can get more with special pieces that prompt you to connect them to tiles of the same type. Each tile can represent several different types of environments at the same time, so one side of the hex may be a river, another a forest, a third and fourth side covered by houses, and so on. Piecing these together cohesively takes just enough planning and strategy to keep your brain active while you drift into the experience.

As the world you’re building comes together, it’s easy to stop and admire the beauty of the gently muted colors of crop fields, quaint villages, and expansive green forests. Considering my haphazard placement, it’s impressive how cohesive it ends up looking and feeling. When you combine this with the soft ambient sounds and placid soundtrack, the whole experience is perfect for getting lost in a trance for hours and losing track of everything. If the auditory experience wasn’t so pleasant, I’d say it was a great game for listening to other music or podcasts as well, but so far I just want to stick with what I’m hearing.

[h1]The Progression Part[/h1]
While the core loop of aligning your hexes to gain more tiles and slowly raise your high score is enjoyable, there are also quests that make the game a little more dynamic. You only get three at most per session, so if you complete one or all of them, that’s all you’ll see until you run out of tiles. It seems the game is geared toward limited sessions, so I’ve never even finished all three available quests on one map. They include basic things like building a certain number of forest tiles or more complex tasks like placing several “perfect connections.” Most of these continue between sessions, so it’s not often required to complete them in a single world.

Finishing these quests will unlock new types of tiles and skins for previously unlocked tiles. New tiles may function almost identically to others, like a clock tower that is essentially just a standard house tile, but they each seem to have some unique aspect that makes them useful. For instance, clock towers usually give you a chance to get more tiles when properly connected. Some new tiles, however, have more unique functionality like connecting dissimilar pieces. One is a “Water Train Station” that can bridge the gap between streams and train tracks – which can be invaluable when things get a little messy toward the end of the game.

There is also a progression aspect in the map itself. As you build into the void, ghostly hexes may appear that you can build your way to and unlock. Once you get to them, they’ll show the new unique tile and display a requirement (much like other tile-gaining hexes) to connect them to a certain number of a specific type of tile. When you complete that little mini-quest, you’ll unlock the new piece and have it added to your randomly assorted stack of future tiles.

[h1]Snapping Together a Release[/h1]
It seems like Dorfromantik has a great start in early access. I’m not entirely sure what future content is being developed outside of the “creative mode” listed in the “new game” menu. However, even as it sits, it’s worth the price. The replayability is outstanding and it’s hard to put down even when you do hit the game over screen. Yet, there are a few quirks worth noting.

The first and most prevalent one is the difficulty to discern what is on each side of a tile. Sometimes it looks like a side is, for instance, a forest, but the forest doesn’t quite extend to that side. If you’re careful, this isn’t much of an issue, but it can easily be a problem if you’re hasty in placement. Even more so down the line when you’re trying to put pieces near already placed tiles.

I also have a more personal issue in that I sometimes feel like I’m playing the game wrong. I’m not sure how to explain that, but it seems like I always get to a point and lose right before I can unlock new tiles. The game is session-oriented and not meant for gigantic maps. The scroll speed becomes painfully slow when you start to get there. Yet, I can’t help but feel like I’m missing something when it comes to keeping enough tiles toward the end of the game.

The future is bright for Dorfromantik though. I plan to keep returning to the experience as more is added and hopefully unlock some cool hexagons to build my fantasy world. Maybe it’s just my environment talking, but I hope they add some rolling hills to the game. Then I can start singing Country Roads…

Having played enough of Dorfromantik's itch.io demo, I don't even need to play the full release to give this game a 10/10. It's single-player Carcassonne with Islanders vibes. It's well worth $10 and even better on sale.

Devs, if you're reading these, don't do what Islanders did. They made a fantastic foundation for a fun little game, and then walked away. Same thing they did with Superflight. While you have no obligation to continue development past full release, I would love to simply request two things that Islanders should have done: Steam Workshop support and small DLCs. Allowing for the community to continue development and expansion of your game after you are ready to move on to another project is a great way to keep your game alive with little to no further attention required. Secondly, I know myself and others would have been more than glad to pay another $5 to $10 for small DLCs that would add more map types, tiles, and expanded mechanics while keeping them completely optional for people who wish to continue supporting the game. I feel board games are a good comparison since this is essentially a singleplayer digital board game. Carcassonne being the obvious one but also Dominion, Kingdom Builder, and others have a simple but solid base game and then a multitude of expansions to really flesh out the game and keep it from getting stale. Really think Toukana should go in this direction with Dorfromantik. /endrant

After 6 additional hours:

Having hidden challenges in the game on top of the already steep quests requirements for tiles is making the game an uphill slope.  I've run into quests which will not terminate even when the available spaces are unable to produce the required number of adjacent terrain edges, multiple tiles that have railroads and rivers crossing making them the hardest to implement,  and a variety of skins that a number of the player base has yet to unlock which do nothing to help with score or make future game play easier.    

I've had tiles with terrain types of similar edges not connect through the center and thus grant no combo to adjacent hexagons.  That is very confusing, as grasslands separate them, and they are on the same hex, but not connected.  

While I go back and play more, attaining 80+ water/raid roads along with random quests to keep the game going isn't happening.  There is no mechanic in place to extend gameplay on a run other than random quests.

*Previous Review*
Most frustrating issues:

First of all there is no option to shuffle tiles. What you are dealt in the order you are given is final. This is extremely infuriating. The game’s goal is to be relaxing, and it deliberately takes away the ability to plan out placement past 3 steps at time. The limitless field can only be created/planned 3 tiles at a time which is judged on score, achievements, and random quests with increasing terrain requirements to adjoin by hexagonal edge only.  

The first tile is always blank grasslands that connect to nothing and won’t adjoin to any terrain.  The start tile of every game never changes.  There is no way to use it, or take advantage of the one constant.

This is all based on RNG of the tiles you start with of which necessary ones are missing and only appear after earning achievements.

The looping music is nice, but the atmosphere doesn’t contribute to gameplay when you are distracted from playing.  I had to disable the ambient music and SFX to actually as it was causing me to neglect adjoining hexagons, of which it is difficult to see which axis can connect to complete chains of a resource.  

Some hexagons will have their resources disjointed, so if you are planning on finishing a quest and place a tile whose terrain doesn’t connect via an edge you will not receive score or credit towards the quest.  

Nothing helps if you are placing down grain/farm tiles. You need to dedicate a ‘dead side’ of the hexagons if you wish to keep accumulating tiles to continue playing/unlocking new materials.  This gets increasingly worse as you are pressured to lay down more tiles blindly past the first three on top of the stack.  

The farm terrain tiles are the easiest to join on the sides since they are the most pronounced visually while the town tiles will only join on the houses with brick road under them that is difficult to see on some tile sides.  

Water tiles and railroad tiles will not cross or interlock without an unlock, and that’s the first problem you will be running into every attempt.  Separating these two till you have an unifying hexagon unlocked and available on the top of the stack is necessary to keep playing.  If you cannot balance water and railroad the attempt is over.  

Empty or grasslands do nothing, and give no combination or score increase.

*

Creative mode is not available. I could have seen what the game directly had to offer like in the advertisement of the beautiful landscape and properly planned out a run.  Maybe seen all the tiles that are unlocked only outside of achievement locks.

Overall the game was not what I was hoping it would be, something to relax and ease out of more strenuous competition/mechanically driven game play. The results are often a mismatch of tiles that need to be placed down somewhere to make room for actual meaningful tiles to accumulate quest reward tiles that afterwards will make game play easier, but ultimately futile.

In windowed mode, tiles will not rotate till you press the mouse button, which places a tile. Knowing this now I can click on the pink space to avoid this. I repeated this several times to confirm it wasn’t a bug. This was intended by the developer.

The tutorial doesn’t teach you about future unlockable tiles, and that placement of them is mandatory. You can create voids in the map until then. That’s just confusing. I cannot do anything with these spaces my first play through, and it isn’t helping to complete quests.

When a tile set is closed off, it’s no longer relevant meaning you have small areas that add up to diminish the run. This is unavoidable.  There is no way to change an existing hex or add elements to it.

Some combinations of interlocking tiles simply don’t exist in the starting games. 3 way railroads/farm/water/forest.houses will never connect.  I’m 5 hours and 20 attempts into the game only to find out I lack all the necessary hexs that will actually simplify/unify game flow.

Tiles are fixed and will not connect in any way the developer didn’t intend, including any sort of “Wild” space that could connect tiles as a reward for multiple combos/quests completed.  Only a pure water tile with all six edges can adapt in this fashion when it touches a side with land, or a river edge.

This game is a prime example of what happens when not enough testing and feedback is given before an 'early release'.  

Broken terrain hexagons that don’t connect a like resource to either edge are traps, and cause failures in quests with no indication that they are meant to disrupt a chain.  Terrain hexs can contain segments of grasslands which will stop linking up adjoining hexs.

Notable Concerns: 

There is no undo, or deletion of tiles. When a tile is placed it's not able to be rotated, nor is it able to be removed. A misplaced tile is often the end of a run.

A quest can require over 200 elements connected, and even then have a triangle near the top signifying that it must be placed separated from an already placed cluster. Rotating and attaching it to other like hexagonal edges fails the quest and does not contribute towards progress.  Larger clusters built over time become invalid and keep you spreading out any planned building past individual quests.

Failed quests even when connected to meaningful tiles produce no reward or score improvement, so if you get a quest tile you have no choice but to complete it. Quests are never optional.

There is no quit button after a “Game Over!” only “Try Again”, and you must navigate back to the menu to terminate.  Should you have a decent game going with no tiles left there is no option to continue playing past this in the same run.  

False Claim: "High replay value - every session is different"
*Every session is exactly the same.*

Dorfromantik is a fun little building strategy and puzzle game. 

You place a bunch of hexagonal cards from your stack to build up a village. The game is over when you don't have any cards left in your stack otherwise it's endless.

Let's say you have 60 cards in your stack. You're just able to play the first one but can see two more. To get more cards in your stack, you need to do little quests like connecting 20+ trees, houses, etc.

Aside from that, you can do challenges like getting a high score of XXX, etc. to unlock new cards. Right now there are 10 cards to unlock and 3 different biomes. 

The main goal of Dorfromantik is to mindlessly play a relaxing game OR to beat your old high score and get a new one. 

Dorfromantik for sure is a fun strategy game. The graphics are nice and the music is relaxing. It's a game to cool down, play a short session here and there or while watching something. Without something to work for (unlocking something, scenarios to do, etc.) I can't pretend it's more. But that's not a bad thing. Dorfromantik is in Early Access and pretty cheap, so if you're looking for a cheap, relaxing, building strategy game - go for it.

[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is the perfect casual and relaxing tile-placing/landscape-building game to spend a few hours, except for the hours might feel like minutes and the weekend is up before you realized. At least for me there was such a strong drive to place a few more tiles or to try to finish up a few more quests before quitting. Before long, I was starting another game right after the previous one just ended, and I was having a blast.

[h1]It's Simple[/h1]
[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is simple, you start with a preexisting blank hexagonal piece and you can join its adjacent edges to tiles that spawn randomly. You can see your current tile plus the next two in the stack, along with the stack size that's easily visible. Once you use up your final tile, the game is over.

Many tile edges can join up if they don't match. Houses, fields, trees, or open space can meet up with each other as your world expands, while river paths and train tracks must meet other compatible tiles to keep linking together on the appropriate edges. 

Occasionally, you may see a tile spawn that is more versatile, a water tile or a water train station. The tile that's entirely water can be matched with adjoining land or any water edge, as long as there's not a hindering edge. The water train station is the wildcard tile that you want to see, because often it will resolve a tight situation.

Some tiles will also spawn quests, such as joining so many houses together, or maybe tress, fields, or water-containing tiles. Completing each quest will earn you 5 extra tiles added to your stack, to keep the game going a bit longer. Starting with 40 tiles may not seem like a lot, but you can make your game last hundreds of turns if you play carefully and with a bit of extra luck.

The game does a good job showing you at any time where you can place the current tile in your hand by highlighting all available spaces, so you won't be left wondering. This feature is great and I found myself subconsciously using it a great deal.

The game gives you a good starting interactive tutorial to get you going. After that, it's entirely up to you to do as you wish.

[h1]No, It's Complex[/h1]
After playing for a while, I began to see more complexity in the game itself. I started to choose placements very carefully, trying to achieve higher scores or to maximize the effectiveness of the placed tiles. Quests become more scarce and more difficult to complete, as the world expanded and the tile stack dwindled quickly due to increasing demand from multiple regions of the map.

The high score can be something that you go after, and locally the game tells you what your overall high score is so that you can try to beat it. Maximizing the number of compatible edges makes each tile score higher, a feature I only started paying attention to after playing a few hours in.

Expanding outward with branching arms may come with a risk, one that spreads your resources out too thin without being able to complete enough quests to keep your game going. Or maybe you could have used some of those tiles in a tighter and well-placed cluster to give some significant points.

There's a risk-reward system of closing off groups of like-joined tiles. Sometimes you will see a flag pop up in a group and that means if you close off the group so that the cluster cannot further expand, you will get a points bonus. But keeping that grouping open might mean an easier way to complete the next quest.

My advice is still to keep it simple, don't over-think it, go and have fun.

[h1]Objectives[/h1]
The game will display 3 objectives on the screen for you whenever you start a new game. It's a random set of 3 from the ones available to you. If you complete these objectives, you will unlock some tiles and some skins that you might see in subsequent games, expanding overall visual appearances, while the overall game stays the same.

To obtain more objectives, you will notice some tiles out in the unexplored areas on the map show a clear outline as you get closer. Even closer, you get a gray tile pop up but it's only revealed when you place a tile adjacent to it. These are all quests that once you complete, you will unlock new objectives for subsequent games. Once again, it's really for people who really want to go after them. These objectives are people who want those extra diversely appearing tiles or the different biomes available on the overall map.

If you just want to casually play the game without worrying about these objectives, that's fine too. Like I already mentioned, the game does not change a lick in basic mechanics no matter how many objectives you finish.

[h1]Gameplay Video[/h1]
My first-look video is here. It's the first game I played after the tutorial, and it lasted almost an hour:
https://youtu.be/h7UgQlsHWBA

[h1]Controls[/h1]
Mouse is all you need. There are some keyboard controls for camera movement, but after your world gets bigger, the mouse is much more efficient to use by itself.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The game has really adorable visuals, you can see right away from the screenshots and videos. You have some degree of zooming in and out also.

[h1]Music & Sounds[/h1]
The music is very subtle, it's nice but if you are playing for hours on end, it might get a little old. It's okay to play your own music. If you zoom into the tiles that have moving locomotives or boats, you can hear a bit louder sound effects. Zoomed out, they are not really audible at all.

[h1]Audience[/h1]
Anyone looking for a casual and relaxing experience that's also a strategic puzzle game.

[h1]Pricing[/h1]
Launching into Early Access, the price is quite reasonable at $9.99 with regional pricing. The game is definitely worth it and has the polish needed to already not feel like it's still in development.

[h1]Personal Wishlist[/h1]
Of course any game can use some improvements, and so these are a few things I have identified as of writing at the beginning stages of Early Access that would make it a better game for me:
1. Wider zooming/movement possibilities. When the map gets rather sizeable at times, rotating and moving to and from different parts of the world can start to feel cumbersome. It would be nice to be able to have a wider zoom or a mini-map toggle that allows the player to click and go to another part of the map.
2. Quest tracker. Sometimes quitting a game and restarting later I feel overwhelmed by the number of quests on-going and have trouble keeping them straight in my head. An optional tracker would be fantastic.
3. Tile saving. I would love to be able to save a tile for later, from time to time. Just a personal wish, nothing more. The game mechanics work fine the way they are.
4. Infinite/Sandbox mode. The completely stress free, no end, just simply building more and more, shaping without worrying about the tile stack dwindling.
5. Optimization. The game runs smoothly, and the playing goes well. But when games have increasing complexity with more tiles added to the map, it starts to really use up computer resources.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[i]Dorfromantik[/i] is pure awesome fun even on Day 1 of its Early Access period. I cannot wait to see the additional updates and further development that may add more content or make it more polished. Its user-friendly interface and family-friendly appearances make this a game that anyone can play and enjoy. And, should you want some challenges, they are there too.

Get this game and start shaping some really neat looking worlds, one tile at a time!

You will soon see yourself making strategic decisions about tile placements, carefully building big groups of tiles and finding ways to fulfill multiple quests using the same groups. 
You set big projects for yourself, like connecting that one giant forest to that other giant forest, gambling that you won't run out of tiles before your mega-project is done.
And all of that comes with a beautiful art style which - together with the user interface, sound effects and music - creates a nicely wrapped package of chill vibes.

+Simple, easy to learn mechanics (with a good tutorial to teach them) that lead to a surprising variety of gameplay.
+Full of smaller and larger goals to keep you engaged.
+It's a puzzle game that feels like a sandbox.
+Just plain relaxing. After a stressful day, sitting and playing a few rounds of Dorfromantik is really calming. Even when you lose, it's not discouraging - it just makes you want to jump right into the next round with new ideas on how to do better.

Issues:
-Creative mode is still in development and not available yet.
-A little too addictive. It's easy to lose a lot of hours to this game without meaning to.

As you can see, overall this is a definite thumbs up from me. Well worth its price, and I can't wait to see what they add to it next.

Dorfromantik is a peculiar game; by many standards it lacks the qualities of a game that can be seen as enjoyable - there is no plot or story; no characters to empathise with; no action-packed adventures to grab your attention. Instead, Dorfromantik is the most relaxing instance of carrot-and-stick I think I'll ever see.

There are points and progression. You fulfill certain easy-to-complete objectives and in return you get more tiles. Your own success becomes the biggest motivator for you to get better at the game; not because you can ever really "fail", but because running out of tiles means starting over from the beginning.
At first it seems like you can just place things wherever, but it quickly becomes a matter of careful planning and management of what tiles you have where, what goals need to be completed, and what you can do to account for six small turns of train track in a row. 

Dorfromantik is by no means a "difficult" game to play, and you don't have to get massive scores in order to enjoy yourself; you can easily become calmly sucked in to this artistically adorable little tile-placing game, regardless of whether you're aiming to do well at it or not. Thoroughly recommend to everyone; it's cheap! Give it a try! You may just find something you love.

[h1]Dorf? Like dwarves? (Nope, no dwarves here.)[/h1]
The Early Access release of [i]Dorfromantik[/i] comes almost a year after the April 2020 pandemic-inspired release of [url= https://www.geeknative.com/72444/free-to-download-official-solo-play-rules-for-carcassonne/]single player Carcassonne rules[/url], which was a mere day before the start of Ludum Dare 46, the 72-hour game jam at which four Berlin-based game design students built the [url=https://ldjam.com/events/ludum-dare/46/dorfromantik]initial prototype[/url] for [i]Dorfromantik[/i]. At first glance, it might indeed look like [i]hexagonal Carcassonne[/i] to players, but [url=https://static.jam.vg/raw/58a/z/3152a.png]the similarity is coincidental[/url] and it's certainly not a clone.

[h1]Gameplay basics & mechanics[/h1]
To continue the comparison, think of the road and city building of Carcassonne, but expanded in complexity. The six edges of each hex can have individual trees, fields, or houses, which you connect to form tile groups. Instead of roads, there are winding railroad tracks and rivers that [i]can only be placed[/i] against matching sides of other tiles – constraining your designs. You start with a stack of 40 tiles and always place whichever is on top. When you're out of hexes, it's game over. Tiles can spawn a quest to connect either a specific or minimum number of its matching map feature together, like 100 trees or 25 houses. Occasionally that's followed by an additional quest to close off the tile group to further connections of that type. On each quest completion, you're given five more tiles, letting you play for longer. You score points for connecting edges that match each other, so that playing perfectly would result in a beautiful map. Of course, as the game goes on, filling map holes with the perfect hex becomes more difficult.

The game picks three progression challenges you can work towards during your playthrough, like 25 sequential flawless tile connections (on all touching hex sides) or building an ultra-long river of 50 tiles; there are also special quest tiles on the outskirts of the map with a unique crown symbol that represent regular quests at a larger-than-usual scale. Both will reward you with new tile biomes, new tile types, and alternative reskins of tiles.

Considering it's a permadeath procedural survival* puzzler and the meta-goals are making it through as many turns as possible, scoring high, and unlocking new content for future runs, I'm tempted to label it a [i]rogue-lite puzzle game[/i]. Of course, nobody forces you to, uhh, run. You can just hang back and watch birds fly by, or build new paths for your tiny little boat and your tiny little steam train. In [i]ISLANDERS[/i], I often felt at the mercy of the available buildings, and obsessed over getting the maximum amount of points, which even meant remembering the best order for placing specific buildings. I had to plan ahead so often that I longed for blueprint outlines of future buildings. Here, I instead just focus on juggling my quest tasks, and scoring is more of a side effect of that.

[h1]Playing to perform, or just to unwind? Both are viable![/h1]
While [i]Dorfromantik[/i] looks like it should be a deceptively simple matter of arranging hexagonal tiles to score said points, it's far from under-designed. That you're not under any immediate pressure to act doesn't mean you won't be racking your brains to optimize the arrangement of your last few tiles, desperate to complete quests and delay the inevitable end with another five or ten chips to play. The game logic that deals your cards is more of a reactive [i]Rimworld storyteller[/i] than a 'dumb' random number generator. At the game over screen I usually know [b]exactly[/b] which one or two tiles I should have used more wisely to reach another round of five, and the feeling that I cannot win with the tools I'm given hasn't really come up. In my best game, I made it through a handful of sequential [i]sudden death[/i] situations, finishing a quest or closing a tile group with one of the last two moves. Each time I was sure the end is near, yet just as sure that focusing and taking it slow could well get me another set of tiles to play. Good enough for #4 in the pre-release leaderboards, and only short [i]one[/i] random railroad tile – of which I of course had at least one in the minutes before. Mea culpa!
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2434059997

On the other hand, nobody forces you to play to win, to strive towards unlocks, or to go conquer online highscore leaderboards, either. With its mellow, calm music and pleasing aesthetics, the game lends itself to being played simply for idle relaxation, and that will be built upon with a Creative Mode the developers already announced for a future release. I've read numerous posts on social media where people express an interest in this game for [i]the exact opposite[/i] of goal-driven gaming. Usually I'm the type to focus on quests and securing unlocks for the next playthrough, but a few times I was so engrossed working on a mini-project that I lost track of the upcoming end and got caught completely off guard by it.

To convey the titular atmosphere – the German word "Dorfromantik" channels something like an idyllic village life, free of worries and pollution – the developers have tried their hardest to keep UI clutter to a minimum. Unneeded complexity and feature creep are things they're very much wary of, hence they haven't implemented popular user suggestions like a joker tile (that connects with everything), the choice to keep a tile as a reserve for later, a limited-use undo button, or a UI popup showing exactly how many points you would score in the current cursor location. Adding everything but the kitchen sink would sure ruin the delicate balance they have maintained a year of careful tweaks.

Expect to see more biomes and tiles added throughout Early Access. If you would prefer this game with a gamepad or touchscreen, it might be worth waiting for support to be added.

[h1]What it ain't & for whom it ain't[/h1]
Speaking of [i]what Dorfromantik isn't[/i], it seems so many people ask the dev team to turn it into an economy management game / city builder, a 4X title, or to add multiplayer, that they even clarify on the Steam Store page that these won't happen. As someone who counts 4X multiplayer to my most favourite game genres, I totally get where those requests are coming from. The great visual style development studio Toukana's graphics guys came up with would be an amazing fit for a deep strategy/simulation/4X game. Other things you won't find here at least for the Early Access release that might put you off are that there are no campaign levels or pre-set scenarios with expected goals ("get three star rating"), there is no endless mode (playing to relax, without the sandbox freedom a true [i]creative mode[/i] implies), and it's not the kind of puzzle game where you can blaze through the progression tree / Steam Achievements (they're the same) in 2–5 hours and call it a day. In ten hours, I've barely collected a quarter, and those likely are the easiest ones to boot. While I definitely get a strong [i]one more tile (turn)[/i] feeling from the game, for me it's more something to play for an hour at a time than something to sink hour and hours into without a break.


Unless you strongly dislike the very idea of procedural game worlds, of survival* puzzling, of needing to unlock content, or of only being able to progress towards a limited amount of goals at the same time, there's little reason to refrain from recommending this game.


*: No, I wouldn't tag it a "survival" game on the Steam Store.
